articles.full_text:
STRASBOURG — The EU will not ease sanctions on Russian fossil fuels even after the U.S. struck a diesel deal with Moscow, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Wednesday morning.
In a speech to EU lawmakers, she warned “Russia is not a trusted supplier of energy because it would, this is our experience, at any time weaponize energy dependencies to blackmail others,” arguing it was Russia that cut gas supply to Europe. “That is a lesson Europe certainly will not forget.”
Earlier this month, U.S. President Donald Trump announced an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to ease sanctions on imports of diesel fuel until April 2027, as global oil prices surge.

articles.title: UK CBAM 2027: Indicative Figures Show a Lighter Burden Than the EU Regime - IndexBox
articles.summary: UK CBAM 2027: Indicative Figures Show a Lighter Burden Than the EU Regime  IndexBox
articles.full_text:
The UK Government has released indicative figures for calculating its national Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, which is scheduled to take effect in 2027, according to Eurometal. An analysis of the published data indicates that the UK regime will be substantially less stringent and less costly for importers of metal products than the comparable mechanism operated by the European Union.
Simplified methodology
The central distinction is the UK approach of using a simplified methodology. Whereas the EU requires importers to track emissions at the level of detailed HS codes or else face strict default penalty values tied to specific countries, the UK is adopting sector-wide and global averages.
The UK CBAM rate is derived with reference to the volume of free allowances allocated to domestic producers under the national emissions trading scheme, known as the UK ETS. The indicative rate has been set at 9.69 pounds sterling per tonne of CO2.
Default emission figures for the UK are calculated for individual product categories but are averaged across all trading partners, without a breakdown by country of origin. They are based on EU data adjusted to reflect the structure of UK imports, excluding imports from the EU.
Diverging cost burden
A comparison of the financial burden under the two systems points to a wide gap. European steelmakers have raised concerns that a soft Brexit would turn Great Britain and Northern Ireland into a transit hub for circumventing the EU's high carbon tariffs.
At a summit planned for November, the UK and the EU intend to discuss integrating their emissions trading systems and providing mutual exemptions from the CBAM. Looking toward 2029, London is considering aligning its rules with those of the EU, including a shift toward country-specific emissions targets.
Domestic industry concerns
British businesses fear that a domestic CBAM could harm the country's manufacturing sector. The UK's plan to introduce its own CBAM in 2027 has numerous shortcomings and could accelerate the decline of British manufacturing, according to these concerns. Industry groups maintain that the UK Treasury, which is responsible for introducing the carbon tax, has not heeded their concerns and is developing a mechanism that would place British manufacturers at a disadvantage.

articles.title: 'Time to make a deal,' Trump tells Zelenskyy as he complains US has got 'nothing back' from Ukraine - Euronews.com
articles.summary: 'Time to make a deal,' Trump tells Zelenskyy as he complains US has got 'nothing back' from Ukraine  Euronews.com‘I don’t care how it’s done’: Trump pressures Ukraine to cut peace deal  Al JazeeraTrump says suspension of Russia sanctions is to keep peace negotiations going  BBCTrump: Zelensky never wanted to end Ukraine war  The TelegraphTrump’s Push for Deals With Russia Powers His Frustration With Ukraine  The New York Times
articles.full_text:
Trump's comments came shortly after Zelenskyy met with a US delegation headed by special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo.
US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that he wanted his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy to "make a deal" with Russia as he complained that the United States had received "nothing back" for its support for Kyiv.
Speaking to the media in the White House, Trump said: "We want Zelenskyy to make a deal. He can make a deal."
"He could have made a deal two years ago when we had our little chat in the Oval Office," he continued, seemingly referencing the pair's heated exchange during a meeting in early 2025. "He's going to have to want to make a deal, because I don't think his people are going to stand for it any longer."
Zelenskyy and Trump have endured a volatile relationship since the US president began his second term in January last year, but it has soured further in recent weeks after Trump struck a diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin and criticised the impact of Ukrainian strikes on Russia's energy sector on global fuel prices.
On Tuesday, Trump - who is gearing up for key midterm elections to determine the make-up of Congress for his final two years in office - seemed to pin the blame for the ongoing war on Zelenskyy, repeatedly saying he had had the opportunity to make a deal and that the US had got nothing in return for its help "except grief, death," and "tremendous monetary loss."
"We have given tremendous amounts to Ukraine; we've got nothing back. Other than high diesel," Trump added. "The American taxpayers are tired of it."
"It's time to make a deal," he said.
Zelenskyy's Oslo talks
Trump's comments came shortly after Zelenskyy met with a US delegation headed by special envoy Steve Witkoff, who is scheduled to travel to Russia for a meeting with Putin on Wednesday.
Following the talks in Oslo, which also involved Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Zelenskyy had appeared relatively positive, telling journalists he had recently held a constructive call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and calling for a trilateral meeting with Trump and Putin.
Zelenskyy also addressed reported restrictions on US intelligence sharing during a press conference with the Nordic leaders, saying he was "thankful" that "intelligence works now."
"I'm speaking about early warning, what is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming," he said.
In a post on social media later in the evening, Zelenskyy added: "It was constructive because all of us want peace – Ukraine, Europe, the United States. And we will see what happens tomorrow."

articles.title: NATO to bolster Black Sea presence with patrol aircraft, drones after attacks on commercial ships - The Kyiv Independent
articles.summary: NATO to bolster Black Sea presence with patrol aircraft, drones after attacks on commercial ships  The Kyiv IndependentNato increases Black Sea deployment amid escalating deadly Russian attacks  The GuardianNATO to send planes and drones to Black Sea after attacks on shipping  ReutersKallas: Russian Black Sea strikes deepen ‘perfect storm’ for world food supplies  Euronews.comRussia, Ukraine and the increasingly fierce conflict in the Black Sea  ...
articles.full_text:
NATO will increase its military presence in the Black Sea, deploying additional maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems, and drones following a series of deadly attacks on commercial vessels in the region.
The announcement came after NATO's main decision-making body, the North Atlantic Council, met at the alliance's Brussels headquarters on Oct. 20 to discuss Black Sea security.
"Allies have or will send additional maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems, explosive exploitation teams, intelligence personnel, drones, and more to the Black Sea," U.S. Army Col. Martin O'Donnell, a NATO military spokesperson, said in a statement.
O'Donnell said NATO's immediate priority is improving its awareness of potential threats in the region through additional surveillance equipment and intelligence sharing.
The decision comes after a series of drone attacks on commercial vessels near the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria, raising concerns about the safety and security of shipping routes used by Ukraine and other countries in the region.
On Oct. 13, drones struck two commercial vessels off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast. The Maltese-flagged, Ukrainian-owned Chelsea 3 was hit by three drones near the coastal town of Byala, while the Guinea-Bissau-flagged HS Dignity sank near Krapets, leaving 11 crew members missing.
Bulgarian authorities subsequently recovered suspected drone fragments from the damaged Chelsea 3 and began the process of examining them to determine the weapon's origin, The Maritime Executive reported on Oct. 20.
Two days later, seven sailors were reported missing after the Wine Trader, a San Marino-flagged chemical tanker, caught fire near the Romanian port of Sulina amid reported drone activity.
NATO has not announced which country they think is responsible for the attacks. Military analysts have identified Russia as the likely perpetrator, although Moscow has not acknowledged responsibility.
"NATO has already strengthened our posture along the eastern flank, including with counter-drone capabilities," NATO spokesperson Allison Hart said on Oct. 20.
"We will continue to stand united and ensure that we are ready and able to address any threat and to keep our one billion people safe."
The attacks have prompted growing concerns among NATO members about the possibility of Russia's war against Ukraine spilling over into neighbouring countries.
On Oct. 17, Romanian F-16 fighter jets shot down two drones over the country's territorial waters, according to Romania's Defense Ministry.
Romanian Defense Minister Radu Miruta said the drones were believed to be Russian-made Geran-4 models, due to their speed and other characteristics.
The Black Sea is a critical route for Ukraine's agricultural exports, but attacks on commercial shipping have raised concerns about the risks faced by civilian crews and maritime security.

articles.title: WAR PROPAGANDA: NATO and the EU will attack Russia to seize its resources - Veridica.ro
articles.summary: WAR PROPAGANDA: NATO and the EU will attack Russia to seize its resources  Veridica.ro
articles.full_text:
European countries are arming themselves in order to attack Russia, seize its resources and save their economies, while Poland, Finland, Sweden and the Baltic States seek to provoke Moscow, counting on a conflict that would increase their international influence, pro-Kremlin propaganda writes.
NEWS: Under the pretext of defending themselves against the “Russian threat”, European countries have for several years been making plans for war against Russia. In October 2025, citing current conflicts and the “growing threats to the Union’s security”, the European Commission adopted the Defense Readiness Roadmap to 2030 [...] However, the European Commission did not conceal the fact that it regards the plan as an integral part of preparations for an armed confrontation with Russia within the specified timeframe. [...]
Germany, which managed twice in history to trigger world wars, is now actively simulating, in the same spirit, a third world war. “The calculation is that enormous sums will be allocated to modernizing the army. Russia, seeing Europe’s strength, will not risk entering into an armed conflict with it. At the same time, there is not a single statement by any Russian official threatening Europe with war”, noted expert Andrey Suzdaltsev [...]
“Europe is a typical empire. It needs to develop, but without Russia’s resources it will not be able to do so. If it wants to survive, it can do so only on the basis of Russia’s resources and capabilities and at the expense of Eastern Europe. Otherwise, it has no way out of this situation, because Europe’s technological advantage is declining, resources are lacking, and the continent is extremely overpopulated”, political scientist Suzdaltsev believes. [...] The expectation is that the wartime economy will develop rapidly, as happened in Germany in the 1930s or in the United States, which overcame the Great Depression only thanks to its participation in the World War II. [...] “We have suitable candidates for acts of provocation: the Baltic states, Poland, Finland, Sweden. They truly count, just as Ukraine counted for a long time, on NATO fighting in their place. They need a conflict in order to occupy a different position in the global hierarchy”, Andrey Suzdaltsev concluded.
NARRATIVES: 1. NATO and the EU are preparing a war of aggression against Russia, using the Russian threat as a pretext. 2. Germany is remilitarizing along Nazi lines and preparing a third world war. 3. The EU needs Russia’s resources in order to save its economy. 4. Poland, Finland, Sweden and the Baltic States seek to provoke a conflict with Russia in order to strengthen their international position.
PURPOSE: To portray Russia as the victim of an imminent Western aggression. To justify the war against Ukraine and the Kremlin’s military policy. To discredit European defense measures by associating them with Nazi militarism. To weaken support for Ukraine and for the strengthening of European security.
Fact: Europe is strengthening its defenses out of fear of a Russian attack
WHY THE NARRATIVES ARE FALSE: The Ukraina.ru article acknowledges that European states are strengthening their defenses because of threats from Russia, but then argues, without providing any shred of evidence, that Europe is preparing an attack on Moscow. On October 16, 2025, the European Commission and the EU High Representative presented the Roadmap, which sets objectives for the development of European military capabilities, including surveillance of the eastern flank, defense against drones and protection of space infrastructure. The document identifies Russia’s aggression against Ukraine as one of the main causes of the deterioration of European security. Its purpose is deterrence and the strengthening of defense, not preparation for an invasion. The same approach appears in NATO’s Strategic Concept, which identifies Russia as the main direct threat to Allied security, while also specifying that the Organization does not seek confrontation with the Russian Federation. Neither NATO nor the EU has ever attacked Russia, nor have they set themselves the objective of seizing its resources. On the contrary, the EU represents one of the most enduring peace projects in the modern history of the continent, built after two world wars to prevent the reoccurrence of such conflicts.
Russia has threatened Europe with its nuclear arsenal and is already waging hybrid warfare against the West
Political scientist Andrey Suzdaltsev’s claim that no Russian official has ever threatened Europe with war is false. On February 18, 2024, former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev, the Deputy Chairman of the Security Council, threatened Berlin, London and Washington with nuclear strikes. In September 2025, the same official again warned of the risk of a nuclear war with Europe.
On the other hand, the absence of direct threats does not guarantee that Russia will refrain from using force. Just a few days before the invasion of February 24, 2022, Moscow denied Western reports about preparations for an attack. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova mocked warnings about the imminence of war. Three days later, Russia invaded Ukraine from several directions. Kremlin statements about its peaceful intentions must therefore be assessed against its actions.
Finally, the Kremlin is contradicted by its own actions. Russia is the only power in this century that has launched wars on the European continent and attempted to alter internationally recognized borders: in Georgia in 2008 and in Ukraine in 2014 and 2022. Russia is also suspected of launching the 2007 cyberattack against Estonia, of being behind a series of assassinations of Putin opponents sheltered in Western countries, and of conducting a wave of hybrid operations (electoral interference, sabotage, drone incursions, etc.), all accompanied by an intensive disinformation campaign.
World War II broke out when Germany and the USSR attacked Poland, after concluding a pact
The article associates Germany’s rearmament with preparation for a third world war, suggesting that Berlin is returning to the expansionist policies of the Nazi era. The comparison ignores the differences between today’s democratic Germany and Hitler’s regime, as well as the responsibility of the USSR for the outbreak of the World War II.
In the case of World War II, which started on September 1, 1939 with the invasion of Poland by Nazi Germany, Moscow omits the initial collaboration between Hitler and Stalin. On August 23, 1939, the two regimes signed the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, whose secret protocols divided Eastern Europe into spheres of influence. On September 17, the Soviet Union invaded Poland from the east. In 2019, the European Parliament condemned the collaboration between the two totalitarian regimes, emphasizing the role of the pact in paving the way to war. The comparison also ignores the distinction between militarizing a state in order to conquer foreign territories and developing defensive capabilities as a response to a war that has already been launched. Nazi Germany pursued territorial expansion by force, whereas European states are strengthening their defenses after Russia illegally annexed Ukrainian territories.
Europe is not seeking to seize Russia’s resources, nor to provoke a war
Russian political scientist Suzdaltsev, quoted by Ukraina.ru, argues that Europe is an “empire” that cannot survive economically without Russia’s resources and seeks to seize them through military conflict. However, the expert provides no evidence whatsoever that such an objective exists. Europe’s economic challenges are turned into an alleged intention of territorial conquest.
Nor does the development of the defense industry demonstrate that Europe needs to start a war in order to save its economy. Military spending may stimulate certain industrial sectors, but it also entails significant budgetary costs. Moreover, the EU is a union of states that cooperate politically and economically, not an “empire” that expands its borders through conquest. By contrast, Russia annexed Crimea in 2014 and attempted in 2022 to annex four additional Ukrainian regions, including territories it did not fully control.
The final part of the article attributes to Poland, Finland, Sweden and the Baltic States an intention to provoke a war with Russia in order to strengthen their international standing. No evidence is presented that these states seek to trigger a conflict that would bring human losses, destruction and enormous economic costs.
The example of Ukraine, invoked by Suzdaltsev, actually contradicts his own argument. Ukraine became the focus of international attention after being invaded by Russia, not because it wanted a war. The military and political support received by Kyiv is a response to aggression, not proof of a plan to provoke it. If war automatically strengthened the international position of attacked states, as the political scientist suggests, then Russia itself would, through its aggression, be contributing to the strengthening of its adversaries.
Moreover, Finland and Sweden abandoned their traditional policy of military non-alignment after the Russian invasion. Finland joined NATO in April 2023, and Sweden in March 2024. NATO enlargement was thus one of the consequences of Russia’s aggression. The article reverses the relationship between cause and effect: Russia invades Ukraine and annexes territories, yet the measures adopted by Europe to prevent the conflict from spreading are portrayed as preparations for aggression.
BACKGROUND: For many years, the Kremlin has promoted the narrative that the West is preparing a war against Russia, using it also to justify the invasion of Ukraine. Following the annexation of Crimea in 2014, the UN General Assembly reaffirmed Ukraine’s territorial integrity, and in March 2022 condemned the full-scale invasion and called for the withdrawal of Russian troops. articles.title: France’s borrowing costs hit 5% for first time since 2002 - Financial Times
articles.summary: France’s borrowing costs hit 5% for first time since 2002  Financial TimesFrench borrowing costs hit 24-year high as civil unrest and budget fears spook markets  The GuardianGermany’s top banker sounds alarm over French debt crisis  The TelegraphRates Spark: France still singled out  ing thinkFrench 10-year bond yields hit 5%, highest since 2002  Reuters
articles.full_text:
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
France’s long-term borrowing costs have hit 5 per cent, a benchmark last reached in 2002, as investors grow increasingly concerned about the stability of the country’s politics and the state of its public finances.
A fresh bout of selling on Wednesday pushed French 10-year bond yields up as much as 0.1 percentage points to 5.02 per cent, taking the jump so far this week to more than 0.2 percentage points. The yield closed at 4.99 per cent on Wednesday afternoon.
The moves come after days of unrest and political recriminations in the country, as peaceful demonstrations over the cost of living and education spiralled into widespread rioting and looting.
France’s borrowing costs have surged from 3.2 per cent in late February, having been the hardest hit in a sweeping sell-off in G7 bond markets, as the Iran war has stoked inflation and put economies with large debt piles and wide budget deficits under particular pressure. Bond yields rise as prices fall.
“The political willingness for any fiscal consolidation ahead of the election is very, very low,” said Jeff Mueller, co-head of fixed income at Morgan Stanley Investment Management, adding there was plenty of room for “the situation to worsen from here”.
The closely watched gap, or spread, between French 10-year borrowing costs and Germany’s rose to almost 1.6 percentage points on Wednesday, matching the intraday high reached in volatile trading earlier this month.
Such a level had previously not been seen since the Eurozone debt crisis more than a decade ago.
Other Eurozone bond markets also suffered on Wednesday, with Italy’s 10-year yield rising 0.07 percentage points to 4.59 per cent, although it is below the post-2023 high it hit earlier this month.
Belgium’s 10-year yield jumped as much as 0.12 percentage points to 4.46 per cent, taking its spread with Germany back to just above one percentage point, its highest intraday level since 2013. It later fell back to 4.43 per cent.
The country, which has one of the biggest budget deficits in the euro area and a higher-than-average debt load at 108 per cent of GDP, is at present holding difficult budget talks.
Prime Minister Bart De Wever has vowed to reduce spending, but discussions stalled again this week as leftwing and liberal coalition partners sparred over proposed cuts.
De Wever told parliament on Wednesday that if the financial situation was not stabilised, “I fear the outbreak of a debt crisis, for which we need to prepare”.
Investors view a broader serious downturn in Eurozone government bond markets beyond France as a key precondition for any intervention by the European Central Bank to support the market.
Lorenzo Bini Smaghi, a former ECB board member, wrote in the FT earlier this month that widening spreads showed “the shadows of the 2011-12 crisis are emerging again”. He said the euro area was in a stronger position, but the ECB could support the market by putting on hold its balance-sheet-shrinking programme, known as quantitative tightening.
Moody’s will issue a ratings decision on France on Friday, with a downgrade a real possibility given the outlook is already negative on the current rating of Aa3.
“The political situation is pretty adverse and [it is] difficult to see that improving anytime soon,” said John Stopford, head of multi-asset income at asset manager Ninety One.
The “path of least resistance”, Stopford added, was for a wider French spread heading towards April’s presidential election, arguing that the ECB would be unlikely to step in without a significant deterioration from current levels.

FRANKFURT, Oct 21 (Reuters) - The European Central Bank can strengthen the euro's global role and amplify the reach of its monetary policy by providing liquidity safety nets to foreign countries, ECB chief economist Philip Lane said on Wednesday.
Speaking at a closed-door event in Shanghai titled "Monetary System Beyond the Dollar", Lane said demand for the ECB's recently expanded euro liquidity facilities had been strong, with more than 30 central banks expressing interest.
"Liquidity lines bolster confidence in the currency and reduce the associated risks, supporting its wider usage," he told the event, part of the annual Bund summit, according to prepared remarks.
The comments come as policymakers globally question the the long-term dominance of the dollar in light of US President Donald Trump's unpredictable economic policy.
Lane argued that greater international use of the euro would enhance the ECB's ability to deliver on its inflation mandate by extending the global impact of euro area monetary policy.
He said the ECB's EUREP facility, which allows foreign central banks to obtain euros against collateral denominated in the single currency, could boost bond markets in the 21-country bloc, particularly through increased purchases by official reserve managers.
ECB President Christine Lagarde said recently that the bank was also reviewing its network of currency swap lines, which allow major central banks, including the US Federal Reserve and the People's Bank of China, to exchange their own currencies for euros.
Lane said such arrangements can encourage borrowing in euros but should be reserved for central banks in economies with close financial links to the euro area and a clear capacity to repay euro liabilities.
(Reporting by Francesco Canepa; Editing by Jonathan Spicer )

New Delhi: Commerce minister Piyush Goyal will be on a 6-day tour to Germany and the Netherlands starting 22 October to strengthen bilateral trade and investment ties and expand industrial and technological cooperation.
Goyal will be accompanied by around 100 business executives during the visit, which will focus on exploring new opportunities for collaboration across manufacturing, clean technology, advanced engineering, information technology and other sectors, the ministry said in a statement on Wednesday.
He will be in Germany from 22 October to 24 October, and in the Netherlands during 24-27 October.
In Germany, Goyal will participate in the Berlin Global Dialogue, where he will engage with international policymakers and global business leaders to highlight India's macroeconomic stability, manufacturing capabilities and role in building resilient global supply chains, according to the ministry statement.
On the sidelines of the event, he will hold bilateral meetings with Germany's federal minister for economic affairs and energy and the economic and financial policy advisor and G7/G20 Sherpa at the German Federal Chancellery. The discussions will cover bilateral trade and investment, technological and industrial cooperation, and market access and investment opportunities arising from the ongoing India-European Union free trade agreement (FTA) negotiations.
India-EU goods trade totalled €118.4 billion in 2025, with EU imports from India amounting to €69.5 billion and exports to India at €48.9 billion, according to official data. The scale of trade underscores the importance of expanding market access and investment opportunities as India and the EU pursue a trade agreement.
The minister will also lead government-to-government engagements in The Hague, where he is scheduled to meet the Netherlands' minister of economic affairs and climate and minister for foreign trade and development cooperation. The discussions will explore opportunities to expand trade channels and cooperation on green transition initiatives.
His engagements in the Netherlands will also include discussions with the King's Commissioner of North Holland and members of the Dutch parliament's committees on foreign trade and European affairs.
The accompanying Indian business delegation will participate in sectoral roundtables with German chief executives and Indian business representatives in Berlin. The discussions will cover automotive, advanced manufacturing, infrastructure and energy; information technology, artificial intelligence and services; agri-food, consumer goods and textiles; and healthcare, pharmaceuticals and wellness.
The delegation will also participate in an India-Germany Investment Roundtable with Germany Trade & Invest (GTAI) on investment opportunities and establishing operations in Germany. It will interact with German innovation and research institutions and think tanks on industrial transformation, deep technology, microelectronics, skills development, and bilateral trade, investment and resilient supply chains.
As part of the Netherlands leg, the Indian business delegation will visit the Port of Rotterdam on 25 October to examine its logistics and supply chain infrastructure.
On 26 October, Goyal will address businesses from India and the Netherlands at the India-Netherlands Business Forum in The Hague, alongside the Dutch minister for foreign trade and development cooperation. The forum will be followed by six parallel sectoral roundtables and business-to-business networking sessions.
The roundtables will cover agri-food and food processing; high technology and innovation; sustainability and renewable energy; logistics and supply chain connectivity; manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, textiles and engineering goods; and services and allied sectors.
The visit comes as India and the European Union continue negotiations on a free trade agreement, with the ministry identifying potential market access and investment opportunities arising from the talks as one of the areas for discussion during Goyal's meetings in Germany.

articles.title: Industry reacts as France and Germany agree automotive deal - Automotive Logistics

articles.full_text:
Trade and policy
France and Germany's new automotive deal proposes changes to emissions targets and 'Made in Europe' eligibility for the UK
On October 16, 2026, France and Germany announced that they have reached an agreement on a joint approach to securing the future of the European automotive industry. This joint plan includes proposals to further soften CO2 emissions reduction requirements and include the UK as a trusted partner in the EU's 'Made in Europe' rules.
In a joint statement, the governments of France and Germany noted that the two countries share the same clear ambition: to successfully transform Europe's automotive industry while maintaining the European Union's climate ambition and ensuring that the cars of the future are produced in Europe.
Both countries reaffirmed their commitment to achieving substantial reductions in CO2 emissions while strengthening Europe’s capacity to develop and manufacture the next generation of electric vehicles. They shared their belief that the "comprehensive package" of policies they've proposed combine an ambitious European decarbonisation pathway with the regulatory flexibility needed to reflect different market realities and technological conditions
"Europe must be a continent that innovates, invests and produces, while protecting the climate and safeguarding jobs," the joint statement read. "This is the purpose of our commitment and the guiding principle of our joint approach."
So what proposals comprise the Franco-German automotive plan?
Changes to the 2035 emissions reduction target
According to reports, France and Germany intend to maintain the 90% tailpipe emissions reduction target that the European Commission proposed in December 2025 – which would replace the EU’s existing plan to phase out the sale of new internal combustion engine (ICE) cars and vans by 2035.
Under the Franco-German plan, however, the requirement to offset the remaining 10% through measures such as the use of low-carbon steel and alternative fuels would be removed.
This is not the only change to the 2035 emissions reduction target proposed by France and Germany, though. The package also proposes multi-year averaging, assessing OEMs' CO2 reduction compliance over multiple years, rather than on a strict annual basis. If this change were adopted, it would allow manufacturers greater flexibility to compensate for higher emissions in one year with lower emissions in another.
Additionally, the proposal seeks to freeze the tightening of the utility factor for plug-in hybrid vehicles (PHEVs) until 2030. This factor estimates the proportion of a vehicle’s driving that takes place on electric power, influencing the CO₂ emissions attributed to it under EU regulations.
A lower assumed electric driving share means a plug-in hybrid is assigned higher calculated CO₂ emissions, potentially making it harder for automakers to meet their fleet targets. Freezing the factor’s tightening would give manufacturers greater flexibility in meeting those targets in the short term, while retaining PHEVs as part of their powertrain mix.
'Made in Europe' eligibility rules
Another significant proposal that is reported to be included in the Franco-German automotive policy package is a plan to ensure the 'Made in Europe' rules for vehicles apply to not just the 27 current EU member states but also any European partner participating within the EU single market as of January 1, 2020.
This would make the UK – which left the EU on January 31, 2020 – eligible for 'Made in Europe' status.
Although officials in Germany have historically supported the widening of 'Made in Europe' status to significant EU trading partners, this joint proposal marks a development in France's position on the matter.
"European taxpayers’ money should support [European] workers and European factories,” France's minister delegate for industry, Sébastien Martin, told reporters as recently as September.
On the UK specifically, Martin noted that a trading relationship between the UK and the EU can still exist, but fundamentally it was the UK's decision to leave the trade bloc.
"At the end of the day, if you are not part of the internal market and if you are not contributing to the financial capacity of the internal market, you don’t get the same kind of protection,” added Benjamin Haddad, France’s minister delegate for European Affairs.
A Downing Street spokesperson told The Guardian that, if confirmed, the UK government would "welcome the objective to have UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act", adding that this would be "good news for the British automotive industry and the jobs and investment it supports across the UK".
At the end of September, Mike Hawes, chief executive of the Society for Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT), warned that the benefits of the trading relationship between the UK and the EU are "at risk if the European Commission’s ‘Made in Europe’ proposals exclude UK-built vehicles from EU market incentives and procurement schemes".
He acknowledged that the EU is rightly focusing on strengthening its industrial base but shared his view that "restricting access for UK manufacturers in their largest market would be self-defeating". He said the move would be mutually detrimental to the competitiveness of both economies "at precisely the moment the industry must invest harder and faster in zero-emission mobility".
France's apparent U-turn on the UK's 'Made in Europe' eligibility is a positive signal for the UK automotive industry's hopes of maintaining a relationship with the EU that supports competitiveness, especially with Chinese OEMs gaining an growing market share in both the UK and EU markets.
However, there is a long way to go before a final decision can be made on this matter, and France and Germany represent just two of the countries at the table as discussions over the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) progress. All eyes will be on the UK-EU summit, which was recently confirmed to be taking place in Brussels on November 20 this year, for further talks around where the UK sits as a trading partner with the EU as the IAA takes shape.
"A threadbare Brexit deal has damaged our economy," UK prime minister Andy Burham has said ahead of the summit next month. "Britain can do so much better, so at this summit I want to take practical steps that pay off for the British public."
In addition to the UK, Norway – which has never been an EU member state but participates in the EU single market through the European Economic Area – could also be granted 'Made in Europe' status if the Franco-German proposal were to be adopted. However, it is understood that other key EU trading partners outside the single market, such as Turkey, would fall outside the proposal's eligibility criteria.
Although this proposal would offer countries like the UK and Norway the opportunity to be eligible for 'Made in Europe' status, it is worth noting that this eligibility would not be automatic and would require some compromise from these countries. It has been reported that the plan outlines that to be eligible for 'Made in Europe', non-EU trading partners would have to agree to full reciprocity and "dynamic alignment with EU conditions for investment from third countries and with EU trade protection measures".
For the UK, which has taken a different approach to the EU on tariffs on Chinese-built electric vehicles, this could present a difficult choice. The UK government would have to weigh the potential benefits of qualifying for 'Made in Europe' status against the implications of aligning more closely with EU measures to restrict trade with non-EU countries.
Recognition of low-carbon fuels as zero-emission
According to reports, the Franco-German proposal also seeks to recognise cars powered by renewable and low-carbon fuels as zero-emission vehicles (ZEVs) for regulatory purposes. This would provide a route for certain ICE vehicles to remain viable under the post-2035 framework, rather than relying exclusively on battery-electric or hydrogen vehicles.
The distinction is that this is a proposed regulatory classification, not a claim that these vehicles produce zero emissions throughout their operation or life cycle. It is not yet confirmed which fuels and vehicles would qualify as zero-emission under these proposals.

The Israeli military has detained about 80 US, Israeli and British volunteers helping Palestinians harvest olives near Bethlehem, including the New York Democratic congressional nominee Brad Lander, several rabbis and Israel’s former deputy attorney general.
“I’ve been detained by the IDF, along with a group of rabbis and volunteers,” Lander posted from a bus taking him to a police station. “We were simply harvesting olives in a grove near Nahalin in the West Bank. The occupation is a crime under international law. Harvesting olives isn’t a crime under any law I know.”
Lander, who is Jewish and an outspoken critic of the Israeli government, describes himself as a liberal Zionist. He believes in the vision of Israel as a safe, Jewish home, but argues that it cannot be a true democracy while it denies Palestinians their human rights and freedom.
An ally of the New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani, Lander’s critical approach to Israel was a key factor in his resounding primary victory against Dan Goldman, a prominent supporter of Israel.
He condemns Israel’s continued occupation of the West Bank and Gaza, supported the restriction of US military aid to Israel and believes that Israel’s military campaign in Gaza after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks amounts to genocide.
Settler militants have unleashed extreme violence on Palestinians attempting to harvest olives from their trees across the occupied West Bank, and anyone accompanying them.
A vicious assault on a US photojournalist and attacks on European diplomats and a French mayor over the weekend drew international condemnation and calls for the Israeli government to crack down on militants.
Wednesday’s olive-picking from trees outside the village of Nahalin was uneventful until a large contingent of Israeli security forces arrived, the organisers Protect the Harvest said in a statement.
“All volunteers were peacefully harvesting on the private land of a Palestinian family who had invited them. For reasons that remain unclear, the Israeli army showed up and detained approximately 80 people who were present.”
Soldiers said the area had been declared a closed military zone, separated the group by nationality and drove them to a nearby police station in minibuses for the Israelis and a larger bus for Americans.
Joshua Schoffman, who served as Israel’s deputy attorney general for more than a decade, described the mass detention as a “complete hallucination” in a post on social media.
“Just now, they told me that I’m being detained for the crime of olive harvesting,” he wrote. “We were asked to stop, and everyone complied. There was no friction whatsoever with settlers or with the security forces.”
Lander was released with a warning but all the others were still being held, Protect the Harvest said. Detainees include Jill Jacobs, the chief executive of T’ruah: The Rabbinic Call for Human Rights, and 11 other American rabbis affiliated with the group.
The detainees have been given water but no food. The Israeli military and police did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
On Monday, Lander made a first post about his journey to Palestine. “Our goals for the trip are to help protect the olive harvest – and to shed a light on the reality of the occupation,” he wrote. “Thankfully, our corner of today’s harvest was peaceful and successful. But violence unfortunately is never far away.”

ECB Economists: Euro Zone Absorbed Energy Shock Better Than Expected
European Central Bank economists said on Wednesday that the euro zone has taken this year's energy shock in stride more effectively than anticipated, according to Reuters. Their assessment, released in an ECB blog, highlights diminished fossil fuel reliance, robust fiscal backing and an artificial intelligence-driven investment surge as forces keeping growth on track.
The euro area encountered a steep climb in oil and gas prices after the Iran war upended energy markets, stirring inflation worries and fueling a worldwide bond selloff. Even so, the bloc has maintained growth, and business surveys point to continued expansion.
ECB economists Oscar Arce, Gerrit Koester and Beatrice Pierluigi calculated that the economy now depends on oil at roughly half the level seen in the early 1990s, which curbs the effect of energy price shocks. Expanded renewable and nuclear generation has further loosened the connection between gas prices and electricity costs in several countries.
The blog called AI-related trade a significant tailwind for the euro area, noting that technology-related export orders and AI-linked sectors have outperformed.
The fiscal impulse reached 0.5% of GDP, double the size anticipated at the end of last year, largely driven by German government spending on defence and infrastructure.
Nevertheless, the economists cautioned that much of this support may turn out to be temporary. Global demand, fiscal stimulus and AI investment could diminish, leaving the bloc vulnerable if geopolitical tensions escalate or energy markets encounter new disruptions.
The findings emerge as the ECB weighs additional interest rate increases to counter an energy-driven inflation surge, with the third hike of the year anticipated in December.

articles.title: Macron rebukes Trump for stoking anti-immigrant anger over France riots - CHOSUNBIZ - Chosunbiz
articles.summary: Macron rebukes Trump for stoking anti-immigrant anger over France riots - CHOSUNBIZ  Chosunbiz
articles.full_text:
French President Emmanuel Macron sharply criticized U.S. President Donald Trump for blaming immigrants and Muslims for riots in France. As protests over high inflation tied to the Middle East war spillover have turned into looting and arson, right-wing leaders in the United States and Europe facing elections are using them to stoke anti-immigrant sentiment, raising the prospect of diplomatic friction among Western allies.
On the 21st, according to a roundup of major outlets including the Financial Times (FT) and Reuters, Macron took issue with remarks by foreign leaders about recent protests in France at a news conference during his visit to Qatar. Macron said, "There is no evidence that foreign powers directly interfered behind the riots," adding, "There has been external information manipulation, and this has led many foreign leaders to make unacceptable and foolish remarks." He specified that "President Trump is one of them."
He added, "We witnessed artificial intelligence (AI) images showing scenes that never happened in France. There are people who said we were invaded by mobs of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false," noting, "These people in some regions or across the Atlantic who are campaigning with France at their back irritate me." European Union (EU) regulators are investigating the widespread online distribution of violent videos unrelated to France and disinformation.
Earlier across France, on the 17th, a large peaceful protest was held to denounce high living costs and education budget issues. During this, some rioters set fire to Limoges City Hall and looted shops, escalating into the most damaging street violence in years. Police in France arrested more than 2,000 people, and authorities suspect that far-left groups, not immigrants or Islamist radicals, are behind the violence.
With midterm elections coming on Nov. 3, President Trump and Vice President JD Vance immediately folded the French riots into an anti-immigration campaign. On the 18th, Trump wrote on the social media site Truth Social, "France is burning! Immigration by people from a completely different world, people with hate in their hearts, has shattered what was once a great country." He warned voters to "just look at France," claiming "Paris will soon become a Muslim city." On the 19th, he told reporters, "Emmanuel should have closed the borders long ago. I told him to do that."
Soon after, other right-wing politicians in countries heading into elections joined in. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces a general election next week, said in an interview with local outlet i24 on the 20th that France had "succumbed to an invasion by Islamist extremists." Santiago Abascal, leader of Spain's far-right Vox party facing a snap general election in November, likewise blamed "Islamist leftist forces" for fueling the riots. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar also pointed to immigration as the cause of the riots.
Inside France, Marine Le Pen, a lawmaker with the far-right National Union (RN) who leads in polls ahead of the French presidential election next spring, went on local radio Franceinfo on the 21st and pressed the attack, saying, "This is migration chaos, security chaos, and budget chaos."
The French government plans to deploy large numbers of police and the military to restore order ahead of additional protests set for the 24th. Macron warned, "Those who seek to spread disorder on the 24th will be stopped."

articles.title: European Commission readies study on 5 DSA dispute settlement challenges - PPC Land
articles.summary: European Commission readies study on 5 DSA dispute settlement challenges  PPC Land
articles.full_text:
The European Commission on October 20, 2026 held a multilateral dialogue with very large online platforms and national Digital Services Coordinators on the out-of-court dispute settlement mechanism in Article 21 of the Digital Services Act, and disclosed that an external study of five problem areas in that mechanism has been concluded and will be published soon.
In Short
When a big platform deletes your post or restricts your account in the EU, you can ask an independent, certified body outside the courts to look at the decision again. On October 20, the European Commission sat down with the largest platforms and national regulators to talk about where that system is not working well, from how users are told it exists to who pays the fees. A study on those same problems is finished but not yet public, and it will feed into how the Commission enforces this part of the law.
What happened on October 20
According to the European Commission, the meeting on October 20, 2026 was a "multilateral dialogue with providers of Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) and Digital Services Coordinators (DSCs) on the out-of-court dispute settlement (ODS) mechanism under the Digital Services Act (DSA)." The Commission published a short news item describing the session on its Shaping Europe's digital future website. The printed copy reviewed for this article was generated on October 21, 2026, and does not display a separate publication date for the news item itself.
The format matters. This was not an enforcement action, a consultation or a guidelines release. It was a closed exchange between the regulator, the companies designated as VLOPs and the national authorities that certify and supervise dispute settlement bodies. The news item does not list which platforms attended, how many representatives took part, or where the dialogue was held. It does not say whether any certified dispute settlement bodies were in the room, although it refers separately to "engagement with certified ODS bodies" as one of the inputs into the Commission's work.
Two sets of presentations took place, according to the Commission. "During the dialogue, platform representatives presented their views on challenges related to the ODS mechanism." National regulators, for their part, "presented their work to establish best practices for Article 21 of the DSA within the European Board for Digital Services (EBDS)." The Commission describes the coordinators as playing "a crucial role in the process, particularly as regards to the certification and functioning of ODS."
The five areas on the table
The core of the Commission's account is a list of the specific implementation problems participants discussed. According to the news item, they were:
- The way platforms inform users about the possibility of using ODS
- Approaches to determining which moderation decisions are eligible for review by ODS bodies
- Exchange of case-related information between platforms and ODS bodies
- Fees charged in relation to ODS disputes
- The implementation of ODS decisions
Each item points at a different fault line. The first concerns the user interface: whether people who lose a moderation decision actually learn that an external route exists. The second is a scoping question that has practical weight, since a platform and a dispute body can disagree about whether a given action counts as a reviewable decision at all. The third involves the flow of evidence, logs and reasoning between a platform and a body that has no power to compel disclosure. Fees, the fourth item, go to the economics of the system, which the DSA loads onto the platform when a user wins. The fifth, implementation, asks what happens after a body rules.
The Commission does not say what positions the platforms took on any of these points, and it attributes no statement to any company. The news item also does not reveal whether participants reached any agreement.
A finished study nobody has seen yet
The most concrete disclosure in the Commission's text concerns research. "To assess these five areas of implementation of Article 21 of the DSA, the Commission engaged an external contractor, to conduct a study - which has been recently concluded and will be published soon," according to the news item. The phrase "external contractor" in the original links to a tender listing on the EU Funding and Tenders portal.
Several basic facts about that study are absent from all four documents reviewed. None names the contractor. None gives a publication date beyond "soon." None discloses the study's methodology, sample or findings. The Commission says only that "the findings of the report, the exchanges held during the dialogue and the engagement with certified ODS bodies, will support the Commission's ongoing work on the implementation of Article 21 of the DSA."
A second account of the meeting came from Tadej Uršič, a Legal and Policy Officer at the European Commission, in a post on his personal LinkedIn profile on October 21, 2026. The post is an individual officer's summary rather than an official Commission statement, and it carries a two-page document titled "ODS Regulatory dialogue." Its wording tracks the news item closely. "An external study on these areas has recently been concluded and will be published soon," Uršič wrote. "Together with the regulatory dialogue and best practices, which DSCs are working on, it will support our ongoing work on Article 21 of the DSA." He summarised the agenda as covering "how platforms inform users about ODS, which decisions are eligible for review, information exchange with ODS bodies, fees, and the implementation of ODS decisions." The post adds no names, figures or dates beyond what the Commission's news item contains.
How Article 21 is supposed to work
The Commission's background page on dispute settlement bodies, last updated on September 11, 2026, sets out the mechanism in some detail. Users whose accounts are restricted or whose content is sanctioned can first appeal through a platform's internal complaint-handling system. "However, the DSA also gives users the right to turn to out-of-court dispute settlement (ODS) bodies, if they think a decision by an online platform was wrong," according to the page. The same right covers people whose notices of illegal content were rejected. Courts remain available throughout: "users may always take the matter to their national courts."
Users choose the body. According to the Commission, users "may select any entity that has been certified as a dispute settlement body in the EU for their type of dispute and request a review of a platform's content moderation decision." The body does not need to sit in the user's own country, provided it handles the relevant language.
The cost structure is asymmetric by design. "For the user, dispute settlement will usually be available free of charge or at a low cost. If the body settles the dispute in favour of the user, the online platform shall bear all the fees," the page states. That clause explains why fees were one of the five discussion points: the party paying the bill in a lost case is the platform, not the complainant.
Enforcement is the weak joint. "Dispute settlement bodies do not have the power to impose a binding settlement of the dispute on the parties, but platforms and users are required to engage with them in good faith," according to the Commission. A body can rule that a removal was wrong, but it cannot order the content restored. That gap sits directly behind the fifth agenda item, the implementation of ODS decisions.
Certification conditions
Organisations apply to the Digital Services Coordinator of the Member State where they are established. Certification lasts a maximum of five years and can be renewed. Only EU-based organisations qualify, and a certificate is valid in all 27 Member States, though it can be limited to particular types of illegal content, particular types of platforms or particular languages.
The Commission lists six conditions. Bodies must show impartiality and independence, including financial independence from platforms and from complainants. They need expertise in one or more areas of illegal content or in the enforcement of terms and conditions for one or more types of platform. Members must be paid in a way that is independent of the outcome of each case. The procedure must be accessible online, allowing complaints and supporting documents to be filed electronically. Bodies must settle disputes "in a swift, efficient and cost-effective manner and in at least one of the official languages of the EU." And they must operate under clear, fair and publicly available rules of procedure.
Reporting duties
Accountability runs upward in two layers. Each certified body files an annual report with its certifying authority. Each national authority, in turn, reports once every two years on the functioning of all the bodies it has certified. According to the Commission, those reports cover "the number of disputes, their outcomes, the time taken to resolve the disputes, encountered difficulties, best practices and recommendations to improve the functioning of the dispute settlement system." A certifying authority can revoke a certification if a body stops meeting the conditions.
Who is certified
The Commission maintains a table of certified bodies on the same page. The printed version reviewed for this article captured only one expanded row, so it is not a complete list. That row shows ADROIT, certified on July 10, 2024 by the Malta Communications Authority. Its listed areas of expertise are online shopping and booking platforms; content sharing and content-driven marketing platforms; crowdfunding and peer-to-peer lending; Web3, DeFi, NFT and fintech platforms and protocols; gaming, gambling and betting platforms; and B2B, B2C and P2P trading platforms and marketplaces. It works in Dutch, English, French, German, Italian, Maltese, Portuguese and Spanish.

articles.title: ECB Finds Euro Zone Oil Dependence Halved as AI and Fiscal Spending Support Growth - ESG News
articles.summary: ECB Finds Euro Zone Oil Dependence Halved as AI and Fiscal Spending Support Growth  ESG News
articles.full_text:
- Lower oil exposure: The euro zone economy is about half as reliant on oil as in the early 1990s, ECB economists estimate.
- Stronger fiscal support: Fiscal stimulus reached 0.5% of GDP, twice the level expected at the end of last year.
- Temporary growth drivers: ECB economists warn that AI investment, global demand and government spending may fade.
The euro zone economy has proved more resilient to this year’s energy shock than expected, according to European Central Bank (ECB) economists. Lower fossil fuel dependence, artificial intelligence investment and stronger government spending have helped sustain growth despite higher oil and gas prices.
Energy Dependence and Economic Resilience
ECB economists Oscar Arce, Gerrit Koester and Beatrice Pierluigi published the assessment in an ECB blog on Wednesday. They estimated that the euro area now relies on oil about half as much as in the early 1990s. This reduction has limited the economic impact of rising energy prices.
The Iran war disrupted energy markets, pushing oil and gas prices higher and renewing inflation concerns. However, the currency bloc has continued expanding, with business surveys showing that economic activity remains positive. Higher renewable and nuclear electricity generation has also weakened the connection between gas prices and electricity costs in several countries.
AI Investment and Fiscal Support
The ECB economists identified AI-related trade as an “important tailwind” for the euro area. Technology-related export orders and sectors linked to AI have outperformed, supporting economic activity during the energy shock.
Government spending has also exceeded earlier expectations. The fiscal impulse reached 0.5% of gross domestic product, twice the level projected at the end of last year. German government spending on defence and infrastructure accounted for much of the additional support.
However, the economists cautioned that several growth drivers could prove temporary. Global demand, fiscal stimulus and AI investment may weaken, particularly if geopolitical tensions intensify or energy markets face further disruption.
Monetary Policy Implications
The findings arrive as the ECB considers further interest rate increases to contain energy-driven inflation. A third rate increase this year is expected in December, following renewed inflation pressures and a global bond selloff.
The ECB assessment identifies reduced oil exposure as a structural source of resilience, alongside shorter-term support from investment and fiscal policy. However, its economists warn that fresh energy disruptions could leave the euro area vulnerable if those temporary sources of growth weaken.
RELATED ARTICLE: ECB Publishes Climate-Related Disclosures Showing Decarbonization Path
Who It Affects
- Euro zone businesses: Lower oil dependence and stronger electricity generation diversity have reduced exposure to energy price shocks in several countries.
- Technology exporters: AI-related investment and trade have supported stronger export orders and activity in AI-linked sectors.
- European policymakers: Energy-led inflation and the possibility of fading fiscal support complicate decisions on further interest rate increases.

articles.title: US lobbying ‘blitz’ seeks to destroy EU’s anti-deforestation regulation, campaign group reveals - The Grocer
articles.summary: US lobbying ‘blitz’ seeks to destroy EU’s anti-deforestation regulation, campaign group reveals  The Grocer
articles.full_text:
Powerful US-based corporations have spent the past two years undertaking a “lobbying blitz” against EU officials, in a bid to “derail and severely weaken” the bloc’s flagship anti-deforestation regulation, a new investigation reveals.
The “unprecedented” lobbying push brought together major US corporations, powerful industry groups and even US government actors as part of a “sustained campaign targeting EU policymakers”, claimed environmental campaign group Mighty Earth.
Based on analysis of EU lobbying transparency records, Mighty Earth’s new report, titled Knives Out: How US lobbyists tried to kill the EUDR, revealed the EUDR was “discussed by major companies and powerful industry association representatives” in at least 173 in-person meetings with MEPs between July 2024 and July 2026.
A further 178 face-to-face meetings were held with senior European Commission officials during the same time period.
Mighty Earth also uncovered “obscured additional lobbying” via an additional 100 meetings in which the EUDR was discussed with EC officials, but were not captured in its transparency register under the meeting subject matter heading.
The group’s probe identified 24 major US companies, trade associations and industry organisations that lobbied EU institutions and/or the US federal government on the EUDR during the time period.
Major agrifood companies that have taken part in the lobbying campaign included Cadbury parent Mondelez – which at eight meetings had the second highest amount of talks of any organisation with MEPs.
Dutch/American coffee and tea giant JDE Peet’s had five meetings, while Cargill had two and Bunge had a single meeting to discuss the regulation with European lawmakers.
Mondelez in particular has voiced strong opposition to the EUDR, with its VP of corporate and government affairs for Europe Massimiliano Di Domenico publicly advocating for delaying the EUDR at events over the past 18 months.
Mighty Earth also discovered evidence of “high-level US corporate engagement with the US Congress, US Department of Agriculture, the Office of the US Trade Representative, the White House, and the US Mission to the EU, based in Brussels”.
In several cases, concerns raised by US timber, pulp and paper and soy interests were closely reflected in representations made by US government officials to their European counterparts, it added.
Even president Trump was directly lobbied to kill off the “unfair and burdensome” EUDR by Representative Austin Scott (Republican, Georgia) at a roundtable meeting on American agriculture held at the White House in December 2025, Mighty Earth pointed out.
Already twice delayed and now significantly watered down from its original ambitions, the EUDR is due to apply from 30 December.
It covers cattle, cocoa, coffee, palm oil, rubber, soy and wood products, and requires companies trading these commodities with the EU to conduct supply chain due diligence and provide farm-level geolocation data to demonstrate that products are not linked to deforestation or forest degradation.
In light of the widespread lobbying activity, Mighty Earth is calling for greater EU lobbying transparency “to see who is seeking to influence EU legislation, on whose behalf and with what demands”.
The group added EU policymakers also needed to “ensure a much more balanced engagement with civil society organizations working to protect forests and the public interest”.
“The knives came out in the most hostile way by US actors in a lobbying blitz to kill off the world’s first, gold-standard legislation to keep forests standing,” said Mighty Earth senior advisor Isabel Fernández.
“The attacks were based on flawed arguments about the negligible US deforestation risk and unwarranted claims of inflation for EU citizens,” she added.
“Our analysis found a relentless and aggressive campaign to further pressure EU policymakers,” Fernández claimed.
“Some of the US companies lobbying the EU include the most egregious forest destroyers who are still linked to the illegal clearing of forests for commodities, such as soy, that make their way into European markets. We hope that will all change when the EUDR comes into effect in December.”

articles.title: ECB promotes the role of the euro, more than 30 central banks are interested. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: ECB promotes the role of the euro, more than 30 central banks are interested.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
|  | 
| ECB headquarters. Photo: Dr. Thomas Liptak/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0) | 
 More than 30 central banks are interested.
 Speaking at an event on the international monetary system held in Shanghai, China , on October 21, Philip Lane, Chief Economist of the ECB, emphasized that expanding access to euro liquidity for foreign central banks could help strengthen the global position of the common European currency and enhance the effectiveness of the ECB's monetary policy implementation.
 The statement was made at an event themed "Monetary Systems Beyond the US Dollar," part of the annual Bund conference. Philip Lane said that the need for the euro-denominated liquidity tools recently expanded by the ECB is enormous, with more than 30 central banks expressing interest.
 Mr. Lane argued that the liquidity provision mechanism helps strengthen confidence in the euro, mitigate associated risks, and encourage wider use of the currency. According to him, the ECB's international liquidity provision mechanisms are designed to be used only in shocks or crisis situations. However, even when not used, the presence of these mechanisms can help prevent adverse developments in financial markets.
 At the heart of this strategy is EUREP, a mechanism providing euro liquidity through secured repurchase agreements for central banks outside the eurozone. Under this mechanism, central banks can access euro funding by using high-quality collateral assets denominated in the common currency. This mechanism aims to help central banks respond to liquidity shortages, thereby limiting the spillover effects on European financial markets.
 In February 2026, the ECB decided to expand EUREP, allowing central banks worldwide, in principle, regular access to the mechanism, except in cases where they do not meet the conditions related to anti-money laundering, counter-terrorism financing, or international sanctions regulations.
 Under the new framework, the maximum limit for each central bank is 50 billion euros. The duration of each transaction ranges from one day to one week and can be extended. The ECB stated that in the past six months, more than 30 central banks have expressed interest in the EUREP mechanism. In early October, the ECB completed the procedures for admitting the first foreign central banks to the expanded EUREP mechanism.
 Expanding the euro's influence and supporting the bond market.
 Besides its role in ensuring liquidity, Mr. Lane believes EUREP could also support the eurozone bond market by encouraging foreign central banks to increase their holdings of euro-denominated debt securities.
 As the ability to convert these assets into euro capital improves, reserve managers will have more incentive to hold long-term bonds, while expanding their portfolios to include bonds from more countries in the region, rather than focusing on the most liquid markets. This could contribute to the integration of the European bond market.
 In addition to EUREP, according to recent information from ECB President Christine Lagarde, the ECB is also reviewing its network of currency swap agreements. These agreements allow major central banks, including the US Federal Reserve (Fed) and the People's Bank of China (PBoC), to swap their currencies for euros.
 Mr. Lane argued that such agreements could encourage borrowing in euros, but should only be reserved for central banks in economies with strong financial ties to the euro zone and a clear capacity to meet their euro repayment obligations.
 According to Lane's argument, the wider use of the euro in international trade, payments, and borrowing also increases the scope of ECB monetary policy. As the cost of capital in euros changes, the impact is no longer limited to the eurozone but can extend to economies that use euros for transactions and capital mobilization.

articles.title: UK fighter jets to protect Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks - DW.com
articles.summary: UK fighter jets to protect Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks  DW.comUK to deploy jets to defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks  BBCWW1 to Houthis: British jets for Saudi Arabia build on long military bond  Al JazeeraRoyal Air Force Typhoons to fly defensive missions over Saudi Arabia  FlightGlobalRAF jets to protect Saudi Arabia’s skies from Houthi rebels  The Times
articles.full_text:
Britain will deploy Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets to Saudi Arabia to help defend the kingdom against increasing attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebels, the UK government announced on Tuesday.
The aircraft will protect Saudi cities and critical infrastructure from drones and missiles, the Ministry of Defense said. They will not carry out offensive strikes against Houthi targets in Yemen.
"The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable," British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said.
He particularly condemned attacks on Riyadh's international airport, which has been targeted 20 times since the beginning of October.
Strikes on the airport have killed at least 18 people and wounded hundreds this month, according to reports.
What additional military support is Britain providing?
The deployment follows a request from Saudi Arabia and expands military assistance announced by London in September.
Britain will also send an Atlas A400M military transport aircraft and military advisers. It has extended its offer to provide air-to-air refueling for Saudi aircraft operating against the Houthis for another 90 days.
The announcement comes as Yemen's civil war continues to escalate following the collapse of a years-long truce in September.
Houthi attacks have increasingly targeted Saudi oil facilities and civilian infrastructure. The rebels have also imposed a naval blockade and attacked tankers, disrupting oil exports and pushing up energy prices.
Inside Yemen, authorities said a Houthi strike on Monday killed 58 people at a training camp for Saudi-backed government security forces.
Saudi Arabia and the United States accuse Iran of supporting the Houthis, an allegation Tehran denies.
How is the conflict affecting Saudi Arabia's economy?
Saudi Arabia has postponed its flagship Future Investment Initiative conference, informally known as "Davos in the Desert," until 2027.
The event, originally scheduled for October 26-29, was expected to attract leading international financiers.
According to media reports, major banks and private equity firms had raised security concerns about attending the event.
The conference is a key part of Saudi Arabia's efforts to attract foreign investment and diversify its economy away from oil.
