articles.title: “Close the Borders and Face a Population Crisis, Open Them and Face Social Conflict”: Europe’s Immigration Policy Dilemma as French Riots Fuel Anti-Immigration Sentiment - https://economy.ac/
articles.summary: “Close the Borders and Face a Population Crisis, Open Them and Face Social Conflict”: Europe’s Immigration Policy Dilemma as French Riots Fuel Anti-Immigration Sentiment  https://economy.ac/
articles.full_text:
Authored On
Modified
Large-scale riots in France prompt calls across Europe for tighter immigration controls
EU population crisis deepens amid low birth rates and aging, highlighting both benefits and drawbacks of immigration
Indiscriminate immigration restrictions could accelerate regional depopulation and weaken the foundations of public services
Anti-immigration sentiment is intensifying across Europe. Some political leaders in the region have linked the large-scale riots and looting that swept across France to failed immigration policies, calling for tough border controls. Experts warn, however, that because immigration has partly offset Europe’s population crisis and labor shortages, a prolonged shift toward reduced immigration could further exacerbate the decline in the economically active population and the depopulation of regions.
Hungary and Poland Signal Anti-Immigration Stance
According to a Euronews report on the 18th (all dates hereafter are local time), Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar and Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk that day characterized the escalating violent protests across France as an example of the failure of Western Europe’s lenient immigration policies, strongly defending their own policies of sealing their borders. On the 18th, Magyar posted footage of burning buildings in France on social media, writing, “Having witnessed senseless destruction and unjustifiable violence, it should now be clear to everyone why Hungary takes the strictest stance on immigration.” He added, “The overwhelming majority of European countries have woken up and are seeking to break with the lenient policies of the past,” saying, “I hope it is not too late.”
That same evening, Tusk also wrote on social media, without directly mentioning France, “Poland will neither repeat the mistakes of other European countries nor pay the price for them.” He emphasized, “We are firmly defending our borders against illegal immigration, implementing our own asylum policy, and deporting those who violate Polish law.” Then, on the 19th, former Polish Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki, who could compete against Tusk ahead of the general election next November, likewise declared, “France is burning, and we must be wise before damage is done.” He stressed that the center-right coalition he leads has a comprehensive solution to make Poland the safest country in the world.
Immigration Also Comes to the Fore in France
Earlier, on the 17th, nationwide protests against rising living costs took place in France. According to the French Interior Ministry, an estimated 550,000 people took to the streets that day, about 2,400 protesters were arrested, and around 1,000 police officers were injured. Shops were looted in Paris, Lyon, and Marseille, while a town hall built in the 19th century was burned in the central city of Limoges. Political symbols tied to immigration issues also appeared at various protest sites. According to local media reports, protesters in the southern city of Toulouse that day placed a yellow vest over the head of an equestrian statue of Joan of Arc, France’s national heroine and Catholic saint, to resemble a hijab, and put a Palestinian flag in her hand. At the Louvre Museum’s pyramid plaza in central Paris, masked protesters climbed a statue of Joan of Arc and affixed stickers bearing political slogans. At Place de la République, a protester was seen waving a Palestinian flag beside a burning bus shelter.
France’s far-right politicians responded by going on the offensive, linking the riots to immigration. On the 18th, Marine Le Pen, a lawmaker from France’s National Rally (RN), said, “We are paying the price for decades of uncontrolled immigration,” directly blaming existing immigration policies for the violence. However, there is no objective evidence that immigrants or people from immigrant families led the unrest, as French police and government authorities have not officially released the proportion of immigrants or second- and third-generation immigrants among those arrested. The French government identified far-left radicals and professional looters who infiltrated peaceful protests as the main perpetrators of the violence.
Immigration Partly Offsets Population Crisis
Population decline and labor shortages underpin the willingness of France and other European countries to accept immigrants from outside the region. According to the third report on demographic change released by the European Commission in July, the EU’s population is projected to rise from its current 450.6 million to a peak of 453.3 million in 2029 before beginning to decline. It is estimated to fall to about 445 million by 2050 and to just 398.8 million by 2100, down 11.7% from 2025. Low birth rates are cited as the biggest cause of population decline. Annual births in the EU fell from 6.8 million in 1964 to about 3.5 million last year—roughly halving over some 60 years.
Population aging is also progressing rapidly. The proportion of EU residents aged 65 and older is projected to rise from about 1 in 5 today to 1 in 3 by 2050. The share aged 80 and older is also expected to more than double, from 6.2% in 2025 to 13.3% in 2070. Immigrants have so far helped partially offset this demographic crisis. Indeed, data from the EU’s statistical office, Eurostat, show that deaths exceeded births in the EU by about 1.35 million last year. Yet population gains from net migration and statistical adjustments reached 2.05 million, resulting in an overall population increase of around 710,000.
Table 1. Sources of Conflict Related to Immigration into Europe
| Category | Main Issues | 
|---|---|
| Social Integration | Insufficient language, education, and employment support; increased risk of poverty and social exclusion | 
| Housing | Concentrated housing demand in major cities; resident opposition to securing refugee reception facilities and temporary accommodation | 
| Public Services | Delays in expanding staffing and facilities to keep pace with increased use of schools and hospitals | 
| Labor Market | Intensifying competition for low-wage jobs; concerns about wage and employment insecurity among existing workers | 
Immigration-Related Social Unrest Also Deepens
Despite this accelerating population decline, calls to restrict immigration are growing across Europe because social conflicts stemming from immigrant arrivals persist. This reflects the failure of social integration policies designed to help immigrants settle into local communities and labor markets to keep pace with the expansion in immigrant admissions. According to Eurostat, 43.8% of non-EU citizens living in the EU were at risk of poverty or social exclusion in 2024, while their unemployment rate reached 12.3%.
Housing shortages are also cited as a factor intensifying tensions over immigration. As immigrants concentrate in major cities with insufficient housing supply, residents have increasingly opposed efforts to secure refugee reception facilities and temporary accommodation. In the United Kingdom, anti-immigration protests took place last July outside a hotel housing asylum seekers in Epping, Essex, while similar rallies followed in London. Meanwhile, insufficient increases in staffing and facilities at schools and hospitals are adding to the burden on public services. In the labor market, concerns are also growing that immigrant inflows could worsen wages and employment conditions for existing workers, particularly in low-wage jobs.
Risks of Prolonged Population Decline
The problem is that indiscriminately restricting immigrant inflows could deepen population decline driven by low birth rates and aging, damaging national economies and social systems as a whole. A shrinking working-age population weakens the tax base and makes it harder to maintain public infrastructure such as schools, hospitals, and administrative offices. These risks are particularly pronounced in regions experiencing concentrated population outflows. In Japan, where population decline has persisted for years, a total of 8,850 public schools closed between 2004 and 2023. According to Japan’s Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology, Hokkaido recorded the largest number of closures at 859, while closures also continued in other regions, including Iwate Prefecture (331) and Fukushima Prefecture (330). As infrastructure supporting daily life shrinks, residents move to major cities at an accelerating pace. The resulting loss of young people reduces labor supply and consumer demand, dampening business activity and new investment in a vicious cycle.
A similar situation is unfolding in South Korea. According to the results of last year’s Population and Housing Census, released by the Ministry of Data and Statistics in July, 26.38 million people, or 50.9% of the total population of 51.82 million, lived in the Seoul metropolitan area. The metropolitan area’s share of the population has continued to rise since first exceeding 50% in 2019, while 147 of the country’s 229 cities, counties, and districts recorded population declines. Low birth rates, combined with the concentration of young people in the Seoul metropolitan area, have weakened the demographic base of other regions. As a result, school mergers and closures are continuing in these regions, while local universities are also struggling to recruit students and facing financial difficulties.

articles.title: European Solidarity proposes UAH 161.5 bln cuts to ministry spending – MP Yuzhanina - Interfax-Ukraine
articles.summary: European Solidarity proposes UAH 161.5 bln cuts to ministry spending – MP Yuzhanina  Interfax-Ukraine
articles.full_text:
Expenditures by ministries and government agencies in the Ukrainian draft 2027 state budget can be reduced by UAH 161.5 billion, with the funds redirected to defense needs.
"This is the next set of our amendments to bill No. 16000," Nina Yuzhanina, a member of parliament from the European Solidarity faction, wrote on Facebook.
The proposal concerns two types of expenditures: consumption expenditures (excluding utilities), which are to be reviewed based on the actual 2026 baseline and the relevant growth indices; and development expenditures, or capital expenditures, which are to be reduced under designated budget programs.
"And here I want to draw attention to a fundamental point. We are not proposing to halt the operations of government agencies or leave them without the funding they need. But how can we continue to accept increases in expenditures amounting to billions of hryvnias across the judicial system, the prosecutor's office, the Ministry of Justice, the Ministry of Digital Transformation and the Verkhovna Rada?" Yuzhanina said.
As is known, European Solidarity is demanding that all populist and corrupt expenditure items be removed from the draft 2027 state budget. Instead, the released funds should be allocated exclusively to defense and strengthening the Armed Forces of Ukraine. According to party leader Petro Poroshenko, reallocating non-targeted expenditures would make it possible to direct at least an additional half a trillion hryvnias to the military.
"Our demands are specific: at least UAH 500 billion in additional funding for the military to purchase weapons and defense technologies; 30% of the military personal income tax revenue to go directly to brigades; indexation of military pay; protection of the energy sector and the economy; cancellation of non-priority and propaganda-related expenditures; fulfillment of European commitments and restoration of our allies' trust," Poroshenko said.

articles.title: ECB Chief Economist Lane: Euro Liquidity Lines Can Widen the Euro's Global Reach - News and Statistics - IndexBox
articles.summary: ECB Chief Economist Lane: Euro Liquidity Lines Can Widen the Euro's Global Reach - News and Statistics  IndexBox
articles.full_text:
ECB's Lane: Euro Liquidity Backstops Can Strengthen the Currency's Global Role
The European Central Bank can reinforce the euro's international standing and widen the reach of its monetary policy by offering liquidity backstops to foreign countries, according to comments from ECB chief economist Philip Lane reported by Reuters. Lane made the remarks at a closed-door gathering in Shanghai titled Monetary System Beyond the Dollar, part of the annual Bund summit.
Lane indicated that demand for the ECB's recently expanded euro liquidity facilities has been substantial, with more than 30 central banks showing interest. He argued that liquidity lines reinforce confidence in the currency and lower related risks, thereby supporting broader use of the euro.
The remarks arrive as policymakers around the world debate the long-term dominance of the dollar, a discussion the report links to the unpredictable economic policy of US President Donald Trump. Lane contended that expanded international use of the euro would improve the ECB's capacity to meet its inflation mandate by extending the global influence of euro area monetary policy.
He said the ECB's EUREP facility, which lets foreign central banks obtain euros against collateral denominated in the single currency, could strengthen bond markets across the 21-country bloc, particularly through additional purchases by official reserve managers.
ECB President Christine Lagarde said recently that the bank is also reviewing its network of currency swap lines, which enable major central banks, including the US Federal Reserve and the People's Bank of China, to exchange their own currencies for euros. Lane said such arrangements can encourage borrowing in euros but should be limited to central banks in economies with close financial ties to the euro area and a clear ability to repay euro liabilities.

articles.title: EUR/USD Price Forecast: Euro at 1.1215 as French OAT Spread Hits 152.5 bps Before Fed-ECB Week — 1.1150 Target - TradingNEWS
articles.summary: EUR/USD Price Forecast: Euro at 1.1215 as French OAT Spread Hits 152.5 bps Before Fed-ECB Week — 1.1150 Target  TradingNEWS
articles.full_text:
Key Points
- The French OAT-Bund spread widened 5.5 bps to 152.5 bps as 10-year OAT yields rose to 4.96%.
- EUR/USD has failed four times at the 1.1260–1.1270 resistance zone since early October.
- Euro area inflation jumped to 3.8% in September, keeping an ECB hike in play for October 29.
EUR/USD traded at 1.1215 in New York on Tuesday, down 0.22% from Monday’s 1.1239 close, after a session that ran from a low of 1.1182 to a high of 1.1235. The European Central Bank fixed its reference rate at 1.1215, down from 1.1225 on Monday and 1.1253 last Friday. The euro opened the European morning at 1.1212, rallied to 1.1235 as the dollar softened on fading October Fed hike bets, then gave the entire move back when Brent crude spiked above $111. The pair has spent October inside a 156-pip band between 1.1114 and 1.1270.
The thesis for this forecast is simple. The euro is carrying a French fiscal risk premium and a rate disadvantage against the dollar, and neither will shift until the Federal Reserve decides on October 28 and the ECB decides on October 29. French 10-year yields rose 3 basis points to 4.96% on Tuesday, and the OAT-Bund spread widened 5.5 basis points to 152.5 basis points. The Fed funds target sits at 3.75% to 4.00% against an ECB deposit rate of 2.50%. Euro area inflation jumped to 3.8% in September, which gives the ECB a reason to hike, but French political unrest gives it a reason to hold.
The longer picture is a steady grind lower. EUR/USD is down 3.78% over the past year and 2.19% over the past month. It traded at 1.2079 at its 52-week high and averaged 1.1588 for 2026 so far, against 1.1276 in 2025. The six-month high was 1.1786 on May 9. At 1.1215, the euro trades 7.2% below its 52-week high and just 0.9% above the October 14 low of 1.1114, its lowest level in 17 months.
The euro failed to join the rally that lifted most major currencies against the dollar on Tuesday morning. GBP/USD firmed to 1.3348 after a stronger-than-expected UK jobs report, and the yen gained as authorities watched for excessive moves. The euro lagged both. A currency that cannot rise on a weaker dollar is carrying its own problem, and in this case the problem is France.
The calendar sets the timing. The Fed decides on October 28, and the ECB decides the following day at 14:15 CET, with President Christine Lagarde’s press conference at 14:45 CET. For the first time this cycle, the ECB will vote knowing whether the rate gap with the United States has just widened again.
OAT Yields at 4.96%, Spread at 152.5 bps: The French Risk Premium
French government debt is the single largest weight on the euro. The 10-year OAT yield rose 3 basis points to 4.96% on Tuesday, after its biggest daily rise in nearly a month on Monday. The yield reached 4.9937% in early October, its highest level since July 2002. The spread over German Bunds widened 5.5 basis points to 152.5 basis points on Tuesday. It hit 158.67 basis points in early October, the widest since November 2011, at the height of the euro zone sovereign debt crisis.
The pace of the widening is what alarms currency traders. The OAT-Bund spread broke above 100 basis points in September for the first time since 2012. By October 1, it was above 130 basis points. By early October it had reached 158.67. A move of almost 60 basis points in a month is a pace matched only during the euro crisis. On Monday, the spread stood at 142.3 basis points, with the OAT at 4.85% against 3.43% for the Bund. Tuesday’s jump to 152.5 basis points erased most of the recent stabilization.
The political trigger is visible on the streets. Protest groups announced a new round of demonstrations for Saturday, and recent street violence included the burning of Limoges city hall. The National Assembly votes on the budget on October 20 and October 27, which puts two fiscal decision points inside the same window as the Fed and ECB meetings. Long-term investors have stepped back ahead of the vote, and market depth in French debt has fallen to less than half its normal level.
The broader bond move adds to the pressure. Since the start of the Hormuz crisis, 10-year OAT yields have risen 150 basis points, against 115 basis points for U.S. Treasuries. France is the hardest hit in the global bond sell-off, mostly because of its own fiscal and political problems. Realized volatility in the OAT spread has jumped to the 90th percentile.
The currency channel is direct. When foreign investors sell French bonds, they sell euros. When the spread widens, it signals that investors see rising fiscal and political risk in France relative to Germany, and that risk feeds into the single currency. A spread of 150 basis points is widely treated as a tipping point. Above it, the risk of contagion into Italian and Spanish debt rises, along with the pressure on the ECB to respond.
The euro’s weakness this month maps closely onto the spread. EUR/USD hit its October low of 1.1114 as the spread approached its peak and recovered to 1.1269 last Friday as it narrowed. Tuesday’s widening to 152.5 basis points coincided with the euro’s slide back to 1.1182.
ECB Deposit Rate 2.50% vs Fed Funds 3.75% to 4.00%
The second weight on the euro is the policy gap. The ECB deposit rate stands at 2.50%, where it has been since September 16, after a quarter-point hike on September 10. The main refinancing rate sits at 2.65% and the marginal lending rate at 2.90%. The Fed funds target range stands at 3.75% to 4.00%. The gap between the two policy rates is between 125 and 150 basis points, and it favors the dollar.
The ECB has been tightening, but slowly. It raised rates in June for the first time since 2023, taking the deposit rate to 2.25%, and became the first major central bank to hike in response to the Middle East war. The September move took it to 2.50%. Lagarde has stressed that the bank is not pre-committing to a path and will decide meeting by meeting. She has also said she sees no signs of second-round inflation effects yet.
The Fed has been tightening faster. The September hike was its first in three years. Futures now price an 82% chance of a hold at the October 27 and 28 meeting and an 89% chance of a hike in December. If the Fed hikes in December and the ECB does not, the gap widens to between 150 and 175 basis points.
Bond yields tell the same story at longer maturities. The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield traded at 5.10% on Tuesday. The German 10-year Bund yielded 3.43% on Monday and edged lower on Tuesday. That leaves a U.S.-German 10-year spread of 167 basis points. Every basis point of that spread is a reason for global investors to hold dollars rather than euros.
Forward pricing reflects the carry. The one-week forward rate for EUR/USD stands at 1.1242, the one-month at 1.1255, the three-month at 1.1284, the six-month at 1.1327 and the one-year at 1.1416. Those forward rates sit above spot because U.S. rates are higher than euro rates. They measure the interest-rate differential, not an expectation that the euro will rise.
Lagarde has added a twist to the policy debate. She said long-term interest rates have climbed since the September meeting, which will slow growth and reduce the pass-through of energy costs by more than the ECB projected. In effect, she counted the bond market selloff as part of the tightening. Currency traders read that as a signal of fewer ECB hikes, and therefore a smaller rate lift for the euro against a dollar backed by the Fed’s higher policy rate.
Euro Area Inflation Hit 3.8% in September, the Highest in Two Years
Inflation is the reason the ECB cannot step back, and it is the strongest argument for the euro bulls. Euro area annual inflation accelerated to 3.8% in September from 3.2% in August, above the 3.6% forecast. That reading is the highest in the past 24 months. Monthly inflation ran at 0.6%, up from 0.4% in August. Core inflation, which excludes energy and food, rose to 2.5% from 2.4%, in line with expectations.
Energy is driving the headline. Energy inflation in the euro area reached 18.8% in September, up from 14.3% in August. The euro area imports most of its oil and gas, so Brent at $106 to $111 hits European consumers and businesses harder than American ones. Germany’s annual inflation rose to 3.3% from 2.9%, its highest in two years. Austria hit 3.5% and Greece 5.1%.
The ECB’s own forecasts show how persistent the problem is. The bank kept its 2026 inflation forecast at 3.0% but revised its projections higher for 2027 and 2028, to 2.5% and 2.1%. Consumer inflation expectations stood at 3.0% in August, and three-year expectations rose to 2.9%. With headline inflation nearly twice the 2% target, the bank has little room to stop hiking.
The core figure is the one that matters for the October 29 decision. Core inflation is closer to the second-round effects Lagarde has said the ECB has not seen yet. A core reading of 2.5% sits at the edge of that line. If core accelerates further, the measured approach to hiking will be tested.
Inflation helps the euro only if it forces the ECB to tighten faster than the Fed. That is the bull case: a hawkish ECB surprise on October 29, paired with a Fed that holds on October 28, would narrow the rate gap and lift the euro. Markets do not price that scenario. Expectations for further ECB tightening point to December rather than October, with an October move possible but unlikely. Earlier in the cycle, the market priced only an 11.7% probability of an October hike.
The risk for the euro is that inflation stays high while growth weakens. Energy at 18.8% eats into household spending, and higher bond yields raise borrowing costs for governments and companies. That combination of high inflation and slowing growth is the stagflation scenario, and it is negative for any currency because it forces the central bank to choose between fighting prices and supporting the economy.

articles.title: Back in the eye of the storm: A Trump-Putin deal would require doing more to protect Ukraine and EUrope | EPC - EPC, European Policy Centre
articles.summary: Back in the eye of the storm: A Trump-Putin deal would require doing more to protect Ukraine and EUrope | EPC  EPC, European Policy Centre
articles.full_text:
It is currently being reported that Putin, Trump and Xi Jinping will meet in November to attempt to end the conflict in Ukraine, now in its fourth year, without involving Ukrainian President Zelensky. In the light of these claims, Fabian Zuleeg revisits and updates his February 2025 exploration of Trump’s earlier ceasefire plans and finds that all his conclusions still hold: EUrope might have bought some time by appeasing Trump but we are still facing the same fundamental dilemma as we did nearly two years ago.
Peace at last?
As President-elect, Donald Trump publicly stated that he wanted to bring the war in Ukraine to an end quickly, aiming also potentially to absolve the US from its responsibility to continue to support Ukraine militarily, financially and politically. He did not succeed at the beginning of his administration, but reports suggest that he may be preparing for another try. By so imposing a ceasefire he would be ignoring that this war was started illegally by Russian aggression, that Russia committed crimes against humanity, as well as various war crimes, or that significant parts of sovereign Ukrainian territory are not only occupied by Russia but have been illegally annexed by Moscow. Making a deal and getting domestic relief for his self-inflicted high energy prices through imports from Russia are Trump’s only aims. But voices around the world believe that the most important goal is to stop the killing immediately. However, any deal must guarantee security in the longer term. If not, the conflict will return in future and is likely to escalate then.
Of course, we do not know whether Trump will be successful. Even if he makes a deal, Ukrainians might not acquiesce, given the existential nature of the threat, although it is very costly to maintain their defences without US support. It is also not clear what Putin wants; this will depend partly on the attached conditions and partly on how the war is developing with the ongoing withdrawal of US support.
Potential implications for Ukrainian and European security
The challenge for the EU and its member states will be to prepare for a working mode of managing the unreliability of Europe’s key security provider. This requires thorough “what if” preparations in Brussels and in European capitals. If Trump approaches the new potential ceasefire in his usual way, what will this mean for Ukrainian and wider European security?
In part, this will depend on the conditions attached to the ceasefire. Who will be the guarantors of any deal? Who will enforce the deal when Russia starts to disregard its provisions, as it has done in the past? Will Kyiv be given the ability to continue to build up its capabilities to resist Russian aggression? Will Ukraine become a part of the EU (now or with a credible path towards membership)? What happens to occupied territories and to sanctions on Russia?
While many in Europe and especially in Ukraine will not believe in such a ceasefire, they must try to set at least some guardrails for the conditions under which it could be agreed and regarding the role of the EU and its members in any settlement touching the very core of European security for years to come.
A ceasefire is not a lasting peace
It is important to emphasise that this is a discussion around ceasefire, not peace. Whatever is achieved now will most likely be an interlude before the next act of Russian aggression – we have been here before. Putin is unlikely to resist the temptation to pick off an already weakened Ukraine if he is not deterred from doing so. It will not be so much a frozen conflict as a temporarily paused one. Even more worryingly, Russia will, sooner or later, turn its eye to other victims. Moldova and Georgia, even the Baltic States, have long been in the firing line of Russian covert warfare and might be next in Putin’s expansionist path, in addition to continued Russian meddling in Europe, Africa and the Middle East. His continuing close alliance with North Korea links the conflict into the Asia-Pacific region.
In addition, a Russian victory would signal to the world that the only guarantor for independence and territorial integrity is nuclear weapons, leading to nuclear proliferation across the board. It would also bury any idea of upholding the UN Charter in future, creating greater insecurity by casting doubt on the independence and borders of all countries with a strong aggressive neighbour.
Putin will also not stop pursuing his stated aim to reverse some of the repercussions of the end of the Soviet Union, continuing to threaten the Baltic States, as well as the whole of NATO’s Eastern flank. With a perceived weakening of the commitment of the US to European security, the temptation to crank up the covert warfare that is already impinging on Western sovereignty will increase. While it is unlikely that he would seek a military confrontation in the short term, a continual testing of the West’s defences strongly increases the risk of a potentially catastrophic accident. In the medium term, it should not be forgotten that Putin’s Russia is expansionist by nature, seeking domination over its neighbourhood. In a few years’ time, Russia will have recovered militarily and might well surpass its pre-war capabilities in a number of areas. Eventually, the next confrontation will become inevitable.
A conditional deal
A ceasefire at this moment in time under these conditions is bad for Ukrainian and European security, as well as for global stability. Rather than resolving the situation and reducing human suffering, it vastly increases the risk of a future confrontation, with even more catastrophic outcomes. But, given the US president’s plans and objectives, it is the most likely next stage in Russia’s long-running war against free Europe.
So, what can the EU and its member states do?
While we could, and should, have done more to support Ukraine to comprehensively win the war, this has been beyond reach for some time. In the near future, it is about damage limitation. This means ensuring that any ceasefire deal contains as many favourable conditions for Ukraine as possible, including credible security guarantees. This must be done in close coordination with Kyiv. At the same time, there should be no limitations enshrined in the deal for Ukraine to arm itself or to be armed, or on any technology Ukraine needs. And Europe should be willing to put boots on the ground in case of a ceasefire; it is the only way to ensure such a ceasefire would hold.
EU membership, or a credible path and timeline to membership, should also be part of the deal, at the very least ensuring that Russia does not exercise a veto on Ukraine’s European future. However, it does not seem that this is a Trumpian priority, given his disdain for multilateral institutions in general and the EU in particular. The Union should nevertheless put this on the table, although it is unclear whether the political will within exists.
Any easing of sanctions should be contingent on the return of illegally occupied territory, as well as mandating the use of Russian funds for reconstruction, which many in the US also advocate, although there is likely to be strong pushback from Russia. Other conditions, linked to Ukraine’s Peace Formula, such as returning prisoners of war, as well as the Ukrainian children abducted by Russia, guaranteeing free passage through the Black Sea and provisions to guarantee nuclear safety all need to be part of the deal. The complete withdrawal of all 8,500 North Korean troops must also be part of any ceasefire.
Putin might not be willing to accept these conditions, but if this leads to a breakdown in negotiations between Trump and Putin, so much the better. However, chances are that in return for a favourable ceasefire, Putin will accept many conditions, even if he intends to break them later on. The challenge will be to ensure that Trump includes these conditions in his dealings with Putin. Appealing to his vanity might help: Trump always needs to win, so if the “best deal ever” is presented as being dependent on these conditions, it might induce him to push for them, i.e. his deal is “great” if, and only if, these conditions are included.
A crucial battleground for EUrope and Ukraine will be US domestic politics. Trump might be constrained in his actions, given that there are many in the US who are opposed to a US–Russia deal. This might become even more salient after the mid-term elections.
Europe will have to do more, not less, in case of a ceasefire
Much of what will need to be delivered under a ceasefire will have to come from Europe, including a commitment to a further continuous strengthening of Ukrainian armed forces and significant funding and risk guarantees for Ukrainian reconstruction. Europe must continue to further strengthen its defence industry, so that it is able to produce the weapons required to defend itself against an expansionist Russia, as well as buying more US weapons. European defence spending will need to continue to rise substantially, consistent with NATO’s June 2025 commitment to invest the equivalent of 5% of GDP in defence and security by 2035. This may entail borrowing more both at national and EU level, potentially also outside the current Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) given the time pressure to strengthen EU capabilities in the immediate future. In many instances, Europe will be expected to sacrifice its economic interest in return for a continuation of the US security guarantee, albeit that this guarantee will be more tentative under Trump than under previous presidents.
As a result, should a Trump-imposed ceasefire become a reality, Europe will have to do – and commit – more rather than less. Europe must listen to the countries bordering Russia, and to Ukraine in particular, to apprehend the nature of Putin’s Russia and the continuous and increasing threat it poses, given the border countries’ correct assessment in the past. articles.title: The ECB annual report 2026: EU Parliament has a chance to ask better questions - PositiveMoney
articles.summary: The ECB annual report 2026: EU Parliament has a chance to ask better questions  PositiveMoney
articles.full_text:

Registered number 07253015.
Registered office: Positive Money c/o New Economics Foundation: 10 Salamanca Place, London SE1 7HB.
T: +44 207 253 0735 
info@positivemoney.org.uk
A resolution that misses the moment: our take on the EU Parliament's draft report on the ECB
This year’s European Parliament draft resolution on the ECB overlooks key threats to price stability, from Europe’s dependence on imported fossil fuels to growing climate risks. We look at what’s missing and how Parliament could push the ECB to better address these challenges while strengthening its democratic accountability.
Every year, one moment keeps us busy at Positive Money Europe: the European Parliament's resolution on the ECB annual report. It isn't legislation, but it matters. It's one of the few times the only directly elected EU institution gets to scrutinise a powerful, technocratic body like the European Central Bank (ECB) and say what it expects of it.
This year's draft, led by MEP Georgios Aftias from the centre-right European People's Party, has some good elements - but it feels detached from what many people across Europe are living through, and in many places are protesting about: a high cost of living that is driven largely by energy and fuel prices, and supply chains shaken by climate-related extreme events.
What the draft says, and what it leaves out
The text puts weight on the ECB’s mandate to maintain price stability - which is right and very relevant with inflation rising again. However, the ECB's secondary mandate is missing entirely. Beyond price stability, and without compromising it, the ECB is also required to support the EU's general economic policies, including sustainable development, full employment, social progress and the green transition.
The draft expresses concern about the cost of living for low-income households, as food and energy prices have climbed since the crisis in the Middle East. We share that concern, of course - but we are also concerned that the draft stops at just describing the problem.
It mentions geopolitical uncertainty and energy security risks, but it doesn’t name what links them: Europe's dependence on imported fossil fuels. As long as Europe relies on fuels priced on global markets, wars and conflicts driven by decisions in other capitals will keep feeding straight into energy bills and supermarket prices. People have gone from one price shock to the next since 2022, and by now these shocks should be predictable - and a report on price stability should say so.
The draft also says little about what renewables could do to keep prices stable over the long term. Producing more energy at home makes prices less dependent on global fuel markets, so renewables are a price stability issue as well as a climate one. That is exactly the kind of long-term view we would expect in a report on the ECB's mandate.
Sadly, in this year’s resolution there is also a renewed mention of market neutrality - the idea that the ECB should mirror the existing composition of financial markets when buying assets or accepting collateral, rather than favouring certain sectors or activities. The draft insists the ECB respect it "in all of its monetary operations at all times". It is a principle the ECB itself has said isn't in the Treaties, and one it no longer follows in practice, as its climate factor on collateral shows. The ECB's own legal analysis is clear: an open market economy does not commit the ECB to an "absolute operational concept" of market neutrality. ECB Board member Isabel Schnabel has also addressed the question in a speech.
On a more positive note, the draft backs the digital euro as essential for Europe's monetary sovereignty, stresses that cash must stay, and welcomes Pontes, the Eurosystem's first step towards making central bank money fit for a tokenised future. We welcome all of this.
Where the report should go further
The good news is that the text can still be improved.
Everything we're asking for starts from the same place: the energy shock. Inflation has been rising again in the euro area since April. Eurostat has since confirmed that it reached 3.8% in September, with energy prices up 18.8% on the year. As the ECB itself has acknowledged, this comes from Middle East-related shocks to oil, petroleum products and gas. Almost 60% of the EU's energy needs are met through imports of these fuels, so global price spikes land directly on European households and businesses. We saw the same thing in 2022. ECB Executive Board member Frank Elderson has warned that repeated energy shocks can turn temporary price rises into lasting ones. We think MEPs should say this clearly: imported fossil fuels are the main driver of current inflation and a structural threat to price stability.
Climate adds to the picture. The ECB expects food inflation to keep rising throughout 2027, partly because of this summer's heatwaves and the ongoing El Niño. Extreme weather is becoming more frequent, and research shows global warming could make El Niño more intense. Nature loss, such as soil depletion and water scarcity, still makes food production more fragile. A report about price stability should recognise that climate and nature-related risks are part of the story.
If fossil fuel dependence is the problem, renewables are part of the solution, and the evidence is there.
Research commissioned by the European Parliament itself finds a strong link between how much a country relies on fossil fuels and how much its inflation rises when fuel prices spike. Our own analysis finds that renewables cut wholesale electricity prices in Europe by an average of 24.4% between 2023 and 2025, compared to a scenario without them.
This is where monetary policy comes in. Clean energy needs large upfront investment, so it is far more sensitive to interest rates than gas-fired generation, where fuel costs matter more. In our analysis, raising rates from 2% to 6% pushes up the cost of electricity from solar with battery storage by 33%, against just 3.7% for natural gas. Across-the-board rate hikes can therefore make the clean investments that would protect us from future shocks more expensive, and prolong our exposure to volatile fossil fuel markets. That is bad news for price stability in the long run. We would like the Parliament to ask the ECB to assess how its decisions affect energy resilience, and to look at tools like green refinancing operations - meaning targeted lending operations tied to banks' lending to renewables and green transition projects. These could protect energy transition investments from higher financing costs, and would serve both the ECB's primary and secondary mandates.
There are two other important points.
On the digital euro, years of delay are enough. The legislation should move forward quickly so Europeans can benefit from a public digital means of payment that complements cash and reduces dependence on private, non-European payment providers.
The draft rightly calls the digital euro essential for Europe's monetary sovereignty, and this is now even more urgent: to preserve the EU's strategic autonomy, and the financial autonomy of its institutions and citizens, in the face of sanctions imposed by foreign powers. The US sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC) show what is at stake: European banks, caught between Washington's penalties and their own clients, can end up putting foreign sanctions compliance ahead of EU rules and interests.
On ECB leadership, the draft is silent, despite important changes ahead. The terms of three of the ECB's six Executive Board members expire in 2027, opening the way for a significant reshaping of the institution's leadership. These appointments are decided by EU governments, with Parliament consulted but having no power to block a candidate. Its hearings are therefore among the few opportunities for public scrutiny of a selection process that remains largely behind closed doors. Parliament should use this moment to call for a more transparent and open process, and for a Board that better reflects Europe's diversity in gender, education and professional background. That would strengthen both the ECB's legitimacy and its accountability to the public.
What's next
This draft is a starting point, and there is still time to improve it. Positive Money Europe will continue to work with MEPs as the report moves through Parliament, and we hope the final resolution will reflect what people are facing today: energy-driven prices, a changing climate, and a central bank whose decisions affect some people and businesses far more than others.

articles.title: Putin and Zelenskyy back three-way US peace talks on Ukraine - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Putin and Zelenskyy back three-way US peace talks on Ukraine  Al JazeeraMissiles hit Kyiv after Russia agrees to US call to resume Ukraine peace talks  BBCUkraine war briefing: New peace proposals lack ‘substance’, says Kremlin after Witkoff-Putin meeting in Russia  The GuardianWitkoff salutes ‘humanitarian’ Putin  The TelegraphPutin agrees to resume 3-way peace talks with Ukraine and US  Reuters
articles.full_text:
Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy have both expressed support for a United States proposal to hold three-way talks to end the conflict in Ukraine.
The Kremlin said Putin conveyed his “in principle” willingness to engage in negotiations during a meeting in St Petersburg with US special envoy Steve Witkoff on Wednesday.
Speaking to journalists via WhatsApp as he returned to Kyiv from Norway, Zelenskyy confirmed Ukraine’s interest in the talks, which he said should take place no later than early November.
Zelenskyy added that he had spoken with US officials following Witkoff’s discussions with Putin.
“We have received feedback that… Russia supports a trilateral meeting at the level of our [negotiating] teams,” Zelenskyy said.
“The American side has proposed holding it as soon as possible and we support that… The Ukrainian side has been in contact with its American partners. They will do everything to ensure that the meeting takes place as early as possible, in November. I think no later than early November.”
Zelenskyy said Kyiv supports “any proposals for a ceasefire, an end to the war, an energy ceasefire as well as humanitarian initiatives”.
The diplomatic effort comes as Washington pushes for an end to the war in Ukraine, which began more than four and a half years ago with Moscow’s full-scale invasion.
Witkoff held talks with Putin on Wednesday after meeting with Ukrainian and European officials in Norway a day earlier.
“Steve Witkoff briefed Vladimir Putin on the substance of the talks held in Oslo,” Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters, referring to talks Witkoff held in Norway with Ukrainian and European officials on Tuesday.
“He mentioned some new aspects in the approaches of the Europeans and Kyiv … but there wasn’t really much substance in them.”
“Our president informed Steve Witkoff that we are, in principle, ready to resume the mentioned talks [with Washington and Kyiv],” he added, saying they could take place in mid-November.
He later told Russian state television Vesti that the talks may be held in Abu Dhabi.
The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February before the United States and Israel launched a war against Iran.
Goodwill gesture
The three-hour talks in a grand imperial palace in St Petersburg, the ninth time that Witkoff has met Putin in person, began with a goodwill gesture from Russia – the release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired US teacher held in Russia.
Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova, reporting from Moscow, said Russia is obviously interested in the lifting of international sanctions, and US sanctions in particular.
“The Trump administration is using economic leverage to encourage Moscow to finish this war, including the temporary lifting of US sanctions on Russian diesel sales,” she said.
Putin also thanked US President Donald Trump and Witkoff for their efforts to end the war.
Ukraine and Russia remain far apart when it comes to the terms of any possible peace deal, but Trump has recently intensified pressure on Ukraine to “make a deal”. He said on Tuesday that it was time for Ukraine to end the war or face “a very bad thing”.
Putin also offered to help Trump in dealing with Iran, saying Moscow had a decades-long relationship with Tehran, which it has repeatedly offered to leverage to address US concerns about Iran’s nuclear programme.
Russia could also supply large quantities of fertiliser to the US to help farmers, Putin told Witkoff.
A potential meeting in China next month with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping was also discussed. The Kremlin said Beijing was already preparing what it said would be the first trilateral meeting of its kind in history.
Oslo talks
The talks in Russia come a day after Witkoff met Ukraine’s Zelenskyy and European leaders in Norway. Witkoff briefed Putin on the Oslo talks, which he described as productive and said had been characterised by “some degree of momentum”.
The prime ministers of Norway and Finland also attended the talks in Oslo. Representatives from the European Union and NATO were present. Following Tuesday’s talks, Zelenskyy said that “very, very important” intelligence from the US had been restored.
US-Ukraine ties have deteriorated sharply since Trump announced a diesel export deal with Russia earlier this month.
Zelenskyy has also accused Washington of slowing down the internet service Starshield, which is crucial for Ukraine’s battlefield operations. Starshield is the military-grade equivalent of Starlink – both developed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.
As diplomatic efforts intensify, Russia and Ukraine continue to trade long-range attacks.
At least one person was killed and two were wounded in a Ukrainian drone attack in Russia’s western Bryansk region on Wednesday, Governor Yegor Kovalchuk said on Telegram.
The Ukrainian emergency service said two people were killed in a Russian attack on a high-rise building in the Sviatoshynskyi district of the capital, Kyiv.

articles.title: Europe’s far right seizes on protest violence to push authoritarian anti-immigration agenda - The Guardian
articles.summary: Europe’s far right seizes on protest violence to push authoritarian anti-immigration agenda  The GuardianKatya Adler: France divided over who to blame for riots and what to learn from them  BBCThe mob is coming to Britain, and the police are woefully unprepared  The TelegraphWho are the Black Bloc?  Financial Times‘I am still traumatised’: French police accused of brutalising minors  Al Jazeera
articles.full_text:
Europe’s far-right leaders have jumped on the violence that rocked numerous cities last weekend, framing it as the inevitable consequence of failed liberal governance and open-border policies and insisting only they can restore law and order.
Months away from key elections in Spain, France and Italy, authoritarian nationalists are eager to weaponise the wave of street unrest, originating in peaceful protests over the cost of living and deteriorating public services but hijacked by violent rioters.
Those in opposition have not held back. In France, where cities such as Paris, Marseille and Lyon faced widespread rioting and looting, the far-right National Rally (RN) has denounced centrist incompetence and promised a crackdown.
The party’s president, Jordan Bardella, said the government was “impotent”. The RN leader, Marine Le Pen, said on Wednesday the state was “collapsing” and had “lost control of everything” amid “migratory, budgetary and security chaos”.
Ahead in presidential polls and seeking voters beyond her base, Le Pen has resisted explicitly racialising the unrest, but has framed it more broadly as a result of state and policy failures leading to “anarchic immigration” and “a total loss of authority”.
In Germany – where there were no major protests – the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has stoked fears rioting could spill over the border. Its co-leader Alice Weidel said France’s “violent excesses” were a “warning for Germany”.
Weidel also linked the unrest to immigration, posting: “The dangerous mix of mass migration and leftwing extremism threatens to lead to civil war-like conditions here too … There will only be a turnaround on migration with the AfD!”
In Portugal, populists have used peaceful protests to blame immigration for the country’s housing crisis, which André Ventura of the far-right Chega party said was chiefly a consequence of an “uncontrolled influx of people from abroad”.
In Spain, where the housing crisis has led to huge protests and a Madrid encampment, and prompted the socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, to call a snap election next month, the far-right Vox party has sought to demonise the protesters. “They’re not defending the right to housing, or asking for work, they’re serving Pedro Sánchez,” the party’s leader, Santiago Abascal, said. “They’re Sánchez’s militias.”
Vox has also attempted to link the housing issue to migration. In a message posted on social media last month, the party falsely suggested that the 87-year-old woman whose eviction sparked the mammoth protests would have had a home had she been an immigrant from north Africa.
In Belgium, where cost of living protests also escalated into street clashes in Brussels and Liège, the far-right Flemish nationalists of Vlaams Belang framed the rioting as a failure of integration and open borders, characterising it as “imported violence”.
Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, has adopted another strategy – as head of a far-right government she has headed for four years, she cannot simply blame failures of the state. Instead, she has expanded her law-and-order agenda, and framed rioters as extremists.
“Demonstrating is a right, but setting our cities ablaze is not,” Meloni said after rioting in Milan and Bologna. “Hooligans have exploited the protests to sow chaos, attack those responsible for ensuring security, and hold entire cities hostage.”
Meloni has previously enacted sweeping security measures aimed at hindering public dissent, including jail terms for blocking roads, tough sentences for resisting police officers, and pre-detention for demonstrators thought likely to cause trouble.
This week she passed emergency decrees creating an offence of violent participation in a demonstration, imposing tougher penalties on rioters and organisers of violent groups, and penalising parents whose children take part in vandalism and looting.
But she too has highlighted immigration as a factor, noting that “nearly half of those stopped or arrested” after the Milan riots were “of immigrant background, including individuals born abroad and second-generation children of immigrant families”.
Beyond Europe’s orthodox far-right parties, anti-immigration polemicists have gone further, interpreting the violence not as state and policy failures but as evidence of a looming civilisational war fuelled by multiculturalism and non-EU immigration.
Éric Zemmour, the founder of France’s Reconquête! (Reconquest) party, demanded an immigration halt and the deportation of “foreign delinquents”, declaring: “These are not riots, but the warning shots in an ethnic war. Either we establish absolute order or we yield.”
The far-right narrative has been reinforced by similar comments from the US, where both the president and vice-president have sought to turn the unrest in France in particular into a cautionary tale for voters before midterm elections.
Donald Trump described France as a once-great nation that had been “conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and communists”, adding on social media that immigration “has shattered that once great country”.
JD Vance echoed the same view, saying: “Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion.” In doing so, they “ignored fundamental questions about assimilation and compatibility”, he said.
Deborah Cole in Berlin, Angela Giuffrida in Rome and Sam Jones in Madrid contributed reporting

articles.title: Trade 'defense' risks becoming a subsidy for EU's inefficiency - China Daily
articles.summary: Trade 'defense' risks becoming a subsidy for EU's inefficiency  China Daily
articles.full_text:
Although German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told reporters on Monday that "we do not want a trade war with China", he was quick to add that at last week's European Union summit in Brussels the 27 member states had been strikingly united on a range of trade and economic issues, ranging from "industrial subsidies" and "manufacturing capacity" to "currency exchange rate" and "trade surplus", that he has repeatedly laid at China's doorstep.
Earlier this month he joined France's president, Emmanuel Macron, in advocating so-called stronger "defense" instruments.
Protection can redistribute economic pain but it cannot manufacture competitiveness. This is the central contradiction in the EU's China trade policy. The EU complains that Chinese manufacturers are too competitive, then proposes measures that would make goods more expensive for European consumers and businesses. Tariffs might protect particular factories, but they also raise costs for downstream industries, delay the green transition and reduce pressure on domestic producers to innovate. Europe's industrial troubles have deeper roots: expensive energy, fragmented capital markets, sluggish investment and a regulatory environment that often makes scaling innovation unnecessarily difficult. None will be remedied by restricting Chinese imports. Indeed, European manufacturers depend on Chinese components, materials and markets. A trade war would therefore disrupt the very industrial ecosystem Brussels claims it seeks to defend. Treating Chinese products' competitiveness as proof of "unfairness" risks turning trade "defense" into a permanent subsidy for European inefficiency.
Fortunately, diplomacy has already produced an alternative. Earlier this month, China and the EU reached understandings during trade and investment consultations in Beijing. Their significance lies in the possibility of replacing reciprocal "defense" with reciprocal accommodations.
Brussels should now concentrate on implementing its part of those commitments. That includes addressing restrictions on dual-use goods exports, improving investment conditions and advancing workable arrangements on trade remedies. The objective should be to expand mutually beneficial commerce, not merely redistribute an existing trade surplus.
A trade deficit is not, by itself, evidence of exploitation. It reflects differences in production, demand, savings and competitiveness. Restricting imports does not create corresponding exports. If the EU wants to sell more to China, improving its products' competitiveness and removing unnecessary restrictions on what it can sell would be more productive than erecting barriers against what it buys.
China has reinforced this argument through intensive diplomacy. Since Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi spoke with his German counterpart, Johann Wadephul, on Sept 21, he has engaged multiple European officials. His recent visits to Croatia, Montenegro and Bulgaria involved discussions with presidents, prime ministers and foreign ministers about investment, infrastructure, technology and trade.
In Sofia, capital of Bulgaria, on Monday, Wang emphasized trust, friendship, cooperation and partnership. Across the three dimensions of state-to-state relations, regional cooperation, and China-EU relations — which develop in parallel and reinforce one another — the core focus is the cultivation of partnerships. Overall, the China-EU relationship is healthy and stable. Differences regarding economic and trade issues have emerged as cooperation has continued to evolve; these can, and should be resolved through dialogue, without undermining the broader China-EU ties.
To that end, trust should serve as the cornerstone of peace, friendship as a precious asset, cooperation as a robust driving force, and partnership as a shared objective.
Merz is right to reject a trade war. But he is plainly talking out of both sides of his mouth. He essentially fears the damage a China-EU trade war would inflict on Germany, yet refuses to acknowledge that Germany, if not the EU, has structural challenges of its own to fix. So he is left oscillating between a carrot and a stick.
Brussels has negotiated a path toward practical accommodation with Beijing. It should follow the path before protectionism becomes a substitute for structural reform.

articles.title: “Deregulation Spurs Investment”: Europe’s AI Ecosystem Gains Momentum as Defense Startups Advance Amid Rearmament - https://economy.ac/
articles.summary: “Deregulation Spurs Investment”: Europe’s AI Ecosystem Gains Momentum as Defense Startups Advance Amid Rearmament  https://economy.ac/
articles.full_text:
Authored On
Modified
Nvidia expands investment in AI startups across Europe, including Germany, France and the UK
EU lays groundwork for industry growth by easing AI regulations, boosting fundraising by local technology companies
Europe’s rearmament drives a surge in demand for defense AI, accelerating growth at drone and autonomous weapons startups
Nvidia is committing substantial funding to Europe’s technology ecosystem. With the European Union (EU) recently delaying the application of high-risk artificial intelligence (AI) regulations and easing some administrative burdens, rapidly growing investment in AI startups is gradually improving growth conditions for European technology companies. Alongside rising defense spending across Europe, investor demand is also spreading to industries where AI technologies are being commercialized rapidly, including defense and robotics.
Nvidia’s European Investment Strategy
According to US business news outlet CNBC on the 20th (all dates hereafter local time), Nvidia announced plans to invest in four German startups at the Invest in Germany Summit held in Berlin, Germany, the previous day. The investment targets are AI-powered robotics developer Agile Robots, hospital information management software developer Avelios Medical, AI-based audiovisual generation company Mirelo, and satellite design and manufacturing company Reflex Aerospace. This is part of Nvidia’s announced plan to invest USD 10 billion (approximately USD 10.2 billion) in companies, universities and research institutions across Europe. Investment amounts for individual companies were not disclosed.
Nvidia has also recently announced a series of investment expansions in European countries beyond Germany. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang previously unveiled plans in France to invest in four local startups and discussed expanding AI infrastructure and developing technology with French President Emmanuel Macron. In the UK, the company announced plans to invest in five advanced technology startups working in areas including AI drug discovery, infrastructure forecasting and quantum computing, and pledged to provide USD 250 million (approximately USD 255 million) worth of computing resources for AI safety research over the next five years. In Sweden, it plans to partner with a local foundation to establish an AI innovation hub supporting healthcare and climate startups, while strengthening its collaboration with Volvo Cars on autonomous driving technology.
Europe’s Once-Frozen AI Market
Market observers are taking note of the rapid pickup in European AI investment. Concerns have long persisted in Europe that a lack of investment and gaps in technology infrastructure could leave the region behind the United States and China in the AI race. For example, at the Hofburg Dialogue in Vienna, Austria, last month, European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde noted, “Last year, the United States developed 59 notable AI models and China developed 35, while the UK and France produced only one each,” adding that “the scale of AI investment being poured in by the United States and China differs greatly from Europe’s.” She also said, “The United States accounts for 75% of global AI computing capacity through its data centers, while Europe accounts for just 5%,” stressing the urgent need to expand computing capacity to keep pace with rising demand.
Institutions have offered similar assessments. In a contribution by Richard Windsor published in April through Telecom Expert Voices, global telecommunications and digital industry research firm Strand Consult described Europe’s AI competitiveness as little more than a “rounding error” in the global market. French AI company Mistral is pursuing plans to build a data center with approximately 200 megawatts (MW) of capacity and deploy 13,800 GB300 chips, but this was assessed as markedly insufficient compared with the United States and the Middle East. Strand Consult identified the regulatory environment and industry culture as key reasons for the weakness of Europe’s AI industry. In particular, it argued that the EU’s AI Act constrains business activity by preemptively regulating an industry that has yet to take shape.
AI Act Raises Regulatory Barriers
The AI Act is the world’s first comprehensive AI regulatory law. Its core approach is to classify AI systems into four risk levels—unacceptable risk, high risk, limited risk and minimal risk—and apply differentiated regulations. High-risk AI includes systems that could significantly affect individuals’ fundamental rights or safety, such as recruitment and personnel evaluations, education and critical infrastructure operations. Companies developing these technologies must fulfill various obligations, including establishing risk management systems, managing training data quality, preparing technical documentation and retaining system operation logs. They must also undergo conformity assessments before launching products. Penalties for violations are stringent. Using prohibited AI technologies can result in fines of up to EUR 35 million (approximately USD 40 million) or 7% of worldwide annual revenue, whichever is higher. Violations of key obligations concerning high-risk AI can result in penalties of up to EUR 15 million (approximately USD 16.9 million) or 3% of revenue.
The problem is that compliance with these regulations requires substantial spending and specialized personnel. Large technology companies can respond through dedicated legal, security and quality management teams, but early-stage startups with limited capital and staff must devote additional resources to data verification, risk assessments and regulatory documentation, separate from technology development. Developers of high-risk AI, in particular, must meet the relevant obligations before launching products and may face heavy pressure from commercialization delays and rising costs associated with certification preparation and regulatory compliance. This delays the launch of new services and revenue generation, while also making it harder to secure follow-on investment.
Table 1. EU Measures to Ease AI Regulations
| Category | Key Details | 
|---|---|
| High-Risk AI | Postpone implementation of regulations for standalone systems involving biometrics, recruitment, education and critical infrastructure until December 2027 | 
| AI Embedded in Products | Postpone implementation of regulations for systems embedded in products such as machinery, toys, elevators and medical devices until August 2028 | 
| Easing Business Burdens | Extend simplified procedures for AI literacy and database registration requirements for small and medium-sized enterprises to some mid-sized companies | 
| Testing Support | Expand national regulatory sandboxes and introduce a joint EU-level sandbox | 
| Addressing Overlapping Regulations | Reduce overlapping application of the AI Act and product-specific safety regulations, and simplify conformity assessment procedures | 
| Maintaining Safety Regulations | Ban AI that generates nonconsensual synthetic sexual content or child sexual abuse material, and maintain transparency obligations for chatbots and AI-generated content | 
Startups Stir as Policy Direction Shifts
Recently, however, the EU’s policy direction has also begun to change. In July, the EU brought into force an amendment simplifying the AI Act and postponed the implementation of key provisions on high-risk AI, originally scheduled to take effect this August, until December 2027. High-risk AI embedded in products such as machinery and toys was granted a grace period until August 2028. The decision reflected concerns that imposing uniform compliance obligations on companies while technical standards and detailed guidance remained delayed could unnecessarily increase development costs and disrupt product commercialization. The EU also introduced measures to reduce administrative burdens on businesses, including extending some simplified regulatory procedures beyond small and medium-sized enterprises to mid-sized companies.
Against this backdrop, European AI startups have begun stepping up fundraising and business expansion. According to the “2026 Sifted AI 100,” released on the 15th by European technology publication Sifted, European AI startups have raised a cumulative EUR 29.6 billion (approximately USD 33.9 billion) this year, more than twice the total raised last year. Growth has been particularly pronounced among companies developing AI technologies tailored to specific industries, including healthcare, finance and industrial automation. Of the 100 promising European AI startups selected by Sifted, 51 were industry-specific AI companies. The number of companies applying AI to physical environments, including robotics, also rose from 11 last year to 14.
Investment Also Picks Up in Defense
The advance of European AI startups is also evident in the defense industry. As European countries increase defense spending following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and accelerate efforts to acquire advanced military technologies such as drones and autonomous weapons systems, funding is flowing into emerging defense companies that use AI. According to the NATO Innovation Fund and market research firm Dealroom, European startups in defense, security and resilience raised USD 8.7 billion (approximately USD 8.85 billion) in venture investment last year, up 55% from the previous year. AI-related companies accounted for 44% of the total investment.
A prominent example of this trend is German defense AI startup Helsing. Founded in 2021, Helsing has developed AI software that analyzes battlefield data to support military decision-making, and has recently expanded into AI-powered unmanned attack aircraft and autonomous fighter aircraft. In July, it raised USD 1.8 billion (approximately USD 1.83 billion) from investors including Dragoneer Investment Group and Lightspeed Venture Partners, at a valuation of USD 18 bill

articles.summary: Armenia Appeals to Eurasian Economic Union for Removal of Russian Trade Restrictions  The Moscow Times
articles.full_text:
Armenia has asked the Moscow-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) to designate Russia’s growing trade restrictions on Armenian goods as illegal market barriers, the newspaper Kommersant reported Wednesday, citing the South Caucasus country’s economic minister.
Russia has issued sweeping bans on a range of Armenian products this year as Yerevan, Moscow’s historical ally, began the process of joining the European Union. Amid the mounting restrictions, the EU relaxed tariffs on around 80% of Armenian exports for the next two years.
“We consider the [Russian] restrictions against us to be unlawful,” Armenian Economy Minister Gevorg Papoyan told reporters, according to the Kommersant.
“If these restrictions are recognized as a barrier, then Russia is obliged to remove them within 30 days per EAEU procedures,” Papoyan was quoted as saying.
He added that Armenia has already submitted individual appeals to each trade restriction introduced in recent months, and in one case, it allegedly secured the support of three other members of the economic union. However, Russia has used its veto power to block those appeals, Papoyan said.
A translation of Papoyan’s comments cited by Kommersant states that the EAEU will consider Armenia’s latest, more sweeping appeal on Nov. 3. “We’ll see if there will be a tangible result,” he was quoted as saying.
Meanwhile, a joint report released Tuesday by the remaining EAEU members Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan warned that Armenia’s exit from the economic union or alignment with the EU would hit Yerevan’s trade, labor and energy markets.
Relations between Russia and Armenia have soured in recent years after neighboring Azerbaijan took control of the disputed Nagorno-Karabakh region in September 2023. Officials in Yerevan accused Russian peacekeepers of failing to protect the region and its Armenian population from advancing Azerbaijani forces during a shock offensive.

articles.summary: Düsseldorf Airport mass casualty response after 'norovirus outbreak' on flight  Daily Mirror'Medics in hazmat suits' board flight after 'several' passengers 'felt very unwell'  AOL.co.uk3 Hospitalized: Suspected Norovirus Outbreak Sparks Panic On Eurowings Flight  Simple FlyingThree Passengers Taken to Hospital After Multiple People On Eurowings Flight Succumb to Mystery Illness  PYOKAmbulances Meet Eurowings Jet From Rhodes After Passengers Feel Unwell in...
articles.full_text:
Düsseldorf Airport reportedly activated its mass casualty response after several passengers fell ill on board a Eurowings flight
Several passengers on board a Eurowings flight fell ill with suspected norovirus amid an outbreak on the Greek island of Rhodes.
Passengers began experiencing gastrointestinal symptoms during flight EW-9631 from Rhodes to Düsseldorf, Germany, on Sunday evening. The cabin crew requested a priority landing at Düsseldorf Airport, a Eurowings spokesperson said.
The airport activated its mass casualty response, according to German news site aero.de, with medics in "hazmat suits" boarding the plane as soon as it landed. Three passengers were taken to hospital.
The illnesses are believed to be linked to a norovirus outbreak on Rhodes that has been ongoing since July. Norovirus, commonly known as the winter vomiting bug, causes vomiting and diarrhoea, the NHS says.
Greek newspaper Kathimerini reported on October 2 that more than 1,400 patients with gastrointestinal symptoms linked to the norovirus had been treated at Rhodes Hospital since August 10.
At the time, the newspaper said the total number of cases recorded since mid-July was close to 1,800. However, it added that the actual figure was likely to be higher, as the total did not include patients treated by private doctors or those who had not sought hospital treatment.
Nathalie Gombik, 28, was travelling back home to Germany with her partner after a holiday when the incident unfolded.
"Seeing so many ambulances and emergency personnel in protective clothing after landing was quite shocking," she said.
"During the flight, several passengers became ill. I know for certain that three passengers were affected, but it appeared that approximately three more were also experiencing symptoms. Some passengers were vomiting during the flight."
Nathalie praised the German airline's cabin crew for remaining "calm" and "discreet" throughout the flight.
"At the time, we had no idea that a mass casualty incident had reportedly been declared, that numerous ambulances had been mobilised or that our aircraft had reportedly been given priority for landing," she added.
She said passengers had to remain on board for around 90 minutes before they were allowed to disembark.
Nathalie added that she began experiencing similar symptoms on Tuesday, two days after the flight.
A Eurowings spokesperson said: "We can confirm that several guests on Eurowings flight EW9631 from Rhodes to Dusseldorf on 18 October 2026 felt very unwell during the flight.
"The flight crew therefore requested a priority landing at Dusseldorf Airport. After landing, medical staff examined and cared for three affected guests on site. As a precaution, these guests went to hospital. All other guests continued their journeys home as normal.
"There were 212 guests and seven crew members on board. The cause of the symptoms is unclear and is being looked into. The safety and health of our guests and crews is always Eurowings' top priority."
The NHS says norovirus spreads through close contact with infected people, contaminated surfaces, infected food or water, and food prepared by someone carrying the virus. Although unpleasant, symptoms usually improve within about two days.

articles.title: Bath, Chippenham and Swindon healthcare staff go on 24-hour strike - BBC
articles.summary: Bath, Chippenham and Swindon healthcare staff go on 24-hour strike  BBCSwindon health workers strike amid fears patients are being put at risk  Yahoo News UKLIVE: Health care workers walk out over workloads and staffing levels  Swindon AdvertiserHealthcare workers in Swindon set to strike  Swindon LinkHealth services affected as 24 hour strike gets underway in Wiltshire  Wiltshire Times
articles.full_text:
Healthcare workers walk out on 24-hour strike
Healthcare workers have gone on strike in protest at workloads and staffing issues.
Staff from the HCRG Care Group in Bath, Chippenham and Swindon who are members of Unison walked out at 08:00 BST on Wednesday until 08:00 on Thursday. Patients have been told to go to appointments.
Joanne Hateley, clinical advisor and ex-nurse, was on a picket line. "I go home and I just cry some nights," she said, because "I don't feel as though I'm making a difference any more".
Ahead of the walkout, Unison ran a ballot with 85% of members voting for strike action. An HCRG Care Group spokesperson said "robust contingency plans" were in place and they recognised "the challenges colleagues have experienced".
The HCRG Care Group is a major private provider of community health and social care services and partners with the NHS and local authorities across England.
It provides community health services, urgent care, sexual health, and wellbeing support.
Picket lines took place at the Orbital in Swindon, Chippenham Community Hospital in Wiltshire and St Martin's Hospital in Bath.
Patients have been told to go to appointments as normal during the strike action.
Many of the healthcare workers told the BBC that when a Single Point of Access (SPA) system - a single phone number for all HCRG services - was introduced in April, it caused difficulties.
On the picket line in Chippenham, Lou Wilson said she had recently left her HCRG role as the pressure had become too much.
She said there had been "no structure" since the SPA was brought in.
"It's been really difficult," she said. "We just want to help the patients at the end of the day.
"We've lost a lot of staff who have not been replaced and the workload fell on the remaining staff," she said.
Beverly Batt, senior community health navigator, said things were not "being followed up", which created "stress" for staff and "concern" for patients.
"Lots of people have gone out long-term sick," she added. "And a lot of people have put in their notice because they can't deal with it any more."
Sam McKechnie, occupational therapist, handed her notice in the day before the strike.
"It's been six months of very difficult decisions and yesterday was the final straw," she said.
She also said the SPA system had caused issues for staff and patients alike.
"It gets embarrassing because as soon as you answer the phone you can see they have been on hold for 23 minutes, these are critically ill people who need help.
"The lack of staff in our team alone is getting desperate."
HCRG Care Group, previously known as Virgin Care, provides community health and social care services across Bath and North East Somerset (Banes), Swindon and Wiltshire.
The HCRG Care Group spokesperson said clinical care had not been disrupted during the strike and that work was ongoing to improve staffing levels.
They said: "We recognise the challenges colleagues have experienced since the introduction of the SPA service and appreciate how hard they have worked to establish it and improve its performance in a relatively short time.
"We have made significant improvements in response to their feedback and remain committed to constructive discussions with staff representatives.
"Our priority throughout is straightforward: patient care comes first."
