articles.title: EU should revive talks on broader China trade deal, top MEP says - Euronews.com
articles.summary: EU should revive talks on broader China trade deal, top MEP says  Euronews.com
articles.full_text:
As EU lawmakers prepare to visit Beijing, the European Parliament's trade chief is calling for a broader agreement that could revive elements of a frozen investment pact and address unfair Chinese trade practices across multiple industries.
The European Union should seek a broad trade agreement with China, potentially including investment, rather than continue negotiating over individual sectors, a senior European Parliament lawmaker said on Wednesday.
Bernd Lange, the German Socialist who chairs the Parliament's Trade Committee, made the call ahead of a visit to Beijing next week by 12 MEPs, as Brussels and China seek to ease mounting trade tensions.
The two sides reached a deal on hybrid cars on 9 October, but the EU views it as insufficient to address a trade imbalance that sees the bloc run a deficit of around €1 billion a day with China.
Brussels and Beijing previously negotiated a Comprehensive Agreement on Investment (CAI), but the European Parliament froze its ratification in 2021 after China imposed retaliatory sanctions in response to EU measures over human rights abuses.
“It is necessary to have a more comprehensive agreement,” Lange told reporters. “I'm also in favour to have an agreement quite soon. Negotiation forever make no sense.”
Lange added that the discussion should include investments. Speaking of the CAI, he also said: “Perhaps it's useful to have a look at that, specifically regarding the investment part.”
Beyond cars, a wider threat to industry
Earlier this month, the European Commission announced a deal under which China agreed to halve its hybrid car exports to the EU over the next four years.
Under the agreement, the EU will introduce country-specific quotas allowing 350,000 Chinese hybrid cars onto the European market annually, with a fixed annual adjustment rate of 6%.
The deal was presented by the Commission as a "first phase" of the negotiation which will continue on a technical level until next political talks scheduled for March 2027.
But French liberal MEP Pascal Canfin, who will join Lange on the trip, warned that the EU needs to look beyond individual industries. He argued that the Commission's negotiations on behalf of the 27 member states should address broader unfair trade practices that threaten European manufacturers across multiple sectors.
“We are open for negotiation, sector per sector, but at the same time, we look at things that it is not a sectorial threat,” Canfin said. “It's the risk of horizontal unfair practices that would have a very detrimental impact on our industries.”
During their visit to China from 27 to 29 October, EU lawmakers will meet representatives of the Chinese Ministry of commerce and members of the National People’s Congress. They are also expected to hold meetings with high-tech business representatives in Hangzhou.
Lange highlighted other issues that should be covered by a future agreement with Beijing, including Chinese export restrictions — Beijing imposes strict licensing requirements on EU businesses seeking to export rare earths, essential to European industry — unfair subsidies in the chemicals and machinery sectors, and a 20% price surcharge on EU bids in public procurement.
The EU is walking a tightrope in its relations with Beijing, pushing for dialogue while simultaneously enforcing trade defence measures to protect its industry.
Last week, EU leaders gave the Commission a political mandate to introduce unilateral quotas to protect the chemicals and machinery sectors, given the urgency of the threats posed by Chinese competition.
However, some member states, such as Spain, favour a softer approach towards Beijing, keen to secure Chinese investment.

articles.full_text:
A family-run pumpkin patch has issued a plea to visitors to stop vandalising pumpkins.
Suffolk Pumpkin Patch, in Barton Mills, reported an increasing number of pumpkins being deliberately smashed and displays being damaged.
The business said: "Every morning, after a busy day welcoming families to our patch, we are faced with the heartbreaking sight of more and more pumpkins deliberately smashed, damaged displays and unnecessary mess left behind.
"We simply cannot understand how anyone thinks it is acceptable to deliberately smash pumpkins, especially at a family attraction designed for everyone to enjoy."
The patch explained that these incidents are one of the reasons for charging an entrance fee.
"Every single pumpkin has cost us money. Every display has cost us money," they said.
"When someone deliberately smashes a pumpkin, that is money straight out of our family's pocket."
The business has stated that anyone seen deliberately smashing pumpkins or damaging displays will be asked to pay for the damage where appropriate and leave the site.
The pumpkin patch has asked parents and carers to supervise children to help preserve the site.

articles.title: Record Chinese turnout puts European carmakers under pressure at Paris show - ET Manufacturing
articles.summary: Record Chinese turnout puts European carmakers under pressure at Paris show  ET Manufacturing
articles.full_text:
The Paris Motor Show is set to showcase a record 20 Chinese car brands next week. European car manufacturers will unveil new electric vehicle models to regain market share. Chinese automakers are focusing on Europe due to challenges in the US market.
European carmakers will use the show to unveil new models and try to reassure investors they can compete, as Chinese rivals gain market share with a growing range of electric vehicles and hybrids.
This year's Chinese contingent will be twice the size of the one at the last show in 2024, with established names such as BYD and Chery joined by newcomers including Aito and Avatr.
"The Chinese are saying 'we've got to try and dominate Europe because we can't do anything in the US'," said Brad Kuntz, a partner at consultancy Grant Thornton Stax. "If the US had allowed Chinese automakers in, Europe ... wouldn't be so much of a battleground."
Data from Schmidt Automotive Research show Chinese brands held a 10.7 per cent share of the European market in the second quarter, up from 5.7 per cent a year earlier and above Japanese rivals who arrived in Europe in the 1970s.
European carmakers play a 'double game'
Pressure from Chinese competition, alongside weak European demand, US tariffs and the costs of electrification, is starting to tell on European automakers.
Volkswagen is cutting thousands of jobs and considering factory closures to slash costs, while luxury rival BMW is also shedding thousands of workers.
The European Union imposed tariffs on Chinese-made fully electric cars two years ago, but Chinese automakers have responded by expanding into combustion-engine models and plug-in hybrids. Chinese brands accounted for more than 26 per cent of the Western European plug-in hybrid market in the second quarter, up from just 2.2 per cent in the same period two years earlier.
Europe's auto industry is now pushing for tariffs on Chinese plug-in hybrids, while the EU is working on legislation that will include "Made in Europe" provisions requiring minimum local content levels for EVs to qualify for key subsidies or government contracts.
While battling Chinese rivals for market share, European automakers are also seeking to benefit from their rise by selling them capacity at underutilised factories and tapping into their EV technology. Stellantis, for example, has partnered with China's state-owned Dongfeng.
"The Europeans are playing a sort of double game," said Pedro Pacheco, vice president of research at Gartner.
'Still strong and still ready'
Chinese automakers have emerged as formidable competitors in EV technology, but European manufacturers are seeking to fight back with a new generation of more affordable electric models.
"This motor show will probably be the most important one in the region since the pandemic," said automotive analyst Felipe Munoz. "This is the platform the Europeans are using to tell the Chinese they're still strong and still ready."
One of the headline European launches at the show, Stellantis' revival of the Citroen 2CV, will test new rules allowing carmakers to cut back on some features in order to offer more affordable EVs and counter Chinese competition.
Meanwhile, previously little-known Chinese brands such as Aito, the premium marque owned by Chongqing-based carmaker Seres Group, will be looking for a breakthrough.
Aito wants overseas sales to account for 20 per cent of total volumes within three years, up from less than 1 per cent currently, and plans to launch four premium electric SUVs for Europe in Paris.
Francois Roudier, secretary-general of the International Organisation of Motor Vehicle Manufacturers, said the arrival of Chinese brands had helped reinvigorate motor shows after interest from some traditional manufacturers waned.
The large turnout in Paris reflects growing pressure on automakers on both sides to compete for buyers in an increasingly crowded market, he said.
"For years people were buying cars, now manufacturers have to sell them," he said, adding that manufacturers who did not attend "have made a mistake".
"It's no show, no sell in a way."

articles.title: Most eurozone states could face extra spending of at least 3% of GDP by 2040 - Nation Thailand
articles.summary: Most eurozone states could face extra spending of at least 3% of GDP by 2040  Nation Thailand
articles.full_text:
European governments face mounting pressure to fund defence, pensions and healthcare while meeting higher debt-servicing costs, with weak growth limiting their options, according to a Morgan Stanley analysis published on July 20, 2026. Without policy changes, those competing demands could raise public spending by at least three percentage points of gross domestic product (GDP) in most eurozone countries by 2040.
Morgan Stanley expects governments to face difficult budget choices over the coming decade as they try to sustain growth without adding to debt. For decades, falling defence expenditure and debt-servicing costs helped European countries expand welfare programmes. Ageing populations, higher interest costs and geopolitical tensions have reversed that advantage.
“Borrowing cannot be the only answer,” said Jens Eisenschmidt, chief Europe economist at Morgan Stanley Research. “Markets will reward plans that boost growth, not debt.”
Europe’s fiscal pressures have also intensified as the Russia–Ukraine war continues into its fifth year and conflict in the Middle East raises energy costs. Governments already carrying high debt and persistent deficits face demands to accelerate defence spending while financing increasingly expensive public services.
Morgan Stanley identified France, Italy and Spain as three of the eurozone’s four largest economies with public debt exceeding 100% of GDP, leaving them with limited room to absorb additional spending pressures through borrowing.
Government expenditure already represents almost half of GDP in many European countries, according to Morgan Stanley. Social benefits and transfers, including assistance and subsidies for individuals and families, account for nearly half of total public spending.
Spain and Portugal could face spending increases exceeding five percentage points of GDP by 2040 without policy changes, Morgan Stanley estimated. Austria would experience the smallest increase, at around 1.5 percentage points.
For the United Kingdom, Morgan Stanley projected that pension and defence expenditure would rise by a combined 1.4 percentage points of GDP by 2040. British debt-servicing costs were already above their pre-Covid-19 levels.
Eisenschmidt noted that the sources of pressure differed between countries, but the direction was shared: lower interest bills and declining defence spending were no longer helping governments accommodate other demands.
Members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) agreed at their June 2025 summit in The Hague, Netherlands, to raise their defence and security spending commitment to 5% of GDP by 2035, compared with the previous 2% defence benchmark.
NATO’s commitment comprises at least 3.5% of GDP for core defence and up to 1.5% for related security spending, including protection of critical infrastructure, cybersecurity and development of the defence industry.
The NATO agreement followed pressure from US President Donald Trump for European allies to take greater responsibility for their own security, alongside concerns about threats from Russia.
Goldman Sachs Research, in an analysis published before the June 2025 summit, projected that annual European Union (EU) defence spending would be around €80 billion higher by 2027, equivalent to approximately 0.5% of GDP. That earlier scenario put eurozone defence expenditure at 2.4% of GDP in 2027, against 1.8% in 2024.
Goldman Sachs estimated that every additional €100 spent on defence would add about €50 to GDP over two years. The benefit would depend on the type of expenditure and how much military equipment was bought from overseas rather than produced domestically.
Financing the higher defence budgets could involve additional national borrowing, joint EU debt or new lending mechanisms through European financial institutions, Goldman Sachs noted. EU fiscal rules constrained borrowing by individual governments, while joint issuance could provide lower-cost, long-term funding but involved complex approval procedures.
Goldman Sachs argued that Europe could secure greater long-term economic benefits by buying more from regional manufacturers, making military equipment compatible across armed forces and expanding research and development.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned that European countries must achieve faster growth or borrow less to keep public debt sustainable. The Fund forecasts eurozone economic growth of 1.1% in 2026 and 1.2% in 2027.
Around three-quarters of European countries need structural reforms to strengthen growth and ease spending pressures, alongside medium-term deficit reductions averaging about 3.5% of GDP, according to the IMF.
Jon Gray, president and chief operating officer of Blackstone, the world’s largest alternative asset manager, has argued that fiscal strains in France, the UK and other European countries present a more urgent risk than those in the United States.
Gray contrasted Europe’s weak growth and large deficits with the US economy’s support from technology investment. Countries carrying debt greater than their annual economic output faced particularly difficult choices, he warned.
High debt burdens aggravated cost-of-living pressures, particularly housing costs, and forced governments to make painful decisions about taxation and welfare, according to Gray.
Fiscal crises were often addressed only when governments were “forced into action by market pressure”, Gray argued, pointing to Greece’s debt restructuring more than a decade ago.
“We are now entering a period where we must face certain realities,” Gray said. He warned that deficits running well above countries’ potential growth rates were fuelling concern because future shocks remained unpredictable.
Morgan Stanley sees Europe’s central challenge as changing the allocation of existing budgets rather than simply reducing total expenditure. Pensions, healthcare, defence, public safety and debt interest are difficult to cut and, in many cases, are expected to become more expensive.
Eisenschmidt argued that slowing the growth of selected spending categories would be more achievable than imposing broad cuts. If expenditure grew more slowly than the economy, its share of GDP could decline over time.
Morgan Stanley’s proposed approach includes limiting increases in selected expenditure to the rate of inflation while protecting public investment, particularly infrastructure that can improve long-term productivity.
Strengthening Europe’s defence industry through more regional procurement would form another part of the approach. Morgan Stanley also advocated reforms to retirement savings systems to encourage household investment and deepen domestic capital markets, alongside support for private investment in industries with stronger growth potential.
Tax increases could contribute in some countries, but Morgan Stanley does not regard them as a universal solution. Existing tax burdens and political constraints mean governments would need different approaches to raising revenue.
Morgan Stanley’s modelling shows how faster economic growth could create more room in public finances, provided governments also restrain spending. The scenario assumes a pool of expenditure initially worth 25% of GDP is frozen in real terms, meaning its cash value rises only with inflation.
With annual real GDP growth of 1%, Morgan Stanley estimates that this approach could create budgetary room equivalent to around 0.25% of GDP a year. By 2030, the cumulative gain would reach approximately 1.2% of GDP, covering roughly half the required improvement in government balances before interest payments under EU fiscal rules.
With real GDP growth of 2% a year and the same spending restraint, Morgan Stanley projects that the available room could approach 2.3% of GDP by 2030. Under that scenario, governments could potentially meet the required adjustment without additional tax increases or outright spending cuts.
Morgan Stanley’s scenarios are conditional calculations, not growth forecasts. The potential gains depend on both the pace of economic expansion and sustained restraint in the selected spending categories.

articles.title: Von der Leyen: “We are paying the price for the lack of an energy union; a plan to revive it” - Eunews
articles.summary: Von der Leyen: “We are paying the price for the lack of an energy union; a plan to revive it”  Eunews
articles.full_text:
Brussels – The watchword in the fight against high energy prices is integration. The President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, is trying to close ranks and is calling for a demonstration of shared responsibility. Because, she laments, “not only are we too dependent on foreign fossil fuels, on gas setting the price, but we are also squandering opportunities by not having a true European Energy Union.“
As is customary, the European Parliament’s plenary session provides an opportunity to report on the summit of Heads of State and Government, and in this context von der Leyen seeks to call for a change of pace, focusing on legislation and reforms. High energy prices are on the leaders’ agenda because they undermine competitiveness, hampered by the fact that a European Energy Union is still lacking. “This is why the Commission will develop a plan for a true European Energy Union,” she announced. A comprehensive strategy for a major revival, “from grids and interconnector to aggregated market power in purchasing.”
For von der Leyen, there are no real alternatives: “we have to make much better use of the potential that we have.” This approach is shared by the President of the European Council, António Costa: “Immediate measures do not solve the EU’s structural problems,” he is keen to make clear to MEPs from all political groups. On the one hand, he warns, “as long as we remain dependent on imports, we remain exposed” to geopolitical turmoil. On the other hand, he notes, the sustainable transition must continue, building on efforts made so far and going even further: “Nuclear and renewables must be combined with modern grids and electrification.”
On the energy front, therefore, there is political convergence between the European Commission and the European Council on the need to complete the Energy Union. This task can no longer be postponed. Costa confirmed that, following the one in February 2026, he would convene “a second summit at Alden Biesen in February to review work on competitiveness”, and in this regard, “energy costs are at the heart of these efforts.”

articles.title: UK inflation: What is the rate and why are prices still rising? - BBC
articles.summary: UK inflation: What is the rate and why are prices still rising?  BBC
articles.full_text:
What is happening to UK prices?
Inflation in the UK rose to 3.5% in the year to September, the highest rate in nearly a year and above the Bank of England's 2% target.
The rise was slightly higher than economists had predicted, driven by higher petrol and diesel prices.
Inflation is widely expected to rise again in the coming months.
What is inflation?
Inflation is the increase in the price of something over time.
For example, if a bottle of milk costs £1 but is £1.05 a year later, then annual milk inflation is 5%.
How is the UK's inflation rate measured and what does it mean for UK interest rates?
The prices of hundreds of everyday items, including food and fuel, are tracked by the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
This virtual "basket of goods" is regularly updated to reflect shopping trends, with alcohol-free beer, dashboard cameras, and pet grooming equipment among items added in 2026, while premium bottled lager and sheets of wrapping paper were removed.
The ONS uses price changes in the basket of goods over the previous 12 months to calculate inflation.
The main inflation measure is called the Consumer Prices Index (CPI), and the latest figure is published every month.
The Bank of England looks closely at the inflation figures when deciding whether to increase, lower or hold its base interest rate, which is currently 3.75%.
Putting rates up makes borrowing more expensive, giving people and businesses less money to spend, reducing demand for goods and slowing price rises.
But it is a careful balancing act – increasing borrowing costs also risks harming the economy.
For example, homeowners face higher mortgage repayments, which can outweigh better savings deals.
Businesses also borrow less, making them less likely to create jobs. Some may cut staff and reduce investment.
What is happening to UK inflation?
Although CPI inflation of 3.5% remains above the Bank of England's 2% target, it is well below the 11.1% figure reached in October 2022 as gas and oil prices soared in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
That was the highest rate for 40 years.
While inflation has fallen significantly since then, prices have not. They have just risen less quickly.
The higher figure for September was mostly caused by higher prices for motor fuel, which rose by 29.8% compared to September last year.
Food price inflation remained at 1.3%.
But it can take a year for changes in the cost of food to filter through to the shop floor because of the way supply chains work, so prices could still rise as a result of the widespread disruption caused by the war in Iran.
How do energy prices affect UK inflation?
Inflation soared in 2022 because oil and gas were in greater demand after the Covid pandemic, and energy prices surged again when Russia invaded Ukraine.
Before the war in the Middle East broke out, UK inflation had been expected to be at or around the target level of 2% over the next five years, according to the official forecasts published in March 2026.
But in April, the Bank of England warned that disruption to global energy markets could push UK inflation as high as 6% in the worst-case scenario.
When the latest ceasefire took effect, analysts said it could limit further inflation hikes. Oil prices initially fell sharply after the deal was announced, but have risen again since the US and Iran resumed attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in July.
As a result, UK petrol prices are likely to climb back up. This - coupled with the 4% increase in household energy bills from 1 October when the latest Ofgem price cap took effect - is expected to push UK inflation higher.
As part of his pledge to provide "breathing space" for households struggling with the cost of living, Prime Minister Andy Burnham scrapped VAT on household electricity bills in October. It is predicted to have a small downward impact on inflation.
Precisely because food and energy prices can be very volatile, the Bank of England also considers other economic measures such as "core inflation", which excludes these costs.
Core CPI was 2.8% in the 12 months to September 2026, up from 2.6% in the 12 months to August.
What is happening to UK interest rates and will they fall again?
The Bank cut interest rates six times between August 2024 and June 2026, which brought rates down to 3.75%, the lowest level since early 2023.
In April, the Bank's Monetary Policy Committee indicated it would act "forcefully" if oil prices did not start to fall, with up to six rate hikes in a worst-case scenario.
At its September meeting, Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey said energy price volatility made it more likely that interest rates would rise.
Are wages keeping up with inflation?
The Bank also looks closely at what is happening to wages and unemployment.
The latest official figures show that regular pay in the UK grew ahead of inflation in the three months to August.
Average annual growth in pay, excluding bonuses, during the three-month period was 3.7%.
After taking inflation into account, it means regular pay grew by 0.8% between June and August.
What is happening to inflation and interest rates in Europe and the US?
The US and eurozone countries have also been trying to limit price increases, but also face challenges with inflation.
The inflation rate for countries using the euro was 3.8% in September, according to EU data - up from 3.2% in August.
The European Central Bank (ECB) has raised interest rates twice in recent months to 2.5%.
US inflation was in 3.7% in September, up from 3.4% in August, with prices there also affected by higher fuel costs.
The Federal Reserve cited "too high" inflation when it raised interest rates for the first time in three years in September, to a range of 3.75%-4%.
The move came despite fierce opposition from President Donald Trump, who had called for rates to be cut.

articles.title: Thousands march in Greece over public education failures as Macron blasts ‘stupid’ commentary on French protests – as it happened - The Guardian
articles.summary: Thousands march in Greece over public education failures as Macron blasts ‘stupid’ commentary on French protests – as it happened  The GuardianThousands of Greek students, teachers protest over education, pay  Reuters'From Greece to France, give money to education': European protesters make clear it's not immigration that has them on the march  FortuneThousands march for school funding in Greece  Al JazeeraSyntagma Square tent protest over housing crisis, ...
articles.full_text:
Crowds are also marching in cities across Greece right now calling for better classroom conditions and higher pay for teachers.
Thousands of students, teachers and civil servants have shown up in Athens, with demonstrations also in Thessaloniki and other cities. Some protesters say they’ve been inspired by the rallies in France and Spain.
The primary school teachers union has launched a 24-hour strike while the high school teachers’ federation has also announced a three-hour stoppage, local media report.
And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today.
Thousands of people joined education protests across Greece, calling for better classroom conditions and higher pay for teachers, in demonstrations echoing demands seen in France (14:42, 16:00).
Two airports have run out of jet fuel, supermarket shelves across southern Italy are standing empty and pharmacies are running short of medicines as Italian lorry drivers continue to blockade roads in protest against soaring fuel prices caused by the war in Iran (13:49).
French president Emmanuel Macron blasted “unacceptable” and “stupid” comments on the protests and riots in France from foreign leaders, accusing them of “campaigning at our expense” (12:22).
More protests in France are expected this Saturday and on Thursday, 5 November.
In other news,
Russia has signalled its readiness to restart trilateral talks with the US and Ukraine on ending the war, despite calling the new proposals emerging from yesterday’s discussions in Oslo as lacking substance (11:19, 12:22, 16:15).
This signal came hours after US envoy Steve Witkoff met with Russia’s president Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg (14:06).
On the margins of the meeting, Russia released a US citizen held by Moscow on allegations of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine (11:24, 13:24).
If you have any tips, comments or suggestions, email me at jakub.krupa@theguardian.com.
I am also on Bluesky at @jakubkrupa.bsky.social and on X at @jakubkrupa.
US, Ukraine discussed the worsening situation in Oleshky, Kyiv's negotiator said
Ukraine and US negotiators discussed the situation in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, Davyd Arakhamia – a member of Kyiv’s negotiating team – was quoted by local media via Reuters as saying.
“We discussed it yesterday, and the informal outcome of this meeting is that there should be some good news next week,” he told media outlet RBC-Ukraine.
Residents of the Ukrainian town, occupied by Russian forces since February 2022, have reported a deepening food crisis as roads in and out are heavily mined and saturated by drones.
Last week, Pope Leo urged Russia’s Vladimir Putin to allow humanitarian aid to the city.
'Ukrainian conflict heading towards its conclusion,' Kremlin aide says, as trilateral talks earmarked for mid-November
We are still getting more lines from the Kremlin, with Interfax news agency reporting that a new round of trilateral Russia, US, Ukraine talks could take place in Abu Dhabi in mid-November.
Curiously, despite his less enthusiastic comments earlier, Interfax also has Kremlin’s Ushakov saying that “the Ukrainian conflict is heading toward its conclusion.”
Government, popular websites go dark as developers race to patch newly-discovered vulnerability
There is also a fascinating story unfolding online, as government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in a widely used programming language sent website operators scrambling to protect their systems, Reuters reported.
Developers of the PHP programming language said Tuesday they had identified two critical vulnerabilities and urged users to update their sites as soon as a fix was released. They said on Wednesday that a new version fixing the vulnerabilities was live.
But with reports that hackers were exploiting the flaws to break into websites, government agencies in the Netherlands and Finland were among those that took sites offline ahead of the fix as a precaution.
PHP underpins large parts of the internet, raising concerns that a significant number of websites could be vulnerable to attack.
Russia open to restarting trilateral talks with Ukraine and the US, but 'not much substance' in Oslo proposals, Kremlin says
Meanwhile, we now have a longer reaction from the Kremlin to the proposals US peace envoy Steve Witkoff relayed to president Vladimir Putin, warning they were “lacking substance.”
“Steve Witkoff briefed Vladimir Putin on the substance of the talks held in Oslo,” Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters, referring to talks Witkoff held in Norway with Ukrainian and European officials on Tuesday.
“He mentioned some new aspects in the approaches of the Europeans and Kyiv... but there wasn’t really much substance in them.”
(That’s very much not what Zelenskyy and the Europeans said last night.)
“Our president informed Steve Witkoff that we are, in principle, ready to resume the mentioned (trilateral) talks,” he added, saying they could take place in mid-November.
More than 10,000 join education protests in Athens
Helena Smith
in Athens
Back again to Greece where tens of thousands of students have joined the burgeoning youth movement demanding better education better prospects amid an ever worsening cost of living crisis in the Mediterranean EU member.
Greece is no newcomer to protests. The massive demonstrations that roiled the country at the height of its debt crisis are still remembered vividly by the parents of the Gen Z protesters now out on the streets.
But for the tens of thousands who marched through Athens, Thessaloniki and other cities today, it was France, as well as the perceived shortcomings of a long under-funded education system, that had spurred them into action.
“From Greece to France we’re fighting for public and free education,” proclaimed a giant banner erected above a stage in front of the Athens parliament in Syntagma Square.
Singing French partisan songs, Greek students participating in the Athens rally, said the French protests were not only admirable but had been an inspiration.
“No one is doubting their message or concerns, even if [media] coverage is mostly focused on the violence,” said Fotini, enrolled at a university in the capital.
“We’re here to say we’re with French youth. Our parents endured so many hardships, so much sacrifice, and they feel really upset and enraged that we, too, have so few prospects. A lot of us are still forced to live with our families, even after we graduate, because the cost of living and house rents are so high.”
The protests, which included a one-day ‘solidarity ‘ strike by teachers, have seen students erect tents infront of the Greek parliament to protest against the soaring costs of education.
Many have privately run colleges – a trend that has included British universities establishing branches in the capital – in their sights. “No to private universities. Free and contemporary studies for all,” read another boldly painted banner erected in the plaza.
Will Europe’s angry protests lead to real political change?
Ashifa Kassam
European community affairs correspondent
Much of the news coverage in recent days has focused on the violence that played out on the fringes of the protests in France and Italy.
The protests themselves, however, point to what seems to be a diverse response to a common crisis: the growing perception, particularly among younger generations, that governments are unable, or unwilling, to deliver when it comes to affordable housing, social equality and robust public services.
“This is the most powerful warning from Europe’s angry youth today, in France and across the continent,” the policy analyst Alberto Alemanno said.
The framing stands in sharp contrast to the many rightwing and far-right voices who have sought to exploit the violence in France and Italy, linking it without evidence to migration while brushing over protesters’ wider demands.
A student protest movement has gripped Serbia for two years. This weekend it will try to take power
Julian Borger
in Belgrade
On Sunday, a mass student movement, Student List, will represent the most serious challenge Aleksandar Vučić has faced in his 12 increasingly authoritarian years in power, by putting forward their own candidates in parliamentary elections.
They hope to emulate the defeat of Vučić’s ally, Viktor Orbán,in neighbouring Hungary six months ago, in a domino effect that could bring a democratic resurgence to central Europe.
Opinion polls have varied wildly, but many expert observers say a close race is quite possible, with neither side prepared to accept a loss as a legitimate result, raising the risk of post-election unrest and clashes.
In order to win, the students’ list of 250 candidates would have to break the mould of Serbian politics, along with Vučić’s grip on the country.
He stepped down as president last month, five months before the end of his second and last term in office under the constitution, but only with the aim of extending his hold on power as prime minister at the head of his Serbian Progressive party (SNS).

articles.title: Brazil’s Pulp Trade Faces EU and US Hurdles Whoever Wins the Vote - Wood Central
articles.summary: Brazil’s Pulp Trade Faces EU and US Hurdles Whoever Wins the Vote  Wood Central
articles.full_text:
Shipments of Brazilian pulp fell 10.5 per cent in the first half of the year, with the winner of Sunday’s presidential runoff taking office six days after the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) starts to apply. That is according to the Brazilian Tree Industry Association (Ibá), which revealed that Brazil’s pulp exports slipped to 9.43 million tonnes, down from 10.53 million tonnes a year earlier.
Export earnings held up better, falling only 4 per cent to US$5.15 billion in the first half, with China and Europe each spending nearly as much as a year earlier. That follows a record 2025, when exports reached 20.7 million tonnes. “This performance reflects the strength of the sector’s investments, with new mills coming online every year and a half,” Paulo Hartung, Ibá’s president, said at the time.
Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, of the Liberal Party, topped the first round with 47.03 per cent of valid votes, ahead of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, of the Workers’ Party, on 45.16 per cent. Datafolha and Quaest polls taken last week both put the senator, the eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, two points ahead in the runoff, within their margins of error.
Brazil’s main share index jumped 7.7 per cent to a record the day after the first round, whilst the US dollar fell 4.1 per cent to five reais. Shares in Suzano, the world’s largest pulp producer, closed 5.4 per cent lower, which Forum Investimentos chief economist Bruno Perri put down to its US dollar revenue, which is worth less in reais as the currency strengthens.
Most wood pulp escaped the 25 per cent tariff the United States imposed on Brazil in July, unlike the paper made from it. The Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) cited “limited availability” outside Brazil in keeping pulp exempt, but removed high-purity dissolving pulp from the list.
North America bought US$1.36 billion of Brazilian pulp last year, 20.5 per cent less than in 2024, making it the third-largest market. Before the tariff was finalised, Brazilian paper exporters said in June that a 25 per cent duty would leave their products unable to compete in the US market.
“Despite having a legal framework for combatting illegal deforestation, Brazil has historically failed to effectively enforce this legal framework,” USTR’s fact sheet states. Illegal deforestation was one of six grounds for the tariff, with USTR saying it will keep monitoring the issues and consider whether changes are appropriate.
Meanwhile, pulp sold into the European Union from the end of the year will need a due diligence statement whichever candidate wins, with Brazil rated standard risk under the EUDR. Europe was Brazil’s second-largest pulp market last year after China, buying US$2.46 billion worth, although that was 13 per cent less than in 2024.
“We will have the goal of eliminating illegal deforestation by 2029, resuming and seeing through the commitment we already made in the Bolsonaro government,” Flávio Bolsonaro’s registered government plan states. His plan also sets fixed deadlines for environmental licences, with a licence granted whenever the agency responsible fails to decide in time.
“In the next term, we will keep working to reach net zero deforestation by 2030, a goal we reaffirm,” Lula’s registered government plan states. His plan also pledges to seek talks with Brazilian industry on traceability and due diligence mechanisms across supply chains.
Both pledges come as Amazon clearing fell to its lowest level since satellite records began in 1988, according to Brazil’s National Institute for Space Research (INPE). Its preliminary estimate showed 3,335 square kilometres were cleared in the year to July, down 41.8 per cent, with Brazil’s environment ministry crediting satellite monitoring and tougher enforcement.
Chile’s Arauco is building a $4.6 billion pulp mill in Mato Grosso do Sul, whilst its rival CMPC has yet to approve a Natureza mill costing the same. Separately, Suzano raised its October asking prices by US$20 a tonne in Asia and US$50 in Europe and the Americas, according to analysts at XP Investimentos.
The analysts see “limited room for short-fibre pulp to stay above approximately $600 per tonne without a significant recovery in demand from paper manufacturers.” For its part, Suzano is due to report its third-quarter results early next month, its first since the vote.
As it stands, polls close on Sunday afternoon in Brazil, which is early on Monday morning in Australia, with nearly 159 million Brazilians eligible to vote. The winner takes office on 5 January, the first president sworn in under a 2021 constitutional change that moved the inauguration from New Year’s Day.

Europe Moves to Curb Chinese Imports as Auto and Chemical Sectors Face Pressure
Europe is taking stepsto control Chinese imports in order to protect key industries including automobiles and chemicals, according to ICIS. The analysis, published by ICIS, notes that China's exports to the region reached a new record last month, rising from 23 billion dollars in September of the prior year to 35 billion dollars, a 25 percent increase, while Europe's exports to China have remained roughly flat at about 25 billion dollars over the past five years.
Autos represent Europe's largest manufacturing industry and support millions of well-paying jobs both directly and through the supply chain. Chemicals are next in line for action, alongside machinery, textiles and metals. According to the source, the approach relies on trade data from partners such as Trade Data Monitor and others, and the EU plans to develop a Warning List of key sectors at risk. Rather than relying solely on anti-dumping tools, which the source describes as slow and easy to circumvent, the bloc intends to limit volumes through quotas, as it has done with hybrids.
Germany has been significantly affected by the imports and, together with France, has asked the Commission to act quickly to protect these vital industries. The source notes that the German push for stronger measures represents a radical shift in the country's approach to China, given Berlin's traditionally cautious stance shaped by its export-driven economy and deep commercial ties with Beijing. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has accused China of keeping the yuan artificially weak and indicated earlier this year that China's power and economic strength had been underestimated.
The EU's action is described as confirmation that China's growth era is over. The source cites a Wall Street Journal interview with the authors of a new IMF book, who describe how a long-standing arrangement between the Chinese state and its people has broken down for tens of millions of young Chinese, with apartments now worth less than their parents paid and career advancement failing to cover rent. The source also points to China's unresolved demographic crisis and cites IMF authors warning of a growing risk of a prolonged slowdown with weak domestic demand and deflation, adding that the longer the wait, the larger the problem becomes.

The Ryanair CEO predicts travellers will face the biggest increase in airfares “in history” next year.
Michael O'Leary made the comments on Tuesday at a news conference in Brussels as airlines remain largely unhedged against higher jet fuel costs.
Mr O'Leary forecast there will be fewer seats available in a matter of months as a result of bankruptcies and takeovers among airlines, which, together with the unhedged positions, would result in fares increasing by as much as 20 per cent.
"You're going to see airfares rise next year in Europe, I think by 10, 15, maybe 20 per cent. You're going to see the biggest increase in airfares, I would say, in history in Europe for the next 12 months," O'Leary said.
The Iran war has driven jet fuel prices sharply higher, squeezing margins for airlines that were unhedged.
O'Leary said that Ryanair and other European airlines had strong hedge positions on jet fuel for 2026, adding that Europe's largest airline was 80 per cent hedged at $67 per barrel to March 2027 when the conflict began at the end of February.
The Ryanair CEO said that from April 2027 most European airlines had very little hedging in place.
Ryanair has just 15 per cent of its fuel costs for next year at $85 a barrel, compared with spot rates around double that level, he said.
Boeing 737 Max 10 certification
O'Leary was in Brussels to announce he was cutting 20 routes and more than a million seats from Belgium for the airline's winter schedule after Belgian plans to increase its aviation tax to €7 in January from €2 now.
The industry veteran also said he was optimistic that US certification of the Boeing 737 MAX 10 will be completed this month, allowing Ryanair to receive 16 planes in early 2027.
"Boeing are hoping to have the MAX 10, the new aircraft, certified before the end of October ... We're pretty optimistic that that date will be hit," O'Leary said.
US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is expected to announce that the Federal Aviation Administration has approved the long-delayed 737 MAX 10 on Tuesday after a glitch with its navigation software threatened further delay to certification.

articles.summary: Booking.com targeted in EU investigation into phishing scams, fraudulent listings  Business Recorder
articles.full_text:
- Big online platforms are required to do more to tackle illegal and harmful content on their sites
The EU is investigating Booking.com under the Digital Services Act for failing to combat fraudulent listings, impersonation, and phishing scams, risking significant fines for non-compliance.
- EU's Digital Services Act and its implications for online platforms.
- Specific types of fraud and scams targeted in the Booking.com probe.
- Potential for hefty fines for Booking.com's non-compliance.
BRUSSELS: EU tech regulators will investigate whether online hotel reservation website Booking.com is doing enough to weed out fraudulent listings and phishing scams to comply with EU online content rules, the European Commission said on Wednesday.
The Commission, which is the EU tech and competition enforcer, said it opened an investigation following a preliminary probe and after analysing risk assessment reports submitted by Booking.com this year and the previous three years.
Big online platforms are required to do more to tackle illegal and harmful content on their sites under the bloc’s Digital Services Act, or risk fines of as much as 6% of their global annual turnover for violations.
The EU investigation will focus on fake listings — such as for non-existent properties — impersonation fraud and non-compliant accommodation offers, and whether Booking.com has properly identified, assessed and mitigated the systemic risks related to these.
Regulators will also look into phishing scams exploiting Booking.com’s reservation and guest data shared with accommodation providers, the Commission said.
A third element will be paid-for boosted listings not clearly identifiable as advertisements. Booking.com is part of Booking Holdings.
“Europeans should be able to book their holidays without fear of being scammed,” EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said in a statement.
“The Digital Services Act sets clear responsibilities on platforms to address these risks, and we must ensure that the leading booking platform in Europe takes those responsibilities seriously,” she said.

articles.title: How Likely Is A Recurrence Of The European Debt Crisis? – Analysis - Eurasia Review
articles.summary: How Likely Is A Recurrence Of The European Debt Crisis? – Analysis  Eurasia Review
articles.full_text:
By Wei Hongxu
Key Takeaways:
- In early October, 10-year French government bond yields approached 5 percent and the spread over German bonds briefly exceeded 150 basis points—the widest since the 2011 eurozone debt crisis—while French financing costs surpassed those of Italy and Greece.
- France’s projected 2026 fiscal deficit of 5.4 percent of GDP (or up to 8 percent on a broader measure) and public debt rising toward 119–122 percent of GDP have prompted a Fitch downgrade, amid political fragmentation that limits fiscal consolidation.
- The article contrasts robust demand for high-yielding U.S. Treasuries with Europe’s structural constraints, warning that ECB limitations, Japanese capital repatriation, and bank holdings of sovereign debt could amplify volatility if French political risks intensify.
As global central banks have entered rate-hiking cycles, the negative impacts of rising interest rates are becoming apparent. Entering October, not only have long-term U.S. Treasury yields remained high, European sovereign debt has also faced a tendency to be sold off, with European sovereign bond yields continuing to climb. On October 7, the yield on the 10-year French government bond rose by more than 0.1 percentage points, touching 4.93% at one point, while the yield spread between French and German bonds rebounded to 140 basis points. In early October, the spread between 10-year French and German government bonds briefly broke through 150 basis points, hitting a new high since the European debt crisis of 2011. The yield on the 10-year French government bond approached 5% during trading, with its financing costs already exceeding those of Italy and Greece. Italy, formerly one of the PIGS nations of the European debt crisis, saw its 10-year government bond yield drop to as low as 4.7% at times since October, rebounding to 4.623% on the 7th, while the Italian-German yield spread rose to around 129 basis points.
As part of the eurozone’s troika, Germany’s government bonds have also shown an upward trend this year. Amid European Central Bank (ECB) rate hikes and the Middle East energy crisis, the 10-year yield rose to 3.631% in late September, the highest since mid-2009. Since October, it has hovered in the 3.4% to 3.5% range, and on October 7 the yield on the 10-year German government bond was about 3.471%. The British bond market has not been spared either. The yield on the 30-year British government bond rose as high as 6.04% intraday, reaching a new high since 1998, before retreating slightly to just below 6%. The yield on the 10-year British government bond rose by 6.8 basis points to 5.442%. On October 8, the yield briefly rose to about 5.50% during trading, approaching its highest level since 2007. Similar to the situation in the U.S., the falling prices of sovereign bonds in major European economies are closely related to mounting global inflation. Meanwhile, under the U.S.-Iran conflict, high energy prices have had a greater impact on Europe. Eurostat announced, based on preliminary estimates, that prices in the 21 member states of the eurozone rose by 3.8% year-on-year in September, reaching a three-year high, with energy product prices surging by 18.8% year-on-year in September. Rising inflation also prompted the ECB to raise interest rates in September. As interest rates rise, the increase in sovereign bond yields can be considered a direct market reaction.
This situation happens to U.S. Treasuries. Like European debt, long-term U.S. Treasury yields have remained high since October, with the yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury climbing to a near 20-year high of 5.36%, and the 30-year Treasury yield reaching 5.73%. However, the results of the U.S. long-term Treasury auction on October 8 showed that at this level, demand for U.S. Treasuries was very robust. That day, the U.S. Department of the Treasury completed a USD 39 billion 10-year Treasury auction at a high yield of 5.3%. This auction yield was the highest since November 2000, yet it still attracted investors seeking stable long-term returns, causing the participation rate of large primary dealer banks acting as a backstop to drop to its lowest level since 2003, which precisely reflects the strength of genuine market demand.
This contrasts with the situation of European debt. Despite facing the same headwinds of high inflation, U.S. economic growth remains robust, and the status of the U.S. dollar remains strong, providing strong support for U.S. Treasuries. Europe, on the other hand, faces more severe stagflation pressures. Considering the geopolitical impacts of the conflicts in the Middle East and Russia-Ukraine, Europe faces a relatively weaker geo-financial situation, which has dragged down the euro and the sovereign credit of its member states. On October 8, the euro fell to 1.1185 against the U.S. dollar. The dollar has become the primary beneficiary of the euro’s weakness, with the dollar index rising to 102.34, close to an 18-month high. The dollar remained generally stable against the Japanese yen at around 158.22, supported by potential intervention risks.
Compared with U.
S.
Treasuries, while both face massive government debt burdens and fiscal deficits, European debt still suffers from the structural flaws of the ECB, contrasting with the strength of the Federal Reserve and the resilience of the U.
S.
economic foundation.
This situation is similar to the European debt crisis during the 2008 financial crisis, except that the main subject in the storm has shifted from Portugal, Italy, Greece, and Spain (“PIGS”) to France, a core member of the European Union.
Eurozone member states are currently still unable to formulate their own monetary policy and find it difficult to coordinate with their governments’ fiscal policies the way the Fed does with the U.
S.
government.
Although the ECB has established related bond-buying mechanisms, it still faces divisions among different member states, making it difficult to effectively constrain sovereign debt risks.
Judging by the current situation, because France’s fiscal deficit fails to meet relevant requirements, French government bonds are not supported by the ECB from a regulatory standpoint.
Some institutions believe that the European Central Bank’s Transmission Protection Instrument requires member states to comply with EU fiscal rules, and France currently does not meet the relevant conditions.
If the French bond market faces further pressure due to fiscal or political risks, the policy buffer space the ECB can provide may be limited.
With the central bank beginning to hike interest rates and shrink its balance sheet, France is unlikely to obtain support on the monetary policy front.
This institutional flaw is the root cause of the inherent weakness of European debt credit and will likely be the source of greater volatility and crisis possibilities in this round of European debt fluctuations.

As it stands, the French government budget and deficit indeed carry the risk of spinning out of control amid economic deceleration. Media reports indicate that market concerns over the fiscal outlook of the eurozone’s second-largest economy continue to mount, demanding a higher risk premium. Data from the French Treasury shows that as of the end of June 2026, the French central government fiscal deficit was approximately EUR 107 billion, 14.4% higher than the government budget plan. Forecast data updated by the French Treasury on September 19 shows that the fiscal deficit is expected to account for 5.4% of GDP in 2026, higher than the previous target of 5.0%, continually and substantially breaching the EU’s 3% deficit red line. Market institutions calculate that if the social security system, local governments, and other generalized fiscal revenues and expenditures are included in the statistics, the total annual government deficit could reach approximately 8% of GDP. Of course, for France, economic sluggishness is also a major factor contributing to market concerns over its debt risk. France’s growth forecast for 2026 has been downgraded three times, with the latest growth forecast standing at only 0.5%. Fitch has downgraded France’s sovereign credit rating from AA− to A+, citing reasons including climbing debt burdens, escalating political uncertainty, and a lack of a credible path for fiscal consolidation.
As investors’ concerns over France’s public finances and policy execution capabilities grow, the yield on the 10-year French government bond has risen by more than 100 basis points this year, even surpassing the yield on Italian government bonds over the same period.
Currently, the French government projects that public debt will reach 119.
3% of GDP in 2026 and continue to climb to 121.
7% in 2027.
Total public debt has already surpassed 3.
5 trillion euros.
Within the eurozone, the only countries with public debt-to-GDP ratios higher than France are Greece and Italy, former PIGS nations, yet Italy’s current government bond yield is now lower than France’s.
Although Italy’s stock of government debt remains larger than France’s, against the backdrop of debt reduction, Italy’s fiscal deficit has already been constrained.
Compared to the continuous growth of France’s debt, Italy’s sovereign credit is superior to that of France.
For the bond market, this means that France’s credit risk is being repriced.
If French government bonds are affected, Italy, which has only recently escaped the troubles of debt, may likewise be dragged down, causing risks in the European debt market to spread continuously.
Amid rising global interest rate levels, not only is the ECB shrinking its balance sheet, but Japan, a country that held European sovereign debt long-term during the low-interest-rate era, is also selling French government bonds and repatriating funds back to Japan.
Currently, Japanese holdings of French debt have decreased by 2.
5% compared to the end of last year.
