articles.title: Nvidia expands open-weight models for European sovereign deployments - news.lavx.hu
articles.summary: Nvidia expands open-weight models for European sovereign deployments  news.lavx.hu
articles.full_text:
Nvidia used GTC Berlin to add document-processing models and an autonomous-driving model that organizations can run on controlled hardware. The releases expand local model control, and deployers must assess their roles under the EU AI Act and meet the data protection and safety requirements that apply to their uses.
At GTC Berlin on Oct. 21, Nvidia released new open-weight AI models that give enterprises and public agencies tools for document workflows and autonomous-driving systems on infrastructure they control.
Nvidia cited demand for sovereign AI, a term for systems an organization or government can operate under its own infrastructure, rules and data controls. Under that model, the operator controls the stack even when Nvidia supplies the hardware and weights. The company said buyers can adapt models and run inference close to their data. Local deployment gives buyers control over system updates. Most companies lack the compute and data pipeline to pretrain a capable model, so they adapt downloaded weights from vendors such as Mistral or Nvidia with their own data. Nvidia's package gives research teams a path to pretrain on the Nemotron architecture as an alternative to fine-tuning.
For European buyers, local deployment offers control over location and system adaptation. Support access remains part of the procurement decision. Teams can keep inference inside a selected region by setting logging and telemetry rules. Remote support must obey the same boundary.
New Nemotron retrieval and reranking models
The refreshed Nemotron Retriever embedding and reranking models range from one billion to eight billion parameters and use the Nemotron 3.5 architecture. They produce embeddings for text and images in a shared space across 34 languages. Teams can then search scanned pages, diagrams and text through one system.
For retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), developers divide source documents into chunks, generate an embedding for each chunk and compare those vectors with the query. A retriever selects the closest matches, and a reranker scores those candidates again. Nvidia's models cover both stages.
Embeddings capture semantic similarity, so a query can find relevant text that lacks exact word matches.
ViDoRe V3.1 measures visual document retrieval. Nvidia says its eight-billion-parameter BF16 models rank first among dense models on the benchmark. The family can run on a DGX Spark while leaving memory for other models, according to Nvidia. Teams should test their own corpus across the languages and document layouts they expect. The Nvidia model catalog and Nvidia's Hugging Face organization provide download and model-card details.
Nemotron Parse targets PDF bottlenecks
Teams that build RAG systems often lose document context when they extract text from PDFs. Scans and complex layouts complicate that work. Charts create another failure point. Nvidia trained the one-billion-parameter Nemotron Parse model to extract information from PDF documents.
Nvidia reported throughput of about 10.5 pages per second on one H100. Teams should benchmark the parser on their own files because scan quality, page layouts and hardware affect speed and accuracy. They should measure page recall and table fidelity, then check reading order and latency.
Run the parser inside the approved environment to keep document content within the compliance boundary. Keep the source file and extracted text in one audit record. Record the model version in the same entry. Compliance teams can use that record to trace a RAG answer to the page that supplied the evidence.
Alpamayo 2 Edge targets vehicle systems
Nvidia made Alpamayo 2 Edge available alongside the Nemotron releases. The compact autonomous-driving model processes streaming video and sensor data in real time on the DRIVE AGX Thor platform. Automakers can use the model as a starting point for perception and planning research on smaller vehicle-compute systems.
Regulated deployment requires a documented safety case and software-process controls. Type approval remains part of market access. Teams should test functional safety under ISO 26262 and intended functionality under ISO 21448. They should check cybersecurity and software-update requirements under UNECE R155 and R156. The UNECE vehicle regulations set the formal path for market access in participating countries. Use the Alpamayo model card as engineering evidence, then record the supporting safety and compliance evidence in the vehicle file.
Nemotron 3.5 Super and Bolt
Nvidia launched the Nemotron 3.5 Super vision-language model before GTC Berlin. The company said it would publish Nemotron 3.5 Bolt on Friday, Oct. 23. Bolt uses a 74-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts design, and Nvidia says it can fit in as little as 24 GB of video memory.
Teams can use that footprint to plan local capacity before they reserve cluster resources. Production teams need to test output quality and memory headroom. They should measure request concurrency against their workloads. The Nvidia model catalog lists each release's supported hardware and license terms.
Open weights and open source
Open weights describe access to trained parameters. Open source covers the software and rights needed to modify and redistribute a system. The OSI's Open Source AI Definition adds requirements for data information and code. The definition includes reproducibility requirements.
Nvidia says it releases training data and recipes alongside weights for many Nemotron models. That package can support independent inspection and new training runs. The Allen Institute for AI follows a similar release approach with OLMo.
Procurement teams should inspect the license and dataset documentation, then compare the model card with the exact training recipe. They should record whether the release includes training code and evaluation scripts. They should list any logs in the same inventory. A weight file lacks evidence of training provenance and dataset consent. Safety evaluation requires separate evidence. Teams need documents and tests to support those claims.
A local model needs controls around remote support. A hosted support service can send data outside the approved region. Telemetry agents and logging pipelines can do the same. Deployment teams should map prompts and embeddings, then trace logs and telemetry to each outside service. Each organization should set data-residency and retention rules. It should limit support access.
EU AI Act and GDPR duties
The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) applies to providers and deployers according to their role and use of a system. Nvidia's release does not change those legal classifications. Open-weight access offers no exemption from the Act.
An open-source license can exempt an eligible general-purpose model from some documentation duties. Duties to publish a copyright policy and a training-content summary remain, and the exemption depends on the license and disclosure package.
Providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk face risk evaluation and adversarial testing. They must report serious incidents and protect model weights. They must disclose energy use. The Act treats training compute above 10^25 floating-point operations as a threshold for presuming systemic risk. A legal team should review the compute record for each model and each fine-tune, then document the classification basis.
Deployers of high-risk systems need risk management and data governance. Their control set must include technical documentation and operating logs. Their controls must cover human oversight and accuracy. They must address cybersecurity. Public bodies and private operators covered by Article 27 need a fundamental rights impact assessment.
The General Data Protection Regulation adds duties for training datasets that contain personal data. Prompts and logs that identify people fall under the same rules. Controllers need a legal basis and purpose limitation. They must conduct a data protection impact assessment when the processing meets the GDPR threshold. A valid transfer mechanism must cover access from outside the EEA.
Before launch, teams should identify the model owner and operator. They should record who supplies the model to the end user. A deployer that substantially modifies a general-purpose model or changes its intended purpose can assume provider duties when the system becomes high-risk. Each organization should sign an operating agreement that names the data controller and processor roles. The agreement should cover update rights and incident contacts.
Compliance timeline
As of Oct. 21, 2026, the EU AI Act's compliance schedule looks like this:
| Date | Requirement | Compliance owner | 
|---|---|---|
| Aug. 1, 2024 | EU AI Act enters into force | EU institutions and member states | 
| Feb. 2, 2025 | Prohibited AI practices and AI-literacy duties | Providers and deployers | 
| Aug. 2, 2025 | Governance rules, general-purpose AI duties and most penalty provisions | Model providers and authorities | 
| Aug. 2, 2026 | Most remaining provisions, high-risk duties for Annex III use cases and fines for GPAI providers | Providers and deployers | 
| Aug. 2, 2027 | High-risk duties for AI used as a safety component of regulated products; deadline for GPAI models sold before Aug. 2, 2025 | Providers and deployers | 
Compliance teams should use the European Commission AI Act page and record the classification and supporting controls. The evidence belongs in the same compliance file. Most AI Act provisions have applied since Aug. 2, 2026. Product-related high-risk duties apply from 2027.
Steps before production
Before a pilot, legal teams should classify the model and use case. They should assign provider and deployer roles, then set review triggers for material updates and new data. Employers should document role-based AI-literacy training for staff and contractors who operate or assess the system.
Security teams should verify the weight publish

articles.title: Rosenberg: US diplomatic push offers little hope for imminent Ukraine peace - BBC
articles.summary: Rosenberg: US diplomatic push offers little hope for imminent Ukraine peace  BBCSee more headlines and perspectives on Google News
articles.full_text:
Rosenberg: US diplomatic push offers little hope for imminent Ukraine peace
- Published
After two days of diplomacy – in Norway's capital and Russia's St Petersburg – is the war in Ukraine any closer to ending?
"Good and constructive" is how Norway's prime minister described Tuesday's talks between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, US President Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and European representatives.
In Oslo, the idea of a trilateral meeting at leaders' level was floated. The hope was that Steve Witkoff's trip to Russia would pave the way for President Vladimir Putin, Zelensky and Trump to meet and agree an end to the fighting.
But Putin has shown little desire to share a table with Zelensky - unless that table is in Moscow.
The Kremlin says it may be willing to resume trilateral talks next month in Abu Dhabi, but only at the technical level.
In a post on X, Steve Witkoff himself conceded that "there is still important work to do", though he claimed "President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end..."
- Russia says it is ready to resume talks with Ukraine and US to end war 
  - Published7 hours ago
- Trump and Zelensky at loggerheads despite new optimism 
  - Published1 day ago
- US citizen Stephen Hubbard freed by Russia as Trump envoy meets Putin 
  - Published8 hours ago
For me, the most telling statement of the day was from Vladimir Putin's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov. He took part in the St Petersburg talks.
Ushakov said that Steve Witkoff had told President Putin about the discussions in Oslo and (as Witkoff viewed them) "new approaches from the Europeans and Kyiv".
The Kremlin adviser was clearly unimpressed by what he heard.
"In terms of resolving the Ukraine crisis, there wasn't much there that was useful," commented Ushakov.
Later Russian state TV asked him about the prospects for peace.
"I don't know how close we are getting," Yuri Ushakov said, "but things are moving in that direction."
All rather vague.
It seems that President Putin doesn't feel under pressure right now to end the war.
He knows that Ukraine's air defences are under severe strain.
He knows that winter is coming and may well view the cold weather as an opportunity to pound Ukraine into submission.
He knows, too, that there is a US president in the White House who clearly wants a bigger, better, more profitable relationship with Moscow.
In recent days Donald Trump has paused some sanctions on Moscow, has agreed to buy Russian diesel and expressed biting criticism of President Zelensky.
That suits Russia just fine. It eases the pressure on the Kremlin leader.
"Right now Trump is the only leader in the Western world who is doing something for peace," Russian MP and TV anchor Evgeny Popov says.
"Doing something for peace, but a peace on your terms?" I respond. "Is that what you want?"
"Of course!"
A Putin-Zelensky-Trump trilateral may not be imminent.
But in China next month a meeting between Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping may well take place on the fringes of the Apec summit.
Some commentators here are already dubbing it "The New Yalta" - a reference to the Yalta Conference of 1945, where Stalin, Churchill and Roosevelt met to plan the political and territorial reorganisation of post-war Europe.
"Russia, China and the United States are the only superpowers right now in the world," Evgeny Popov says. "Of course, it will be good for the entire world if our leaders meet in China."
After nearly five years of war, that would put Vladimir Putin exactly where he wants to be - at the top table of global politics.

articles.title: Booking.com faces EU probe over scams and paid listings not labelled as ads - PPC Land
articles.summary: Booking.com faces EU probe over scams and paid listings not labelled as ads  PPC Land
articles.full_text:
The European Commission today opened formal proceedings against Booking.com under the Digital Services Act, examining whether the travel platform failed to assess and curb fake listings and phishing scams, and whether listings that accommodation providers pay to push up its search results are clearly labelled as .
In Short
The European Union's executive has started an official investigation into Booking.com, the hotel and holiday rental website. It wants to know whether the company did enough to stop fake properties and scam messages from reaching travellers, and whether listings that hotels pay to rank higher are honestly marked as ads. Nothing has been decided yet, but the case could end in binding orders, a non-compliance decision or promises from Booking.com to change how its site works.
What the Commission opened
According to the European Commission, the proceedings assess "whether Booking.com may have breached the Digital Services Act (DSA) by not having diligently assessed or effectively mitigated risks related to fraudulent listings and phishing scams." A second strand concerns transparency. The platform "may also have breached the DSA when it comes to transparency because it did not clearly label as ads those listings whose providers paid for a higher ranking in search results shown to users," the Commission states.
The announcement carries the reference IP/26/2223 and is dated Brussels, October 21, 2026. Three captures of it were reviewed for this article: the Commission's press corner web page, the press corner's print version, and a news item on the Shaping Europe's digital future website, which is managed by the Directorate-General for Communications Networks, Content and Technology. The two press corner versions carry identical wording, figures, dates and legal references. The Shaping Europe's digital future item is a shorter summary that lists the three investigation areas and points readers to the full release; it adds nothing that contradicts the main text. None of the three documents gives a separate date for the formal decision opening the proceedings, so the opening and the announcement are treated here as falling on the same day.
The Commission framed the case around three areas.
Fraudulent and non-compliant listings
The first concerns what appears on the platform itself. According to the Commission, it "will examine whether the provider of Booking.com has properly identified and assessed the systemic risks linked to the dissemination of illegal content." The release names the categories it has in mind: "Fake listings, such as for non-existent properties, impersonation fraud, and non-compliant accommodation offers may have negative effects on consumer protection."
Assessment is only half of the obligation. The investigation, the Commission says, "will also assess whether the platform has put in place effective measures to mitigate these risks, including by removing fraudulent and non-compliant listings." The term "non-compliant accommodation offers" is not defined in the release. It sits alongside outright fraud, which suggests the Commission is looking beyond invented properties toward listings that may exist but break applicable rules, though the document does not say which rules.
Phishing through reservation and guest data
The second area is the one most likely to be familiar to travellers. According to the Commission, the investigation "will focus on risks related to the way reservation and guest data is shared with accommodation providers, and the design and functioning of Booking.com's messaging service."
That wording places the platform's own architecture at the centre of the inquiry. Booking.com passes booking details to the hotels and hosts listed on it, and it runs an internal channel through which guests and properties exchange messages. The Commission wants to know whether the company "has put in place sufficient safeguards to prevent data from being misused to carry out phishing and solicit fraudulent payments." The release does not describe any specific incident, does not quantify how many users were targeted, and does not say whether the data reached fraudsters through compromised partner accounts or by another route. Phishing is a form of fraud built on impersonation, and in this case the question is whether the platform's design gave impersonators the material they needed.
The third area is where the case touches the advertising business directly. According to the Commission, "Accommodation providers can make their listings more visible in Booking.com's search results by paying a higher commission. Users should be able to clearly recognise that these 'boosted listings' are in fact advertisements."
The distinction matters for how the platform makes money. Booking.com is paid by commission on stays, and the release describes a mechanism in which a higher commission rate buys prominence in the ranking. Under the Commission's reading, that paid prominence is advertising, and it carries the disclosure duties that apply to any ad on an online platform. The Commission "will also examine whether, for each advertisement shown on Booking.com, users can easily see who is behind, who paid for it, why they are seeing it and how they can change the settings that determine which ads they see."
Those four questions map onto the four elements of Article 26(1) of the DSA: recognising that something is an ad, the person on whose behalf it is presented, the person who paid for it if different, and meaningful information about the main parameters that determine who sees it, along with how to change them. The Commission's rationale is plain. "Under the DSA, users are entitled to understand when, and on whose behalf, an ad is shown to them. Without this, they cannot tell whether a listing appears prominently because it matches their search or because the accommodation provider paid for that visibility."
The release does not name any Booking.com programme, product or label, and it does not say whether the boosted listings currently carry any marking at all. The Commission's phrase is "not clearly identifiable as advertisements," which leaves open whether the problem is the absence of a label or a label that falls short.
The legal basis
According to the Commission, "If proven, these failures would constitute infringements of Articles 34 and 35 of the DSA, which oblige Very Large Online Platforms and Search Engines to identify, analyse, assess, and mitigate systemic risks; and of Article 26(1), which requires providers of online platforms to ensure that users can clearly identify advertisements and the information about them."
The split is significant. Articles 34 and 35 apply only to services designated as a Very Large Online Platform or Very Large Online Search Engine, and they are built around the concept of systemic risk: the platform must identify the risks its service creates, assess them, and adopt measures proportionate to them. Article 26(1) is broader. It applies to all online platforms, regardless of size.
That difference explains one of the more technical sentences in the release. "The opening of formal proceedings relieves Digital Services Coordinators, or any other competent authority of EU Member States of their powers to supervise and enforce the DSA in relation to the suspected infringement of Article 26(1) as regards the conduct covered by the proceedings." Because the obligations reserved for the largest platforms are enforced by the Commission in any case, only the advertising duty, which a national authority could otherwise police, needed to be taken out of national hands. For the conduct covered here, the advertising question now belongs to Brussels alone.
Booking.com's status is not in doubt. According to the Commission, "Booking.com was designated as Very Large Online Platform under the EU's Digital Services Act on 25 April 2023." The release does not mention any designation as a search engine, and it gives no current user figure for the platform.
How the Commission got here
The proceedings did not come out of nowhere. According to the Commission, its decision "follows a preliminary investigation, which included an analysis of the risk assessment reports submitted by Booking.com in 2026 and the preceding three years, information published in its transparency reports, and the company's replies to the Commission's formal requests for information sent on 23 September 2025 and 26 May 2026."
Read literally, that means four annual risk assessments were reviewed, covering 2026 and the three years before it. The release does not name those years individually, and it does not describe what the requests for information asked or what Booking.com said in reply. Thirteen months passed between the first request and today's opening, with a second request roughly eight months into that period.
The Commission also names its national partner. It "cooperates with the Dutch Authority for Consumers and Markets, the Digital Services Coordinator of the Member State where Booking.com is established, in the supervision of Booking.com under the Digital Services Act." Booking.com is established in the Netherlands, which places it under the Dutch authority for DSA coordination purposes. The release does not describe what that authority contributed to the preliminary investigation.
Henna Virkkunen, Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy, provided the only quoted statement in the documents. "Europeans should be able to book their holidays without fear of being scammed," she said. "The Digital Services Act sets clear responsibilities on platforms to address these risks, and we must ensure that the leading booking platform in Europe takes those responsibilities seriously."
Next steps and possible outcomes
According to the Commission, it "will carry out an in-depth investigation as a matter of priority, continuing to gather evidence, for example by sending additional requests

articles.title: Europe Risks AI Startup Exodus as Regulation and Funding Gaps Grow - The420.in
articles.summary: Europe Risks AI Startup Exodus as Regulation and Funding Gaps Grow  The420.in
articles.full_text:
Europe risks losing some of its fastest-growing artificial intelligence startups as regulation, funding shortages and skills gaps make it harder for companies to scale, a senior Amazon Web Services executive has warned.
AWS EMEA Managing Director Tanuja Randery said nearly four in 10 European startups surveyed would consider relocating outside the region to expand their businesses.
Among the fastest-growing companies, the figure rises to more than half.
The warning comes despite rapid growth in AI adoption across European businesses, suggesting that using AI and building globally competitive AI companies are becoming two very different challenges.
Startups Say Europe Is Becoming Harder to Scale In
Randery said startups increasingly tell AWS they are reconsidering where to build their businesses because they cannot access enough capital or support in Europe.
Funding is only part of the problem.
European companies also face a complicated regulatory environment, shortages of workers with advanced AI skills and limits on computing and energy infrastructure.
Randery said some businesses report spending as much as 40 cents of every euro on regulatory compliance instead of technology investment.
That figure reflects feedback from companies rather than an official EU-wide measurement.
Still, it highlights the growing tension between Europe’s effort to regulate AI safely and its ambition to build globally competitive technology companies.
The European Union’s AI Act has created one of the world’s most comprehensive regulatory frameworks for artificial intelligence.
Supporters argue that clear rules around safety, transparency and high-risk systems can increase trust.
Critics worry that compliance costs may weigh more heavily on smaller companies than on technology giants able to maintain large legal and regulatory teams.
AI Adoption Is Rising, but Transformation Remains Limited
AWS research suggests Europe is not struggling to persuade companies to experiment with AI.
Around 54% of European businesses now use the technology, up from 33% two years earlier.
But only about one in five businesses has developed what AWS describes as a clear AI strategy, governance structure and investment plan capable of fundamentally changing operations.
That gap matters.
A business using a chatbot to summarise documents counts as an AI adopter.
But that is very different from redesigning production, customer service or internal workflows around AI systems.
Randery said Europe needs to focus more heavily on inference.
AI inference is the stage where a trained model is actually used to generate answers, analyse information or carry out tasks.
Training advanced models attracts much of the attention because it requires enormous computing resources.
But most of the practical economic value comes when those models are deployed at scale inside businesses.
Europe therefore does not necessarily need to build every frontier model itself to capture value from AI.
It does, however, need companies capable of turning available models into productive commercial systems.
Skills and Funding Could Widen US-Europe Gap
Europe already trails the United States in the scale of venture capital available to technology startups.
AI makes that financing gap more important because companies often need large amounts of capital for computing infrastructure, technical talent and rapid expansion.
A promising startup may therefore decide that operating from the US gives it better access to investors, customers and specialised workers.
Skills shortages add another constraint.
Building advanced AI systems requires machine-learning engineers, data specialists, cybersecurity professionals and people capable of redesigning business processes around automation.
AWS says the availability of those skills has not kept pace with demand.
The problem can become circular.
If successful startups relocate, Europe could lose both jobs and experienced employees who might otherwise help create another generation of technology companies.
Europe Also Faces Energy and Computing Constraints
Capital and regulation are not the only issues.
AI infrastructure requires large amounts of electricity and computing capacity.
Europe controls a relatively small share of global AI computing infrastructure compared with the United States.
Several countries are trying to expand domestic data centres, but electricity-grid capacity, permitting delays and environmental requirements can slow new projects.
That leaves European AI companies more dependent on large foreign cloud providers and technology companies.
The dependence has already become a policy concern.
UK government advisers recently warned that Britain could become a high-value AI customer rather than a creator if it fails to strengthen domestic computing, data and model-development capacity.
Similar concerns are emerging across continental Europe.
Randery said the answer should not be to choose between innovation and safety.
Instead, she argued that Europe needs both stronger safeguards and faster development.
The bigger question is whether policymakers can create rules that protect consumers without making it significantly more expensive for smaller companies to compete.
What this means for you:
Europe’s AI challenge is shifting from adoption to scale. If promising startups cannot find enough capital, computing capacity or skilled workers locally, more could move to markets where expansion is easier.

articles.title: Booking.com under investigation by EU regulators over fake listings and scams | European Union - The Guardian
articles.summary: Booking.com under investigation by EU regulators over fake listings and scams | European Union  The GuardianEU investigating Booking.com over action on fraud cases  RTE.ieEU wants Booking.com to check out of its scam problem  The RegisterBooking.com under investigation over fraudulent listings concerns  The Irish TimesBooking.com targeted in EU investigation into phishing scams, fraudulent listings  Reuters
articles.full_text:
EU regulators have opened an investigation into Booking.com, alleging that the accommodation website has not done enough to protect consumers from fake listings and scams.
The European Commission, which regulates the world’s biggest tech companies operating in the EU, said Booking.com may have breached the EU’s Digital Services Act (DSA) with its “absolutely substandard” approach to tackling fraudulent listings and phishing scams, where criminals impersonate a third party to trick people to hand over money.
A commission official said Booking.com should be carrying out risk assessments and acting to prevent fraud as required under the DSA. “We feel that what they have done is absolutely substandard,” said the official. “Although they take measures, they could go much further and they could have much more solid systems to prevent fraud.”
EU officials will also investigate whether Booking.com has breached advertising transparency rules, by potentially not making clear to users that some accommodation providers had paid to make their business more visible on the website.
Under the EU’s DSA, which aims to protect people from harmful and illegal internet content, a company could be fined 6% of its worldwide annual turnover.
The commission said that opening the investigation did not prejudge the outcome.
Booking.com, which is headquartered in Amsterdam and claims to have 28m accommodation listings, said it was engaging constructively with the commission. “Security, trust and the protection of personal information are top priorities at Booking.com,” a company spokesperson said. “We remain committed to working with relevant governments, regulators, law enforcement and industry partners to combat cybercrime and online fraud, and protect travellers and partners.”
The investigation comes after researchers at the UK consumer group Which? exposed security lapses at Booking.com when they used the site to set up – and accept payment for – a fake offer to stay at 10 Downing Street.
EU officials are investigating similar scams, with less high-profile addresses, where consumers thought they had booked a stay, only to find on arrival at a property that it had been fraudulently listed on Booking.com.
Officials are also assessing a second category of scams, dubbed “reservation hijacks” where scammers use hacked data to impersonate an accommodation provider. Criminals send WhatsApp messages and have even used Booking.com’s own platform to request payments from Booking.com’s customers, supposedly to secure a stay. Cases seen by Guardian Money in 2025 involved the theft of several hundred pounds.
EU officials will examine whether the company has sufficient safeguards to prevent data from being misused.
The Dutch consumer association Consumentenbond said it had received 200 reports of scams costing people €65,000 that involved Booking.com in 2025, up from 89 reports worth €25,000 the previous year. These cases were “just the tip of the iceberg”, it said, as many victims would not report to its fraud helpdesk.
Booking.com told the BBC in 2024 it had seen a 500 to 900% increase in scams in the previous 18 months, driven by generative AI tools that enable fraudsters to create very realistic-looking fake emails and internet booking links.
Agustín Reyna, director general of the pan-European consumer group BEUC, said: “It is positive to see the European Commission investigating Booking.com for failing to meet EU digital rules. This is a systemic problem.”
Henna Virkkunen, the commission’s lead official on tech policy, said: “Europeans should be able to book their holidays without fear of being scammed. The Digital Services Act sets clear responsibilities on platforms to address these risks, and we must ensure that the leading booking platform in Europe takes those responsibilities seriously.”

articles.full_text:
Formal proceedings under the Digital Services Act will assess Booking.com’s risk controls related to scams and its advertising disclosures.
The European Commission has opened formal proceedings to investigate whether Booking.com may have breached the Digital Services Act (DSA). The investigation seeks to understand whether Booking has adequately assessed and addressed risks linked to fraudulent accommodation listings and phishing scams. It will also investigate whether paid-for boosted listings are clearly identified as advertisements under the DSA’s transparency rules.
The Commission will assess how the platform identifies and mitigates risks associated with fake or non-compliant accommodation listings, including properties that do not exist and cases of impersonation. It will also examine whether the handling of reservation and guest personal data, alongside the platform’s messaging service, provides sufficient safeguards against phishing and fraudulent payment requests.
The Commission will further investigate whether users can clearly recognise listings promoted through higher commissions and identify who paid for advertisements, who is behind them and why they are being shown. The proceedings will assess Booking’s compliance with the DSA’s requirements on systemic risk management and advertising transparency, under articles 34 and 35 of the legislation.
According to the European Commission, the investigation follows a preliminary review of Booking’s risk assessment reports, transparency reports and responses to requests for information. The Commission intends to gather further evidence through additional requests, interviews and inspections.
Why does it matter?
This is an important step in the ongoing investigation into Booking.com’s activities under the DSA. Whilst not a preliminary decision, the steps taken, with the support of Digital Service Coordinators, send a strong signal to online services to ensure compliance with the legislation, particularly regarding transparent ads and assessing systemic risks.

articles.title: ​EU Investigates Booking.com Over Fraudulent Listings and Phishing Risks - The420.in
articles.summary: ​EU Investigates Booking.com Over Fraudulent Listings and Phishing Risks  The420.in
articles.full_text:
Online travel platform Booking.com has come under formal regulatory scrutiny after the European Union opened an investigation into allegations concerning fake accommodation listings, deceptive phishing schemes, and the mishandling of consumer data. The European Commission announced the inquiry on Wednesday, focusing on whether the company failed to implement sufficient safeguards to protect travellers from digital fraud and unlicensed holiday properties. Regulators suspect that the platform may have underestimated the reach and severity of fraudulent operations conducted across its ecosystem, while failing to stop bad actors from using customer details to orchestrate deceptive booking communications.
Scrutiny Grows Over Consumer Risks Under Digital Services Act
The action marks the first formal proceeding against Booking.com under the European Union’s landmark Digital Services Act, a regulatory framework crafted to hold digital platforms accountable for illegal content, consumer harms, and unsafe online practices. European authorities are probing whether the company allowed fraudulent property advertisements and uncertified rentals to proliferate unchecked. Such listings risk luring holidaymakers into paying for non-existent or unauthorised lodgings, resulting in direct financial harm while exposing user records to illicit operators.
European officials are evaluating the platform’s internal mechanisms for flagging suspicious properties, managing user complaints, and defending personal data against cyberattacks. The inquiry also covers deceptive phishing techniques where fraudulent operators target customers with bogus payment requests or messages designed to steal sensitive account credentials. European Commission Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy Henna Virkkunen affirmed that Europeans must be able to book travel arrangements without fear of falling prey to scams, noting that the Digital Services Act sets explicit obligations that the continent’s dominant travel portal must take seriously.
Probe Focuses on Unlabelled Commercial Search Placements
In addition to fraud prevention, European investigators are reviewing the platform’s handling of commercial search rankings to determine whether properties that pay for higher prominence are properly identified to consumers. The Commission is examining whether Booking.com failed to disclose paid placements clearly as commercial advertisements. Because elevated positions in search results significantly boost property visibility and booking rates, undisclosed commercial arrangements can impede a user’s ability to distinguish between organic search relevance and paid positioning.
The investigation will examine whether the platform’s ranking disclosures comply with transparency obligations mandated under European digital rules. A finding against Booking.com on this matter could set a wider precedent for commercial disclosure standards across the broader online hospitality sector. European regulators noted that no definitive determination of wrongdoing has been established on the labelling of paid search results, and investigators are continuing to review internal algorithmic and interface practices.
Booking Pledges Cooperation as Regulators Weigh Financial Penalties
Booking.com has stated that it is cooperating fully with the European Commission’s inquiries, maintaining that security, user trust, and personal data protection remain core commitments across its services. The company affirmed that it works alongside governments, regulatory bodies, and law enforcement agencies to counter fraud and safeguard travellers as well as hotel partners. The platform retains the ability to propose corrective operational commitments during the investigation to resolve regulatory concerns and demonstrate compliance with statutory standards.
Should the European Commission conclude that Booking.com violated the Digital Services Act, the company could face financial penalties of up to 6% of its total global annual turnover. The legislation provides European authorities with substantial punitive powers against non-compliant technology firms, though no statutory deadline governs the duration of the probe. The ongoing investigation is set to determine whether the travel giant fulfilled its legal duties to weed out fraudulent listings, protect consumer data, and provide complete clarity on commercial search listings.

articles.title: UN warns El Nino could be strongest on record as it urges world to prepare - Euronews.com
articles.summary: UN warns El Nino could be strongest on record as it urges world to prepare  Euronews.comFive ways El Niño is affecting the weather around the world  BBCEl Nino 'wrecking ball' could cause record Pacific temperature rise, UN says  ReutersCould history repeat itself? How past Super El Niño winters offer clues about what's ahead  FOX WeatherEl Niño and humanitarian action  World Meteorological Organization WMO
articles.full_text:
The UN's aid chief says the humanitarian system cannot cope alone, as $50 million is released for 11 frontline countries including Chad and Somalia.
The current El Nino could reach a strength never seen in modern records, United Nations officials warned on Wednesday, calling on governments to act now to limit the damage.
"The current El Nino event could be unprecedented in strength. Literally off the monitoring charts that we have used for the past four decades," Celeste Saulo, secretary-general of the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), told reporters in Geneva.
"El Nino will peak towards the end of 2026, but its impacts will be felt long after that," she added.
According to the WMO's latest global seasonal climate updates, sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific, where the phenomenon originates, could climb as high as 3.8C above average between November and January. That would be far beyond what is normally seen during an El Nino.
"This will have far-reaching consequences for weather patterns across the world," Saulo said.
The agency expects the event to push up temperatures across much of the globe, adding to the warming already driven by human-caused climate change.
A call for early action
Saulo appeared alongside Tom Fletcher, the UN's under-secretary-general for humanitarian affairs.
"Today, we are issuing a joint call for urgent and coordinated anticipatory action... We cannot stop El Nino, but we can prevent many of its worst human consequences," she said.
Fletcher described the coming El Nino as a "wrecking ball" of extreme heat, drought and flooding, warning it would bring "massive humanitarian consequences".
"The damage will not stay in the countries in the immediate path of this El Nino," he said. "It will create economic shocks for the global economy and drive further conflict, displacement, migration.
"I am sounding the alarm that the humanitarian system... cannot alone cope with a threat on this scale." He urged governments, development banks and international financial institutions to release funding "before that damage is done, not afterwards".
"The choice is clear: we can wait for disaster or we can invest in resilience. We cannot prevent El Nino but we can be serious about the challenges ahead."
Fletcher said he had already released $50 million to support 11 of the most exposed countries, among them Chad, El Salvador, Ethiopia, Somalia and South Sudan.
What is El Nino?
El Nino is a naturally occurring climate pattern in which surface waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific become unusually warm. This shifts winds, air pressure and rainfall around the world. It usually returns every two to seven years and lasts between nine and 12 months.
The climate swings between El Nino and its cooler counterpart, La Nina, with neutral periods in between.

articles.title: Resilience of the euro area economy – weathering one shock, preparing for the next - Zprávy Kurzy.cz
articles.summary: Resilience of the euro area economy – weathering one shock, preparing for the next  Zprávy Kurzy.cz
articles.full_text:
Despite a sharp rise in energy prices in early 2026, the euro area economy has proved resilient. This blog examines how decreased vulnerability to energy shocks, policy support and the global AI upswing have helped cushion the impact, and explores what is needed to sustain that resilience.
The latest shock follows years of economic turbulence. The euro area has navigated the pandemic and post-pandemic global supply shortages, the energy crisis following Russia’s war against Ukraine, Red Sea disruptions to global shipping, and trade tensions linked to US tariffs.[2] Although distinct, the events of early 2026 posed a stern, and still ongoing, challenge to the euro area's resilience. These events disrupted global energy markets amid geopolitical uncertainty, which can have significant and durable adverse effects on activity and amplify business cycle fluctuations.[3]
A series of shocks
Since 2022 euro area GDP has continued to follow a moderate upward trajectory, despite successive shocks.[4] Adverse shocks have not resulted in declines in output (Chart 1, panel a)[5], even though growth has slowed compared with the long-term average. So far, the latest energy shock has been no exception.
When excluding the volatile Irish data, real GDP in the second quarter of 2026 was 0.6% above the level reached in the fourth quarter of 2025. Incoming data point to a continued expansion. Compared with the previous quarter, the euro area economy (excluding Ireland) has fared better than forecasts expected, with a stable growth rate of around 0.3% in each of the last four quarters (Chart 1, panel b).
This raises an important question: why has the latest energy price shock had only a limited impact on the euro area economy so far?
The concept of economic resilience can help answering this question. It encompasses three complementary dimensions: absorptive capacity, the ability to limit the immediate impact of a shock; recovery capacity, or the ability to return quickly to the pre-shock path; and adaptive capacity, which refers to the ability to adjust economic structures and institutions in ways that reduce vulnerability to future shocks.
The experience of the latest energy shock illustrates how all three dimensions have strengthened in the euro area in recent years, although each also has its limits. It is important to distinguish between lasting structural improvements and support from policy measures and the AI-driven upswing, which may prove more temporary.
Chart 1
Macroeconomic developments in the euro area
| a) Real GDP - levels | b) Real GDP - growth | 
|---|---|
| (first quarter of 2022 = 100) | (quarter-on-quarter percentage changes) | 
|  |  | 
| Source: Eurostat. Notes: Long-term average corresponds to the period 2000-26. The latest observations are for the second quarter of 2026. | Sources: Eurostat and ECB calculations. Note: The latest observations are for the second quarter of 2026. | 
Is the economy less vulnerable to energy shocks?
The conflict in the Middle East initially sent oil prices soaring, but they eased after the June US-Iran memorandum of understanding (Chart 2, panel a). A second wave of the shock starting in July saw another significant increase in oil prices, along with sharp increases in refining margins and a sustained rise in gas prices.
The euro area economy has become structurally less exposed to fluctuations in fossil energy commodity prices. This explains why the impact of the latest energy shock has so far been relatively limited. Over the past three decades, firms and households have improved energy efficiency and reduced reliance on oil and gas[6].
Economic activity has gradually shifted towards less energy-intensive sectors, particularly services. The euro area economy is for example only half as reliant on oil as it was in the early 1990s (Chart 2, panel b).
ECB analysis suggests that this decline has reduced the impact of oil supply shocks on growth, consumption and investment in the euro area, making the economy more resilient.[7] The green transition can reinforce this development, as a growing share of renewable energy reduces the dependence on imported fossil fuels.[8]
This shift is increasingly shaping electricity prices in the euro area. The expansion of renewable generation capacity is reducing wholesale electricity prices in many countries.[9] This is linked to a higher share of renewables reducing the share of hours in which gas-fired plants set the marginal price of electricity, decreasing the pass-through from wholesale gas to electricity prices.
In Spain, for example, where renewable electricity generation is particularly high, the share of hours in which gas plants set electricity prices has fallen from around 80% in 2020 to just above 20% in 2026, considering the first nine months of each year. A similar decline has occurred in France, where nuclear power often dominates the generation mix, with the share falling from around 60% to around 20%.[10] Unlike during the 2021-22 energy shock, when electricity prices closely followed gas prices, the latest shock has had a smaller impact in countries with larger renewable and nuclear energy shares in the first half of 2026.[11]
Although Europe remains exposed to developments in global energy markets, the economy is now less vulnerable to fossil fuel and gas price shocks compared with a few decades ago.
Chart 2
Oil price developments and sensitivity to oil supply shocks
| a) Oil price | b) Oil sensitivity of the euro area economy | 
|---|---|
| (USD per barrel) | (index: 1990 = 100) | 
|  |  | 
| Sources: Bloomberg, Refinitiv and ECB staff calculations. Note: The latest observations are for 20 October 2026. | Sources: Eurostat, New Area-Wide Model database and ECB staff calculations. Notes: Oil intensity is measured in kilograms of oil equivalent per euro of real GDP and indexed to 100 in 1990. The latest observations are for 2024. | 
At the same time, the public sector has been playing a larger role in the economy in the post-pandemic period, acting as a buffer against the impact of the energy shock linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
Chart 3, panel a, shows that non-market services have been consistently growing above their long-term average and faster than other sectors in recent years. And fiscal policy has again helped to absorb the energy shock.[12] Fiscal support of the economy, which can be measured by the fiscal stance, has been increasing over the year. While the December 2025 projections expected an expansionary fiscal stance of 0.25 percentage points for 2026, this has gradually increased to reach 0.5 percentage points, thus doubling the expected fiscal support for the euro area economy over 2026 (Chart 3, panel b).[13] This mainly reflects higher spending on defence and infrastructure in Germany, and to a lesser extent, fiscal support measures of euro area countries aimed to cushion the impact of higher energy costs.
However, part of this support is temporary, fiscal space is limited in several countries, and the projections point to less fiscal support in the coming years. Therefore, fiscal policy might not be able to cushion further shocks to the same extent.
Chart 3
Sectoral developments and fiscal stance
| a) Sectoral developments | b) Fiscal stance | 
|---|---|
| (index: 2022 = 100) | (percent of GDP) | 
|  |  | 
| Sources: Eurostat and ECB calculations. Note: Long-term averages (trends) correspond to the period 2000-26. The latest observations are for the second quarter of 2026. | Sources: September 2026 ECB staff macroeconomic projections, June 2026 Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections, March 2026 ECB staff macroeconomic projections and December 2025 Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections. Notes: The fiscal policy stance is measured as the change in the cyclically adjusted primary balance. The figures shown are adjusted for the fact that revenues from grants under the Next Generation EU programme are not withdrawn from the domestic economy. A negative figure implies a loosening of the fiscal stance, while a positive figure implies a tightening of the fiscal stance. | 
Which factors supported growth?
Four factors that helped the economy get back on track stand out: a moderation in the degree of uncertainty perceived at the initial stages of the Middle East crisis, a more favourable external environment driven partly by AI, an AI-related boost to domestic investment, and a resilient labour market.
Uncertainty shot up after the start of the conflict. Production expectations collapsed, and uncertainty shot up, amid fears of disruption to energy and non-energy commodities, such as fertilisers, and a swift deterioration in global supply bottleneck indicators.
However, some of these fears started to fade as early as May. Production expectations gradually moved back to their pre-war levels in August and September (Chart 4, panel a). When the worst conflict-related scenarios did not materialise, uncertainty receded and confidence returned, supporting the euro area economy.
Activity may also have been temporarily supported by precautionary behaviour. Because the conflict raised the risk of outright fuel shortages and higher costs, some firms may have brought forward orders and production to secure supplies.
A second factor is that the global environment has been more supportive than many anticipated. While the December 2025 Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections expected global trade to grow by 2%, the latest projections see global trade growth in 2026 as more than twice as high, at 4.7% (Chart 4, panel b).
Strong AI-related trade is an important driver of this more positive outlook. AI-related trade has provided an important tailwind for the euro area economy, helping to cushion the effects of the energy shock.[14]As a highly open economy, the euro area benefited from stronger external demand for capital goods and specialised manufacturing products linked to AI-related investment, as reflected in th

articles.title: Airbnb bans check-out chores like taking bins out - Euronews.com
articles.summary: Airbnb bans check-out chores like taking bins out  Euronews.comAirbnb hosts can no longer make guests strip beds and wash dishes under new rules  BBCAirbnb bans making guests do dishes and take out the trash  The VergeAirbnb Hosts Are Furious They Can No Longer Make Guests Do Their Chores  WIREDAirbnb limits chores for guests, sparking backlash from hosts  TechCrunch
articles.full_text:
Hosts can no longer ask guests to do anything that would take “significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner”.
A common complaint around staying at an Airbnb is the dreaded check-out chores, like stripping the bed linen or taking the bins out.
But now the short-term rental service has updated its rules to prevent hosts from including such tasks in their house rules.
According to its community policy update, guests can’t be asked to do things that require “significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner”.
As an example, hosts can’t ask you to wash and put away dishes, but they can ask you to put used tableware in the sink.
In a statement shared with Euronews Travel, Airbnb said: “House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we've heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage.
“So we've redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises.”
Airbnb’s house rules updates
As part of the update, house rules are now shared on the listing page, in the trips tab, and in reservation reminders.
There are seven standard house rules hosts can share, which cover check-in and check-out times, the number of approved guests, smoking, approval for pets, designated quiet hours, and commercial film and photography.
Hosts will also be able to add “reasonable” requests, and these can be updated at any time.
Airbnb will flag any requests that do not fall in line with the new policy, and the host will need to remove them, or make an appeal.
The cleaning fee should only cover a standard tidy up between guests, and hosts are not allowed to charge guests for not doing something listed in the checkout tasks.

articles.title: Macron hits out at ‘stupid’ Trump remarks about riots in France - Financial Times
articles.summary: Macron hits out at ‘stupid’ Trump remarks about riots in France  Financial TimesMacron accuses foreign leaders of exploiting French riots for political gain  BBCMacron accuses Trump and other foreign leaders of ‘stupid comments’ about France unrest  The GuardianProtests banned in parts of Paris as Macron swipes at Trump  Le Monde.frMacron slams ‘stupid comments’ from world leaders after Trump blames France unrest on migrants  CNN
articles.full_text:
Your guide to what Trump’s second term means for Washington, business and the world
President Emmanuel Macron hit out on Wednesday at what he called “unacceptable and stupid” comments by foreign leaders, including Donald Trump, about the riots in France allegedly being carried out by migrants.
Trump, whose Republican Party is facing midterm elections in two weeks, has repeatedly brought up the violence and looting in France since demonstrations spiralled on Saturday.
The US president warned voters to “just look at France”, blaming immigration for the violence and stating that “Paris is going to be a Muslim city very soon”.
Macron on Wednesday said there was no evidence that foreign interference had stoked the riots.
“However, there has been a foreign manipulation of information since then, and that has led to some unacceptable and stupid comments from many foreign leaders,” Macron told reporters on a visit to Qatar. He later specified that Trump “was among them”.
“We’ve seen AI images that show scenes that never happened in France. There are people who have stated that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false,” Macron said, hitting out at those who “campaign on our backs in some regions or on the other side of the Atlantic”.
“These people irritate me,” he added.
The riots across France over the weekend marked some of the worst street violence in the country for years. A largely peaceful mass demonstration over the high cost of living and education funding descended into chaos when rioters attacked city halls and looted stores.
Macron and his government have come under fire for a lacklustre police response and for underestimating the size of demonstrations and the threat from the ultra-left groups authorities suspect of being behind some of the most violent acts, including the torching of a city hall in Limoges.
Ahead of new protests called for this coming Saturday, they have pledged a “massive” police presence and help from the army.
Macron, who was in the Middle East partly to shore up diesel supplies as high energy prices add to discontent, said: “People who want to sow disorder next Saturday will be stopped from sowing disorder.”
The French president then made an unscheduled stop in Riyadh later on Wednesday as part of his Gulf tour, where he was due to meet Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the Élysée Palace said.
Macron is the first western leader to visit Saudi Arabia since Iran-backed Houthi militants intensified their attacks in recent weeks, forcing Riyadh airport to shut. The visit was a mark of “solidarity”, the president’s office added.
Images of buildings on fire and a tear gas-ravaged Paris made front pages worldwide, but the riots also spawned misleading online content including widely watched footage of violent scenes that were not recorded in France. EU regulators are now probing these possible disinformation campaigns.
Police made more than 2,000 arrests but have not made any explicit link to immigration or Islamist radicals.
That has not stopped several foreign leaders from weighing in. With Israelis set to head to the polls in legislative elections next week, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday warned in an interview with i24 that France had “ceded to an invasion by Islamist extremists” as he lamented the destruction in Paris.
In Spain, where Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has called a snap election for November, the leader of far-right party Vox, Santiago Abascal, this week blamed the “Islamist left” and “Sánchez’s allies” for what had happened in France.
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar also blamed immigration for the riots while defending his country’s tough stance, as did Polish PM Donald Tusk.
Trump and his vice-president JD Vance were among the quickest to seize on the French protests. “France is burning! The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country,” Trump posted on his Truth Social platform on Sunday night.
On Monday he told reporters: “Emmanuel should have closed his borders a long time ago. I told him to do it.”
France faces its own high-stakes election next spring with the race to succeed Macron after his two terms in office. Marine Le Pen of the far-right Rassemblement National is the frontrunner, and her party had gained in polls since Saturday’s riots, one first estimate showed, as it vowed to bring “order” to France.
Le Pen on Wednesday pointed to “chaos” under Macron on Franceinfo radio: “It’s a migratory chaos, a security chaos, a budgetary chaos.”

articles.summary: Sichuan-Chongqing Connects with EU, Industrial Chains Embrace the World  FinancialContent
articles.full_text:
PARIS, France - October 21, 2026 - The 5th Chengdu-Chongqing Economic Circle Global Investment Promotion Conference themed “Sichuan-Chongqing Connects with the EU, Industrial Chains for a Global Future” concluded successfully in Paris, France on October 16. Co-hosted by the Sichuan Provincial Bureau of Economic Cooperation and the Chongqing Municipal Commission of Economy and Information Technology, this marks the debut of the conference in Europe. The event serves as a practical follow-up to the important consensus reached during French President’s visit to Sichuan-Chongqing, advancing bilateral economic and trade ties and deepening integration into global industrial and supply chains.
Cao Daixue, Deputy Secretary-General of Sichuan Provincial People’s Government; Wang Zhijie, Director of Chongqing Municipal Commission of Economy and Information Technology; Wang Dong, Minister-Counsellor of the Chinese Embassy in France; and Paulo de Carvalho, Mayor of Dourdan, France, attended and delivered addresses.
Photo caption: The 5th Chengdu-Chongqing Economic Circle Global Investment Promotion Conference kicks off in Paris, France on October 16. Representatives from Chinese and European government agencies and enterprises attend the event.
European Enterprises Gather to Build High-end China-EU Industrial Matching Platform
Europe is a key source of foreign investment for Sichuan and Chongqing. Sichuan-Chongqing and France share a long-standing foundation for industrial cooperation. As of August 2026, 197 French-invested enterprises and institutions have set up operations in Sichuan, including Airbus, Alstom and Veolia. Suez, STMicroelectronics and Mersen have also established presences in Chongqing.
The conference drew strong attention from French and EU industrial communities. More than 200 representatives attended, including Fortune Global 500 enterprises such as Saint-Gobain, Schneider Electric, La Poste and Richemont, as well as authoritative industry associations including Movement des Entreprises de France (MEDEF) and France-China Economic and Trade Promotion Association. Participants covered aerospace, high-end equipment, green energy, artificial intelligence, premium consumer goods and modern logistics — sectors highly aligned with priority industries of Sichuan and Chongqing, laying solid groundwork for targeted industrial collaboration.
Pragmatic Promotion Unveils Hundreds of Billions-level Global Cooperation Opportunities
Centered on building world-class industrial clusters in the Chengdu-Chongqing area, the conference connects high-quality EU resources in a targeted, efficient manner to unlock new avenues for cross-border industrial collaboration.
Sichuan and Chongqing jointly promoted six key industries: electronic information, biomedicine, aerospace, intelligent connected new-energy vehicles, new materials and high-end equipment, highlighting regional industrial strengths and cooperation tracks. Suining City of Sichuan Province and Dadukou District of Chongqing Municipality delivered special presentations on local featured industries and development priorities. Matthieu ELRIZ, Executive Vice-President of Advanced Materials Division at Mersen, shared investment outcomes and practical experience as an established French investor in the Chengdu-Chongqing region, offering valuable references for global market players.
As a flagship highlight of the event, the “Chengdu-Chongqing Twin-City” Investment Projects & Cooperation Opportunity List was officially released. More than 200 high-quality investment projects were jointly rolled out by Sichuan and Chongqing, with total planned investment exceeding RMB 750 billion, covering Sichuan’s six competitive industries and Chongqing’s “33618” modern manufacturing cluster system. A batch of cooperative projects between local entities (including Suining City, Dadukou District, Chongqing Bonded Port Group and Tongwei Co., Ltd.) and well-known EU enterprises were showcased on-site, demonstrating the strong appeal of the Chengdu-Chongqing Economic Circle for global investment.
Solid Industrial Foundation Empowers Global-oriented Cooperation
Six years into the development of the Chengdu-Chongqing Economic Circle, its aggregate economic output has crossed three trillion-yuan milestones, hitting over RMB 9 trillion in 2025. It accounts for 6.5 % of China’s national GDP and 30.3 % of Western China’s total GDP, growing into a critical growth engine driving high-quality national development. Backed by robust economic fundamentals and opening-up momentum, Sichuan and Chongqing have cultivated advanced modern industrial systems with global competitiveness, creating vast opportunities for international investors:
Electronic Information Industry: In 2025, the output value of the Chengdu-Chongqing electronic information advanced manufacturing cluster surpassed RMB 2.05 trillion, representing over 11.8 % of China’s national total. Sichuan hosts leading multinationals including Huawei, Intel, SK Hynix, ARM, Texas Instruments and IBM. Chongqing is the world’s largest laptop manufacturing base, with output ranking No.1 globally for 11 consecutive years. The local supporting rate for electronic-information industries across Sichuan-Chongqing exceeds 80 %, making it one of the world’s top-10 electronic-information industrial hubs.
Automotive Industry: Sichuan-Chongqing has become China’s third-largest automotive industrial cluster. In 2025, total vehicle output reached 3.72 million units, among which new-energy vehicle output hit 1.528 million units (a year-on-year increase of 47.3 %). One out of every 9 new-energy vehicles manufactured in China comes from Sichuan-Chongqing.
High-end Equipment Manufacturing: Sichuan-Chongqing is a core R&D and production base for high-end equipment nationwide. In 2025, its equipment manufacturing output exceeded RMB 1.2 trillion, with profound technological accumulation in rail transit, general-purpose machinery, industrial robots, large-scale agricultural machinery and nuclear-power equipment, alongside strong capacity for research commercialization.
Biomedicine Industry: Listed as a national advanced manufacturing cluster, Chengdu-Chongqing’s biomedicine sector generated around RMB 270 billion in revenue from above-scale enterprises in 2025, accounting for 9.1 % of China’s national total. In the past three years, cumulative overseas licensing revenue of locally-developed innovative medicines has exceeded USD 25 billion.
New-materials Industry: Sichuan boasts world-leading vanadium production capacity, a complete industrial chain for crystalline-silicon PV products, top-tier fluorine-silicon new-material capacity, and a national-rank-one lithium-battery-material cluster. Chongqing features competitive strengths in high-performance light-alloys, high-performance fibers and specialty inorganic new materials.
Aerospace Industry: The sector maintains robust growth. In 2025, Sichuan’s aerospace industrial revenue reached RMB 249.4 billion, rising 18.8 % year-on-year. The Chengdu-Deyang-Mianyang-Ziyang-Liangshan aerospace cluster is recognized as a national-level advanced-manufacturing cluster, gathering nearly 1 000 upstream and downstream enterprises. Aero-engines manufactured in Banan District, Chongqing, capture more than 60 % of China’s civil-drone engine domestic market share.
The successful Paris event marks further international expansion of the Chengdu-Chongqing Global Investment Promotion Conference. It exemplifies Sichuan-Chongqing’s efforts to pursue global industrial-chain allocation and foster a new landscape of high-level opening-up. Going forward, Sichuan and Chongqing will deepen industrial exchanges with the EU and the rest of the world, keep building a market-oriented, law-based and international-grade business environment, and work with global enterprises to unlock shared growth, advance industrial innovation, and elevate the development of the Chengdu-Chongqing Economic Circle to new heights.
Relevant officials from the Sichuan Provincial Bureau of Economic Cooperation and the Chongqing Municipal Commission of Economy and Information Technology attended the conference.
About The 5th Chengdu-Chongqing Economic Circle Global Investment Promotion Conference
The 5th Chengdu-Chongqing Economic Circle Global Investment Promotion Conference was held in Paris, France, on October 16. Focusing on key industries such as aerospace, new energy vehicles, and electronic information, the conference facilitated industry matchmaking and exchanges, released a list of more than 200 high-quality investment projects with total investment exceeding RMB 750 billion, and showcased a number of cooperation projects between Sichuan-Chongqing and Europe. The event served as a platform for industrial matchmaking between Sichuan-Chongqing and the EU, helping the two regions integrate more deeply into global industrial chains and open up new prospects for international cooperation.

articles.title: Booking.com targeted in EU investigation into phishing scams, fraudulent listings - ET BrandEquity
articles.summary: Booking.com targeted in EU investigation into phishing scams, fraudulent listings  ET BrandEquity
articles.full_text:
EU tech regulators are launching an investigation into an online hotel reservation website for possible compliance issues. The probe focuses on fraudulent listings, phishing scams, and accommodation offers that do not meet requirements. There are risks involving fake properties and the abuse of reservation and guest data from users. The European Commission emphasized the need for enhanced safety and compliance under the Digital Services Act. Booking.
                                    
Highlights
- EU investigates Booking.com for fraudulent listings compliance.
- Digital Services Act mandates stricter rules for online platforms.
- Booking.com pledges to enhance security and combat online fraud.
                    
                    
                    
                                        EU tech regulators will investigate whether online hotel reservation website Booking.com is doing enough to weed out fraudulent listings and phishing scams to comply with EU online content rules, the European Commission said on Wednesday.
The Commission, which is the EU tech and competition enforcer, said it opened an investigation following a preliminary probe and after analysing risk assessment reports submitted by Booking.com this year and the previous three years.
Big online platforms are required to do more to tackle illegal and harmful content on their sites under the bloc's Digital Services Act, or risk fines of as much as 6 per cent of their global annual turnover for violations.
Booking.com said it was engaging constructively with the Commission. "Security, trust and the protection of personal information are top priorities at Booking.com," a spokesperson for the company said."We remain committed to working with relevant governments, regulators, law enforcement and industry partners to combat cybercrime and online fraud, and protect travelers and partners."
The EU investigation will focus on fake listings - such as for non-existent properties - impersonation fraud and non-compliant accommodation offers, and whether Booking.com has properly identified, assessed and mitigated the systemic risks related to these.
A third element will be paid-for boosted listings not clearly identifiable as advertisements. Booking.com is part of Booking Holdings.
"Europeans should be able to book their holidays without fear of being scammed," EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said in a statement.
"The Digital Services Act sets clear responsibilities on platforms to address these risks, and we must ensure that the leading booking platform in Europe takes those responsibilities seriously," she said.
