articles.title: Germany's Cost-of-Living Squeeze Exposes Deeper Economic Strains - Sada Elbalad English
articles.summary: Germany's Cost-of-Living Squeeze Exposes Deeper Economic Strains  Sada Elbalad English
articles.full_text:
Rising energy bills, persistent inflation, and higher prices for everyday essentials are forcing German households to cut spending, while adding pressure to the country's already struggling industrial sector, Xinhua reported in its latest feature.
For Manuela, a middle-class resident of Berlin, the decision to turn on the heating has become a matter of careful consideration. Instead of switching on the heat at the first sign of cold weather, she now reaches for a sweater to avoid additional expenses.
"Before turning on the heating, we have to think twice and ask ourselves whether it is really necessary at this temperature," she said.
Her family's annual spending on electricity, heating, and hot water amounts to around 3,500 euros, or nearly 300 euros a month. With fuel, food, and other necessities also becoming more expensive, the family has been forced to reassess its household budget.
Rising Energy Bills Deepen Household Concerns
According to the Household Energy Price Index for European Capitals, residential natural gas prices in Berlin increased by approximately 22% between February and September 2026. Manuela is particularly concerned about the possibility of additional heating costs when annual bills are adjusted against monthly payments.
Her experience reflects broader concerns among German households. A survey by insurer R+V, titled "The Fears of Germans in 2026,'' found that 59% of respondents identified a sharp increase in the cost of living as a major concern.
Isabelle Borucki, a political scientist at Philipps University of Marburg, said rising prices for essentials such as energy, housing, and food were leaving households with less money for leisure activities, holidays, and other discretionary spending.
Official figures indicate that inflationary pressures have intensified. Germany's Federal Statistical Office reported that the annual inflation rate reached 3.3% in September, its highest level since December 2023.
Energy prices rose by 14.9% year on year, while motor fuels increased by 37.1% and heating oil surged by 74.9%.
As consumers cut back on nonessential purchases, the effects can extend beyond individual households, weighing on retailers, hospitality businesses, and tourism operators by weakening domestic demand.
Industrial Sector Faces Mounting Cost Pressures
The cost-of-living squeeze comes as Germany's manufacturing and export-orientated industries face growing challenges from high energy prices, transport expenses, and raw material costs.
Energy-intensive industries, including chemicals, are particularly vulnerable to higher gas and electricity prices. Other manufacturers are also facing increased operating expenses, while businesses that cannot pass these costs on to customers risk lower profits, reduced investment, and weaker job creation.
Volker Treier, chief analyst at the German Chambers of Industry and Commerce, has warned that high oil and gas prices could increase Germany's energy import bill by as much as 40 billion euros, equivalent to nearly 1% of the country's gross domestic product.
Pressure is already evident in the chemical industry. According to German industry publication KunststoffWeb, LEUNA-Polyamid, a plastics producer serving the automotive and electronics industries at the Leuna chemical complex in Saxony-Anhalt, is gradually shutting down production after failing to secure an investor.
The company reported that combined energy and raw material costs had risen by 80% since it filed for insolvency in June. Around 400 jobs are at risk.
The potential loss of industrial capacity highlights the broader consequences of high operating costs for Germany's manufacturing base, particularly as companies weigh whether continued production and new investment remain economically viable.
Energy Security and Economic Competitiveness
Germany's energy-cost challenges are unfolding amid a major restructuring of Europe's energy supply. Following the outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine conflict, Germany reduced its reliance on Russian energy, while European countries increased imports of liquefied natural gas. Rising tensions in the Middle East have added further uncertainty to global energy markets.
Germany now faces the challenge of balancing energy security and affordability with the need to maintain industrial competitiveness. Diversifying energy supplies and investing in cleaner energy sources could reduce exposure to fossil-fuel price shocks, but households and businesses continue to face immediate cost pressures.
If energy prices remain elevated, companies could postpone investment or reduce production, while households may further restrict discretionary spending. Such decisions could reinforce pressure on domestic demand and complicate efforts to strengthen economic growth.
Families Rethink Spending as Costs Rise
The financial strain is also changing how German families approach everyday decisions and holiday plans.
During the autumn school break, Manuela's family would normally travel abroad with their children. This year, they have decided to stay home and save the money for more pressing expenses.
For households like hers, the choice reflects a wider adjustment to rising living costs. For Germany's economy, the cumulative effect of these decisions could extend from household budgets to consumer demand, business investment, and the future of its industrial base.

articles.title: It’s Banana Time: Ecuador’s largest sector convention targets sustainability and supply chain strength - FreshFruitPortal.com
articles.summary: It’s Banana Time: Ecuador’s largest sector convention targets sustainability and supply chain strength  FreshFruitPortal.com
articles.full_text:
A produce aisle staple is getting its moment in the spotlight. Bananas, famous for their convenient price and grab-and-go perks, will be front and center at the 23rd Banana Time Guayaquil, to be held between October 28 and 30 in Ecuador.
Gathering under the slogan "Connect to Grow," the convention will bring together growers, exporters, suppliers, shipping lines, port operators, government officials, academics, and international experts.
"Ecuador is the world's largest banana exporter, which is why this meeting carries a shared responsibility," said José Antonio Hidalgo, Executive President of the Association of Ecuadorian Banana Exporters (AEBE).
Organizers expect more than 5,500 attendees at the event, which comes on the heels of robust export growth. Between January and August, Ecuador exported 282.28 million boxes of bananas, a 10 percent increase from 2025 numbers. As usual, Europe accounted for nearly half of that growth, importing 91.6 million boxes during that period, representing a 15 percent year-on-year surge.
Ecuadorian growers to assess production, biosecurity, and trade
The three-day technical agenda focuses on strengthening the production base, protecting crops against phytosanitary threats, and preserving fruit value through final delivery.
Opening day sessions will address measuring and strengthening production through satellite mapping tools, soil and water management, and farm preparation for El Niño weather events.
The program will also cover plant health, specifically preventing and containing Tropical Race 4 (TR4) Fusarium wilt and moko disease through international phytosanitary frameworks, risk-based surveillance, and verifiable biosecurity protocols across farms, public roads, and packing facilities.
The final day will cover export integrity and market demands, including customs controls, post-harvest care, packaging and refrigerated freight costs, disease-resistant varieties, and compliance costs associated with destination market regulations such as the European Union Deforestation Regulation (EUDR), maximum residue limits, due diligence, and living wages.
"These are the concrete challenges facing the industry today," Hidalgo told FreshFruitPortal.com. "We want what is shared at Banana Time to translate into practical tools so that producers and exporters can make better decisions."
Culinary competitions and networking for international buyers
The trade show floor will feature more than 90 exhibiting companies and 101 brands representing agricultural inputs, banking, shipping, box manufacturing, ports, and technology, with nearly a quarter of exhibitors originating from outside Ecuador.
On October 29, the event will host the Banana Innovation Challenge, a culinary competition featuring live cooking demonstrations that highlight bananas' gastronomic potential.
Parallel events include a multilateral meeting with executives from the World Bank and the International Finance Corporation on sector financing, as well as an executive breakfast with IFEMA Madrid leadership, the organizer of Fruit Attraction.
Additional program highlights feature the first Agro Woman Meeting, part of AEBE's "Sowers of the Future" initiative, featuring Rosa Rodríguez of the Heifer Ecuador Foundation and Josselyn Vega, recognized as a Top Agri-food Pioneer 2026 by the World Food Prize Foundation. Olympic champion Richard Carapaz will also speak about professional athletics and banana consumption as an energy source.
"For a buyer, it is the opportunity to meet producers and exporters in one place and discuss quality, traceability, logistics, and destination market requirements," Hidalgo noted, recommending attendance for industry professionals seeking reliable information and stronger supply chain collaboration.
*Photos courtesy of AEBE.

articles.title: Booking: EU investigation into scams and sponsored adverts - Il Sole 24 ORE
articles.summary: Booking: EU investigation into scams and sponsored adverts  Il Sole 24 ORE
articles.full_text:
The investigation centres on compliance with the Digital Services Act. The company says: “We are cooperating fully with the proceedings.”
The EU Commission has launched formal proceedings against Booking to assess its compliance with the Digital Services Act (DSA), with particular regard to the handling of fraudulent adverts, phishing scams and the transparency of paid listings. “European citizens should be able to book their holidays without fear of being scammed. The DSA sets out clear responsibilities for platforms to address these risks, and we must ensure that Europe’s leading booking platform takes them seriously,” said Commission Vice-President Henna Virkkunen. The investigation launched by the Italian Competition Authority in April this year.
The key issues in the investigation
The investigation will focus on three aspects. Firstly, it will seek to ascertain whether the platform has adequately identified and assessed the risks associated with the publication of false adverts, such as those relating to non-existent properties; non-compliant accommodation listings, and cases of fraud involving identity theft. The Commission will also assess whether the platform has taken effective measures to mitigate these risks, including the removal of fraudulent and non-compliant listings.
The risk of phishing
Also under scrutiny are phishing scams and risks associated with the way in which guests’ and bookings’ data is shared with accommodation providers, as well as the design and operation of the platform’s messaging service. Brussels will also assess the adequacy of safeguards against the misuse of data to send fraudulent payment requests. The third area concerns sponsored listings. Accommodation providers can gain greater visibility in search results by paying higher fees. The Commission intends to verify whether such adverts are clearly recognisable as advertising and whether users can find out who is promoting them, who is paying for them and why they are being shown, and whether they have the option to change the settings that determine which adverts they see.
Violations of the DSA
If proven, the breaches would constitute infringements of Articles 34 and 35 of the DSA, which require large online platforms to identify, assess and mitigate systemic risks associated with their services, and ofArticle 26, which requires advertisements to be clearly identifiable and to provide information on who promotes and funds them. The investigation, which has been launched as a matter of the highest priority, will continue with the gathering of further evidence, including through requests for information, interviews and inspections. The Commission may also adopt interim measures, issue non-compliance decisions or accept commitments proposed by Booking to remedy the issues under investigation. The opening of the proceedings does not prejudge the final outcome.
The company’s response
For its part, Booking.com states that it ‘is cooperating fully with the European Commission and is engaging constructively in discussions on the issues raised under the Digital Services Act. Security, trust and the protection of personal data are top priorities for Booking.com. We reaffirm our commitment to working with relevant governments and regulatory authorities, law enforcement agencies and industry partners to combat cybercrime and online fraud and to protect travellers and partners’, reads a statement.

articles.title: EU Regulators Open Probe Into Booking.com Over Fake Listings and Phishing Scams - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: EU Regulators Open Probe Into Booking.com Over Fake Listings and Phishing Scams  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
European Union technology regulators are examining whether Booking.com does enough to remove fraudulent property listings and phishing schemes, opening a formal investigation that could expose its parent company to a penalty of up to 6% of global annual revenue.
The European Commission, which enforces the bloc's tech and competition rules, said the probe follows a preliminary review and an assessment of risk reports the hotel reservation platform filed this year and in each of the three prior years. Large online platforms are required under the Digital Services Act to take stronger action against illegal and harmful content, or face fines of as much as 6% of worldwide annual turnover.
The inquiry centers on three areas:
| Focus area | What regulators will assess | 
|---|---|
| Fake and non-compliant listings | Properties that do not exist, impersonation fraud and accommodation offers that breach EU rules | 
| Phishing schemes | Scams that exploit reservation and guest data Booking.com shares with accommodation providers | 
| Paid boosted listings | Whether promoted placements are clearly identifiable as advertisements | 
Investigators will also determine whether the company properly identified, evaluated and mitigated the systemic risks tied to those problems. Booking.com is a unit of Booking Holdings (BKNG).
"Europeans should be able to book their holidays without fear of being scammed," EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said in a statement. "The Digital Services Act sets clear responsibilities on platforms to address these risks, and we must ensure that the leading booking platform in Europe takes those responsibilities seriously."
The Digital Services Act took effect for the largest platforms in 2023, obliging them to audit their own risks and submit regular compliance reports to Brussels. The Commission has used the framework to press major travel and e-commerce operators on how they police listings and advertising on their sites.
The opening of a formal proceeding does not establish wrongdoing, and the company has not publicly responded to the allegations. A finding of infringement could bring a penalty of up to 6% of Booking Holdings' global annual revenue, a sum that would run into the billions of dollars for a group of its size.
For investors, the investigation adds a regulatory overhang to a platform whose European accommodation business is central to its earnings. Beyond any fine, the case could force changes to how listings are verified, how guest data is shared with hotels and other partners, and how paid placements are labeled, all of which touch on the fees and visibility that drive the marketplace's economics.

articles.title: EU probes Booking.com over online fraud risks - ETLegalWorld.com
articles.summary: EU probes Booking.com over online fraud risks  ETLegalWorld.com
articles.full_text:
The European Union opened an investigation into online travel agent Booking.com on Wednesday over alleged failures to tackle fake listings and phishing scams. The EU will also investigate whether Booking.com is doing enough to address the risks that phishing scams pose to European consumers.
Brussels, Oct 21, 2026 -
The European Union opened an investigation into online travel agent Booking.com on Wednesday over alleged failures to tackle fake listings and phishing scams.
The EU fears Booking.com has underestimated the impact of fraud and unlicensed accommodation, and is not sufficiently protecting users' data from being misused for scams.
"Europeans should be able to book their holidays without fear of being scammed," EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said in a statement.
The EU said it was also looking into whether the Netherlands-based firm breached rules "because it did not clearly label as ads those listings whose providers paid for a higher ranking in search results shown to users".
Booking.com said that it was "cooperating fully" and that "security, trust and the protection of personal information are top priorities".
"We remain committed to working with relevant governments, regulators, law enforcement and industry partners to combat cybercrime and online fraud and protect travellers and partners," it added.
Booking.com is among over 20 very large online platforms that must comply with the DSA's stricter rules or risk fines that could go as high as six percent of their global turnover, or even a ban for serious and repeated breaches.
There is no legal deadline for the completion of the probe but the targeted company can offer commitments to address the European Commission's concerns.
- Suspicions over data -
A senior EU official was critical of Booking.com and its risk assessment efforts since 2023.
"We feel that what they have done is absolutely substandard," the official said on condition of anonymity.
The commission -- the EU's digital watchdog -- said it would assess whether the online platform "properly identified" risks linked to the spread of illegal content such as non-existent properties and fraudsters portraying themselves as the owner of a property and putting it up for rent.
In some cases, customers discover on arrival that the property they thought they had booked does not exist, or more often, photographs or property descriptions do not accurately reflect reality.
The EU will also investigate whether Booking.com is doing enough to address the risks that phishing scams pose to European consumers.
Phishing is broadly defined as the practice of tricking people into sharing sensitive information through deceptive messages.
The EU said it would look at how reservation and guest data is shared with accommodation providers, and whether Booking.com has put in place "sufficient safeguards to prevent data from being misused".
"We suspect that Booking is not sufficiently protecting the data of... private users and business users, and (this) makes the system vulnerable for this kind of phishing," the senior official said.
Meta is also under investigation over potentially fraudulent advertising on its platforms in a probe that began in 2024.

articles.title: EU Kids Act: New proposal to protect kids online - Arthur Cox LLP
articles.summary: EU Kids Act: New proposal to protect kids online  Arthur Cox LLP
articles.full_text:
The European Commission published its proposal for the EU KIDS Act on 17 September 2026. This proposal specifies and expands on existing child safety principles and guidelines under the Digital Services Act (DSA). It is intended to harmonise online child safety rules on access, safety-by-design and age assurance. The headline provisions would restrict access to social media and video platforms for children under 15. The proposal contains prescriptive safety-by-design requirements which will apply, not only to social media and video platforms, but also to providers of online games, AI companions, chatbots and app stores. The proposal is open for public consultation until 3 December 2026.
Key takeaways
- Evolution on DSA principles: Builds on digital child safety rules and guidance under the DSA
- Expanded scope: Will apply to online games, AI companions, chatbots, app stores and operating systems accessible to children, in addition to social media and video platforms (which are already regulated under the DSA)
- Age-based access restrictions: Children under 15 will not be able to access or create a social media or video platform account where the service poses a risk to their privacy, safety or security subject to limited derogations
- Safety-by-design: Prescriptive safeguards will include restrictions on addictive design features, default safety settings and limiting behaviour-based recommendations. Guardians must also be provided with specific controls.
- Age verification: Age verification for social media and video platform account access and creation must be based on EU-approved age verification methods
Beyond social media and video platforms
The EU KIDS Act proposal will apply to social media and video platforms (similar to the DSA) but also to the following services, where those services are accessible to children under the age of 18:
- App stores
- Online games
- AI companions
- Chatbots
- Operating systems
The proposal will not apply to not-for-profit online encyclopaedias, certain not-for-profit educational and scientific services, open-source code development and sharing platforms (like GitHub), services solely for scientific research and development purposes, and systems operated for or on behalf of public authorities. It also excludes certain narrowly designed chatbots whose functionality is limited to a specialised service/task or a pre-defined set of functions (e.g. customer service or technical support chatbots).
Evolution in child safety obligations
Since 17 February 2024 (and earlier for Very Large Online Platforms or VLOPs), the DSA requires providers of online platforms that are accessible to children to implement appropriate and proportionate measures to protect their privacy, safety and security. The types of measures that providers are expected to implement were detailed in non-binding guidelines from the Commission published in 2025. The EU KIDS Act proposal can be seen as a mechanism for codifying these soft law requirements and it will expand both the scope and depth of binding digital child safety rules.
Video platforms must also currently comply with Ireland’s Online Safety Code in relation to restrictions on harmful and illegal content and obligations relating to age assurance, parental controls and user reporting tools. In September 2026, Coimisiún na Meán opened its first formal investigation under the Online Safety Code, into X’s age assurance measures and parental controls, stating that age assurance based solely on self-declaration is not considered effective. Once finalised, the prescriptive requirements of the EU KIDS Act may prompt updates to the Online Safety Code.
Age-based access restrictions
Under the proposal, age-based access restrictions apply to social media and video platforms only.
| Default rule Children under 15 – no access or account creation | Children under 15 will not be able to access or create an account on social media or video platforms where the service poses a risk to their privacy, safety or security. The proposal lists a number of circumstances or features that would pose such a risk, including the use of recommender systems based on profiling (as defined in the GDPR). | 
| Exception Children between 13 and 15 – Limited access via guardian-controlled account | As an exception to the default rule, providers may allow guardians to set up social media and video platform accounts for children between 13 and 15 subject to limitations on those accounts. | 
| Exception Children under 13 – Limited access to video platforms designed for under 13s via guardian’s account | For video platforms specially designed for children under 13, providers may enable a guardian to allow a child under 13 access through the guardian’s account subject to certain conditions and limitations. | 
Within six months of the restrictions applying, providers of social media and video platforms must assess existing accounts and disable accounts of children under 15 or accounts where the account holder’s age cannot be established. To establish an account holder’s age, the provider will be required to use EU-approved age verification methods unless they can establish, with a high degree of confidence, that the user is 15.
Separately, app stores must assess their users’ age and put in place an age-rating system to ensure that children are accessing apps that are appropriate for their age. Unless a provider can establish, with a high degree of confidence, that the user is over 18, they must assess their age using an age assurance method such as biometric age estimation. App store providers are not mandated to use EU-approved age verification methods, but they can offer these methods if they wish.
Prescriptive safety-by-design rules
The proposal would:
- Restrict addictive design features and require time-limited access and breaks to protect school and sleep time
- Give children greater control over recommender systems (e.g. ability to easily reset), protect against repeated harmful recommendations (“rabbit holes”), prohibit the use of children’s data from outside the platform and restrict use of behavioural data when making recommendations
- Mandate default safety settings (e.g. geolocation, microphone, camera access turned off by default)
- Oblige certain providers to implement safeguards relating to contact and interaction by children with others
- Require providers to make children aware of purchases in real time
Certain additional requirements would apply to VLOPs designated under the DSA.
Age assurance
Age assurance generally means a method for determining, estimating or verifying age. Age verification is a more specific concept which means establishing with a high degree of certainty whether a person has attained a particular age using identification documents and reliable verified sources. See our article on the EDPB’s age assurance statement.
Under the proposal, age verification is mandatory for higher risk areas such as determining if the user is 15 for access and account creation on social media and video platforms. Providers can use age assurance methods (e.g. biometric age estimation tools) to meet certain safety-by-design obligations, to distinguish adults from children for child-protective settings and for the purposes of applying app store age ratings.
Tools for empowering children and guardians
Under the proposal, providers must create tools that allow children to report content and control their settings. Controls must also be provided to guardians so that they can set time limits on access, manage settings and submit reports on behalf of their child. Interestingly, VLOPs designated under the DSA must ensure that their tools are interoperable with controls offered by third parties in accordance with the interoperability requirements under the Digital Markets Act (DMA).
Enforcement
The proposal does not create a new enforcement and supervision framework but instead refers to the existing frameworks under the DSA (for social networks, video platforms, online games and app stores) and the AI Act (for AI companions and chatbots).
It does, however, specifically state that fines for AI companions and chatbots must not exceed 6% of total annual worldwide turnover. (For reference, the AI Act has two tiers of fines: 3% for non-compliance with most rules and 7% for non-compliance with prohibited AI systems rules.)
Due to the heightened risk that children face online, the proposal also envisages a fast-track enforcement mechanism which would require the Commission to adopt preliminary findings within 30 working days and a final decision within 90 working days.
Next steps
The European Commission opened a consultation seeking feedback on the proposed regulation which will close on 3 December 2026. The feedback will be incorporated into amendments tabled and debated by the European Parliament and Council as part of the ordinary legislative procedure. If the proposal is adopted, the legislation is unlikely to become applicable before 2028.
A recent report from the Joint Committee on Children and Equality welcomed the EU KIDS Act proposal. The Committee recommended that, at a minimum, children under 13 should not hold traditional social media accounts. However, evidence shows that a blanket social media ban for children under 16 would, on its own, be unlikely to provide a comprehensive solution to the harms experienced by children online. Access for younger teenagers should be limited, age appropriate and subject to parental supervision. Autonomous accounts should only be permitted on services shown to be safe by design.
While it is too early to say what the final text of the EU KIDS Act will look like, it is clear that the direction of travel is towards mandated age verification for online services that are accessible to children and prescriptive safety controls. These requirements are likely to require significant product changes so organisations should consider what lead time is required

articles.title: Rioting in France gives Trump a new talking point as he tries to stave off GOP midterm losses - Egypt Independent
articles.summary: Rioting in France gives Trump a new talking point as he tries to stave off GOP midterm losses  Egypt Independent
articles.full_text:
As Kansans were waiting for President Donald Trump to arrive at his rally in Wichita this week, they were treated to a new addition to the pre-show program: footage of this weekend’s violent protests in France, most of it clipped from Fox News, aired on large screens.
That the unrest was unfolding 4,700 miles away from the Heartland Credit Union Arena seemed immaterial to the point Trump and his team were trying to make. This could happen here, Trump would later warn his crowd, if Democrats win in November’s midterms.
“When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember that is what the radical ‘Dumocrats’ want to do to America,” he said Monday.
France, he claimed, was being “conquered, looted and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists and communists who hate Christianity” and “the Western civilization itself.”
It’s a theme the president briefly returned to Tuesday night in North Carolina. “Do you believe what’s going on in France? That’s never going to go on over here,” Trump told rally attendees. “I promise you, that’s never going on in here.”
With a narrowing window for harsh political winds to shift, Trump and Republicans have seized on the violence as they make their final arguments to American voters. To some of Trump’s advisers, the unrest has looked a little like an “October surprise” that some believe could help improve what had been dire prospects for victory in just two weeks.
The torched cars, graffiti and looted shops are all a cautionary tale, they have warned, and the inevitable result of liberal policies — particularly on immigration — that they have been warning against for years.
There is little evidence the violence in France over the weekend was carried out by illegal immigrants, or immigrants of any kind. The demonstrations began as a student movement demanding better funding and improvements at schools. Labor unions and other groups joined to protest high living costs and record fuel prices.
What led to the scenes of violence is a matter of dispute among France’s political leaders, and has led to a round of finger-pointing.
Trump, along with right-wing leaders in France, used the scenes to accuse French President Emmanuel Macron and other European centrists of failing to get a handle on uncontrolled migration from the Middle East and Africa.
“Our country is caught in a vice…between violence and powerlessness,” Marine Le Pen, the far-right leader, said, suggesting only her firm hand could restore order amid Macron’s “chaos.”
Le Pen, who is standing in the presidential election for the far-right National Rally party, has sought to inject the issue of migration into the debate, blaming the violence on delinquents from France’s banlieues, poor urban areas where much of the country’s migrant population lives.
Trump stopped short Tuesday of saying whether he would endorse Le Pen in next year’s election, where she is a front-runner. But he nonetheless appeared to be echoing her arguments, and insisted Macron had ignored his advice to crack down on migration.
“Some people think it’s a little controversial. I don’t care,” Trump said in the Oval Office on Tuesday. “It’s an immigration problem. We have people that poured into France, and they were also unchecked, unvetted, like with (President Joe) Biden when he was doing. We don’t do that.”
Earlier in the day, he specifically invoked “what is taking place in France” in pledging that the spending in outside money he oversees will top $400 million by Election Day.
It may be too early to tell whether Trump’s decision to seize on the images from France will have a determinative effect among American midterm voters. Most say their primary concerns are the high cost of living, and Trump’s immigration agenda has become unpopular, with majorities of Americans saying in polls his administration has gone too far in deporting undocumented immigrants from the United States.
Trump, however, has chafed at recommendations from political advisers that he not mention immigration as much as he stumps for Republican candidates. As he shines a spotlight on the situation in Europe, he has once again made a hardline approach to immigration a centerpiece of his pitch.
“If you want to see what is at stake in this election,” Trump said ominously in Kansas on Monday, “just look at what’s happening in France.”
Other Republicans have followed suit. Vice President JD Vance wrote on X that immigration was to blame for the violence.
“Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion,” he wrote in a post that featured video of the fire that destroyed the historic town hall in Limoges, the town in central France famous for its porcelain. “They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility.”
Trump referred approvingly to Vance’s post in the Oval Office on Tuesday, and insisted that concerns about education or costs were not driving the scenes of unrest.
“It’s not about education. It’s about immigration,” he said. “It’s about illegal people coming in who basically hate France. They hate the people. They hate everything.”
This story has been updated with additional details.

articles.title: Every Road Leads East: German Factories, Polish Railways, and the Need for a European Logistics Systems Test - Modern War Institute -
articles.summary: Every Road Leads East: German Factories, Polish Railways, and the Need for a European Logistics Systems Test  Modern War Institute -
articles.full_text:
Mika, Poland, November 15, 2025. Night has already fallen over the Masovian countryside when an explosive charge detonates on the Warsaw–Lublin railway. Farther south, on the same route near Puławy, the overhead power line is damaged, and a clamp is placed on the tracks. After an investigation, Polish authorities identified two Ukrainian nationals suspected of cooperating with Russian services. It was established that they had escaped across the Polish-Belarusian border. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the attacks unprecedented, and prosecutors treated the incidents as acts of sabotage carried out by a foreign intelligence service.
Events such as the one in Mika show how fragile wartime logistics are. The Warsaw–Lublin railway is a key route for military and humanitarian aid to Ukraine. A small device placed on the tracks triggered a whole sequence of repairs, further inspections, and disruptions. In a confrontation in the Baltic region, similar attacks would likely be repeated on a much larger scale.
Therefore, the current European discussion on rearmament cannot be concentrated solely on defense budgets. It should also include such prosaic questions as how European states plan to move equipment from warehouses to deployed units in the opening hours of a crisis, and how quickly damaged vehicles can be taken from the front line to rear-area workshops and returned to service. The critical sections of this chain will run through Germany and Poland. Testing whether this system can operate under repeated pressure should be an essential part of Europe’s war planning.
The Clock Is Already Running
Credible military and logistical readiness remains one of the strongest means of deterring Russia. The Kremlin’s main advantage at the outset of a conflict in the Baltic region would be a war economy already in operation. Four years of full-scale war have forced Russia’s industry, public finances and state administration to adapt to sustained mobilization. This head start would give the Kremlin an advantage in a conflict’s opening weeks and months. Sabotage such as the attack at Mika could cost Europe precious hours in inspections, diversions, and repairs. From the outset of a crisis, the speed of its response would matter as much as the forces and equipment it had prepared.
The industrial component of such response would be especially beset by delay. Germany’s chemical, automotive, optical, and machine-tool industries could support a rapid expansion of military production, but only if government, industry, and the Bundeswehr had prepared for it together. They would need to decide in advance which plants must remain operational, which civilian orders could be postponed, and how scarce electricity would be allocated when civilian and military demand collided.
During the Cold War, a significant part of NATO’s continental industrial and logistical base was located in West Germany, close to the expected central front. Today, Germany hosts much of the relevant industrial base, while Poland must provide secure and resilient routes toward the east, where the Baltic states would form the most exposed part of NATO’s northeastern flank. The geography has changed, but the division of responsibility has not fully caught up. German planning and Polish infrastructure would have to function as one system, yet it remains unclear who would be responsible for keeping it moving after the first disruption.
What the Next Zloty Buys
What Warsaw surely knows is how to increase its defense budget. In 2026 Poland will spend 200 billion zlotys, which is 4.8 percent of its GDP. More than half of this sum will be spent on new military equipment. The scale is impressive, but it raises a harder question: What should the next zloty buy? Instead of being put toward another 500-million-dollar military platform the next zloty may be better spent on recruiting and training repair units, developing antidrone and missile-defense capabilities, and strengthening the security of transport routes. Yet the repair network depends on another vulnerable system: energy.
In 2024, the EU was 96.6 percent dependent on imports of crude oil and petroleum products; Germany’s overall energy dependency rate was 67 percent. Europe has multiple suppliers, storage capacity, and a large refining system, so its fuel reserves would not disappear overnight. The more immediate problem is distribution: Fuel may be available elsewhere in Europe but fail to reach a factory if a port or railway connection is disabled.
Gas and electricity create different vulnerabilities. Military production would increase demand just as civilian industry tried to preserve its own output. Households would eventually bear part of the cost. A more immediate operational risk would be a blackout caused by sabotage against the power grid. The loss of a large power transformer would be particularly difficult to manage. According to an International Energy Agency report, a replacement may take up to four years to manufacture and deliver.
A blackout would not only shut down factories. It could also halt operations at workshops and railway facilities needed to return damaged equipment to service. In a prolonged conflict, repair would become as important as replacement. A new armored vehicle may take months to produce and deliver, while a damaged one could return much sooner if the right parts, tools, and mechanics were available. Poland would therefore serve not only as a corridor for equipment moving east, but also as a repair base for vehicles arriving from the opposite direction. This would expose another weakness: European armies operate many different platforms, each requiring its own spare parts, diagnostic tools, and maintenance procedures. The result can be absurd: A machine worth millions may spend weeks waiting for one certified part or one mechanic authorized to touch it. Poland, Germany, and the manufacturers would need to agree in advance what could be repaired locally, which components should be stored nearby, and when substitutes could be used. Such arrangements should be tested before a crisis rather than improvised after damaged vehicles begin arriving.
When the Chain Breaks
The European Union’s military mobility package is intended to allow troops and equipment to move across Europe at speed and on a large scale. NATO has its own Logistics Action Plan, covering military movement, host-nation support, interoperability, and the sustainment of deployed forces. Poland and Germany have also signed a new defense cooperation agreement, which includes closer industrial cooperation, joint training, and exercises, with particular attention paid to the Baltic region. Publicly available documents, however, do not make clear whether the same exercise follows equipment from a German factory, through a Polish depot, and toward a Baltic unit, while assuming that a railway line, power connection, or port has been disabled. They say even less about the journey in the opposite direction, when damaged vehicles begin returning to workshops.
The expansion of German ammunition production shows why such planning cannot be left until a crisis. When Rheinmetall opened its new plant in Unterlüß in September 2025, the company planned to produce 25,000 artillery shells before the end of that year. It expected to deliver 140,000 in 2026 and reach an annual capacity of 350,000 only in 2027. The figures show the delay between a political decision and actual production. When Unterlüß reaches its planned capacity, Europe’s transport routes and depots must be ready to move the additional ammunition.
The Flags Will Be Fine
Poland is spending heavily, Germany is expanding production, the EU is addressing military mobility, and NATO is exercising the reinforcement of its eastern flank. The weakness lies in counting each improvement separately. These efforts now need to function together. Europe’s preparations should therefore be tested as one system—starting with a broken link to measure how quickly the rest of the system adjusts.
Poland and Germany already have enough institutions, declarations, and flags around conference tables. What they still need is an exercise that begins with a failure. A railway line is cut before dawn or a transformer fails at the workshop just as the first damaged vehicles are due to arrive. Such a test would bring the exercise closer to wartime reality.
Fortunately, Europe has friends who already know what to do. Ukrainian personnel have spent years recovering equipment from fields, replacing unavailable components, and keeping damaged infrastructure alive with whatever remained at hand. Their methods may lack the elegance of Brussels corridors, but they have been tested under fire.
Mika was a small warning. In a Baltic conflict, such incidents would become part of Europe’s daily reality. If that day ever came, we would quickly find out whether Europe’s leaders had prepared its infrastructure and industry for the demands of war.
Paweł Witczak is an analyst specializing in European security, Germany, and transatlantic relations. He works at the Institute for Eastern Studies Foundation in Warsaw and writes on European security, geopolitics, and strategic dependencies. He holds a postgraduate diploma in Eastern studies and a master’s degree in American studies from the University of Warsaw.

articles.title: GBP/EUR Surge: Can the Rally Continue? - investingLive
articles.summary: GBP/EUR Surge: Can the Rally Continue?  investingLive
articles.full_text:
Summary
- GBP/EUR hits May 2025 highs amid BoE rate hike bets and euro instability.
Sterling has strengthened against the euro as expectations of higher UK interest rates collide with growing uncertainty across European financial markets. On October 20, the pound reached its strongest level against the single currency since May 2025, with the exchange rate trading around 83.95 pence per euro (after a low at around 83.89). The currency was mostly supported by UK labour-market data that reinforced expectations of a Bank of England (BoE) rate increase on November 5.
EUR/GBP Daily Chart - Source: TradingView
However, the pound's advance is not simply a reflection of improving UK economic fundamentals. Political unrest in France, rising European sovereign borrowing costs and surging energy prices are also shaping currency markets. With money markets almost fully pricing in a 25-basis-point BoE rate hike, the key question is whether sterling can extend its gains or whether expectations have already gone too far.
BoE Rate-Hike Expectations Support Sterling, but the Labour Market Sends Mixed Signals
The latest UK employment figures have strengthened the case for monetary tightening, although they do not provide an unequivocal signal that the economy can withstand a prolonged cycle of rate increases.
Annual growth in regular wages reached 3.7% in the three months to August, exceeding economists' expectations of 3.6%. The unemployment rate also edged down to 4.7%, its lowest level since mid-2025, while preliminary payroll estimates suggested that employment conditions may be stabilising. These developments followed a run of stronger-than-expected UK economic data.
Employment Rate and Wage Growth in the UK - Source: Reuters
For the BoE, the combination matters because persistent wage growth can contribute to domestic inflation, particularly if labour costs remain elevated. If policymakers believe that inflation will stay above their 2% target for longer than expected, tighter monetary policy may be necessary.
Markets have responded accordingly. Money-market futures were almost fully pricing in a 25-basis-point increase at the November 5 meeting, which would lift the Bank Rate from 3.75% to 4%. Investors were also anticipating further increases into 2027, although expectations for a sustained tightening cycle remain less certain.
Higher expected UK interest rates can support sterling by improving the relative return available on pound-denominated assets. However, the latest employment report contains an important counterpoint.
The number of vacancies fell to 691,000 in the July-to-September period, its lowest level outside the pandemic era since 2014. The decline suggests that businesses, particularly smaller firms facing higher employment costs, remain reluctant to recruit. The Office for National Statistics also reported that payroll employment remained weaker than a year earlier.
This creates a gap between market expectations and the underlying economic picture. Wage growth and falling unemployment strengthen the argument for a November rate increase, but declining vacancies point to fragile labour demand.
The data therefore provide a stronger case for a possible near-term hike than for assuming that several additional increases will necessarily follow. If the BoE raises rates as expected but signals caution about subsequent decisions, some of sterling's monetary-policy support could fade.
European Political Turmoil Adds to the Euro's Vulnerability
Sterling is also benefiting from pressure on the euro, as investors reassess the political and fiscal outlook across Europe.
France has become a particular source of concern. Renewed demonstrations and unrest have added to uncertainty surrounding the government's ability to pass its 2027 budget and address the country's sizeable deficit. At the same time, French government bond yields have approached levels last seen in 2002, while the spread between French and German 10-year yields has widened significantly.
These developments matter for the single currency because persistent sovereign bond-market stress can undermine confidence in the eurozone's economic and financial stability. If investors begin to demand higher risk premiums across several member states, concerns about financial fragmentation could intensify. Of course, France's difficulties should not be treated as an automatic signal of a wider eurozone crisis. The implications for the single currency will depend on whether political and fiscal pressures remain concentrated in France or spread to other European markets.
For the GBP/EUR, the distinction is important. Sterling can appreciate because investors become more confident in the UK outlook, because they become less confident in the eurozone, or through a combination of both.
The Oil Shock Could Complicate the BoE's Next Move
The Middle East conflict introduces another variable that could reshape the outlook for sterling and the euro: energy prices.
Brent crude climbed above $111 per barrel on October 20, reaching its highest level since May, amid persistent disruption risks around the Strait of Hormuz and limited progress towards ending the conflict. The prospect of further interruptions to energy shipments has kept markets concerned about supply and inflation.
Daily UK Oil Chart - Source: ActivTrades
For the UK, higher oil and gas prices could push inflation higher through transport, household energy bills and business costs. If these pressures persist, the BoE may face greater difficulty bringing inflation back towards its 2% target, strengthening the argument for higher interest rates.
That could initially support sterling, particularly if investors expect the BoE to tighten policy more aggressively than the European Central Bank (ECB). Yet the relationship between energy prices, interest rates and currencies is not straightforward.
Higher energy costs also reduce households' disposable income, squeeze corporate margins and potentially weaken economic growth. If the shock becomes sufficiently severe, markets could begin to question whether further monetary tightening would damage the UK economy rather than simply contain inflation.
The BoE has already warned that prolonged energy-price volatility could make inflation more persistent and increase the likelihood of further tightening. Its September decision left Bank Rate at 3.75%, while acknowledging the risks arising from the conflict. The ECB faces a similar dilemma, although the consequences differ according to each economy's exposure to energy imports, inflation dynamics and fiscal position.
The key risk for sterling is therefore that the energy shock initially supports rate-hike expectations but eventually undermines the growth outlook. If markets begin to focus more heavily on the economic damage, the pound could lose some of its current advantage.
Can GBP/EUR Extend Its Rally?
The outlook for the GBP/EUR will depend on whether the BoE delivers the expected rate increase and how policymakers assess the risks beyond November. Three scenarios stand out.
Sterling could extend its gains if UK inflation remains persistent, the BoE raises rates and French political uncertainty continues to weigh on the euro. A further widening in expected UK-eurozone interest-rate differentials could provide additional support, although much will depend on how much tightening is already reflected in market prices.
The currency pair could consolidate if the November hike is delivered but the BoE signals that subsequent decisions will depend on incoming data. With vacancies falling and hiring demand remaining weak, policymakers may be reluctant to validate expectations of a prolonged series of increases. If European market tensions also ease, sterling's relative advantage could diminish.
The euro could recover if energy prices retreat, political risks in Europe subside or markets reassess the expected pace of UK monetary tightening. A deterioration in British growth prospects could also undermine sterling, particularly if higher energy costs squeeze household spending and corporate profitability.
For traders, the distinction between the expected November decision and the outlook for rates in 2027 is important. A widely anticipated rate increase may provide limited additional support if it is already priced into the GBP/EUR evolution. Future price movements could depend more on the BoE's guidance, inflation data and developments in the Middle East.

articles.title: Spain’s DANA claims 5 lives: What is the deadly weather phenomenon? - Euronews.com
articles.summary: Spain’s DANA claims 5 lives: What is the deadly weather phenomenon?  Euronews.comResidents winched from rooftops as torrential rain hits eastern Spain  ReutersTwo dead and thousands evacuated as Dana Adam dumps over 600mm of rain on Valencia and Alicante  Sur in EnglishDrivers rescued from rising floodwaters in Costa Blanca motorway tunnel after deadly Storm Adam dumps 700mm of rain in less than an hour  Olive Press News SpainIs it safe to travel to Spain?...
articles.full_text:
A DANA caused the deadly flooding in Valencia in 2024 which killed 200 people.
A storm in eastern Spain has killed five people and left cars and streets submerged in water, and the DANA weather system is behind it.
Storm Adam dumped 700 litres of rain per square metre in just 24 hours in some areas of the Valencia region. Floodwaters swept away parked cars, submerged roads and cut off residents, some of whom had to be airlifted to safety by emergency crews.
The coastal resort of Oliva was one of the areas worst hit by Sunday night’s storms. A 79-year-old woman was found dead in her home, while a man suffered a fatal heart attack at a local campsite. The third victim was a man who drowned while swimming at a beach in Sagunto. Firefighters in neighbouring Catalonia also reported the death of a woman who fell into a rain-swollen stream.
Storm Adam is reminiscent of the sudden downpours that devastated Valencia in 2024, when some areas saw a year’s worth of rain in just 24 hours. 200 people lost their lives, making it one of the worst flood-related disasters in Europe since the late-1960s and the worst in Spain for many decades.
The government came under heavy criticism for the lack of warnings to the public about what was to come. Thankfully they appear to have learnt their lesson: warnings were sent to mobile phones before Storm Adam hit, urging people to avoid travelling, stay away from rivers and ravines, and seek shelter on higher ground or on the upper floors of buildings.
The 2024 storm introduced many Europeans to a weather phenomenon that often hits Spain: DANA. What is it and is it becoming more deadly as the climate warms up?
What is a DANA?
DANA stands for ‘Depresión Aislada en Niveles Altos’. It’s not easy to translate into English but it essentially means periods of heavy rain, stormy weather and a sudden drop in temperatures.
The bigger the temperature difference, the bigger the storm. This is why the worst DANAs are usually at the end of summer in September and October, and are more likely to happen in parts of southern and eastern Spain.
Put simply a DANA is a very intense wind current that forms when it breaks away from a polar jet, a sort of pocket of cold air surrounded by warmer air that can move around and cause extreme weather. It’s the meeting of hot and cold air fronts causing extreme weather.
Southeastern Spain is particularly vulnerable to DANAs because it’s where the Atlantic and Mediterranean meet, meaning that cold air fronts can meet warm air fronts at certain times of year. It’s also an area where mountains favour the formation of storm clouds and therefore rainfall.
DANA is increasingly used in everyday language in Spain
Some Spanish people now use the term DANA to refer to a big storm, but this hasn’t always been the case.
For many years Spaniards have used the phrase ‘gota fría’, literally meaning ‘cold drop’, The Local Spain explains. But as technology has advanced, and it has become easier to predict and understand the weather, meteorologists say that DANA is a more useful term because it’s more specific.
On its website, Spain’s meteorological agency Aemet explains that: “The term gota frìa is a relatively old concept and has been superseded over the years. New ways of understanding tropospheric processes and new observational tools have made us revise and redefine the ideas linked to these isolated pockets of cold air at higher levels.
“We believe that the concept of DANA, which we associate with the Anglo-Saxon term ‘cut-off low’, is more accurate and realistic than that of gota fría. As the concept of a gota fría is not very precise and incomplete, it is understood that it should be replaced by a more modern one.”
Is climate change making DANAs worse?
The Valencia floods in 2024 made worldwide news, with many shocked by the scale of loss and devastation in a wealthy European country. Much analysis followed, with climate scientists asking what role global warming played.
It was confirmed that a DANA was to blame and that global warming very likely made it worse.
“No doubt about it, these explosive downpours were intensified by climate change,” Dr Friederike Otto, lead of World Weather Attribution at the Centre for Environmental Policy, Imperial College London, said in 2024.
The floods were caused by a ‘cut-off low pressure storm system’ that had migrated from an unusually wavy, stalled jet stream. This system then got stuck over the region, pouring down a year’s worth of rain in eight hours.
Unusually warm sea surface temperatures, made much more likely by human-caused climate change, and our warming atmosphere, however, directly impact how much rain these storms can hold. The ground in many parts of eastern and southern Spain had also been left less able to effectively absorb rainwater following severe drought.
A rapid partial analysis done by Dr Otto’s group of international scientists suggested that human-caused climate change made Spain’s rainfall around 12 per cent heavier. It also found that the weather event the region experienced was twice as likely.
Though it isn’t a full, detailed attribution study, they said climate change is the most likely explanation for the extreme downpours.
“With every fraction of a degree of fossil fuel warming, the atmosphere can hold more moisture, leading to heavier bursts of rainfall. These deadly floods are yet another reminder of how dangerous climate change has already become at just 1.3°C of warming,” Otto adds.

articles.title: Automakers warn against excluding Türkiye from ‘Made in EU’ plan - PressReader
articles.summary: Automakers warn against excluding Türkiye from ‘Made in EU’ plan  PressReader
articles.full_text:
Excluding Türkiye from stricter “Made in EU” auto rules, backed by France and Germany to counter Chinese competition, could raise costs, disrupt supply chains and erode Europe’s competitive edge, industry representatives have warned.
French President Emmanuel Macron’s plan to protect the European automotive industry against China has sparked debate. Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz agreed to lower the 2035 emissions target from 100 percent to 90 percent and tighten “Made in EU” measures. Under the plan, internal combustion vehicles would still be allowed to be sold after 2035, while EU production requirements in public procurement would be strengthened and vehicles would be required to contain 70 percent European-origin parts.
However, manufacturers such as Toyota, Ford and Hyundai warn that excluding trade partners such as Türkiye would raise costs and weaken both supply chains and Europe’s competitiveness.
Yoshihiro Nakata, President and CEO of Toyota Motor Europe, said in Brussels that Europe should adopt a “Made with Europe” approach rather than “Made in Europe.” Nakata said that including reliable trade partners such as Türkiye, the U.K. and Japan would expand Europe’s production and market scale to around 31 million vehicles, which is necessary for global competitiveness.
Toyota also proposed increasing the European-origin content requirement to 70 percent after a three-year transition period and called for Customs Union partners such as Türkiye to remain within the framework.
Jim Baumbick, President of Ford Europe, also objected to the proposed rules. Baumbick said production in Türkiye and the U.K. should be evaluated together with factories inside the EU.
“Made in Europe should be measured by where value is created, not where the last bolt is tightened,” he said. Using the electric Ford Transit Custom produced in Türkiye as an example, Baumbick noted that the vehicle is engineered in the U.K. and Germany, its electric motor is produced in the U.K. and its battery in the EU. More than half of the vehicle’s component value originates from EU countries, he added.
“By any economic measure, this is a European vehicle,” Baumbick said, warning that excluding Türkiye would also weaken manufacturing inside the EU.
Xavier Martinet, CEO of Hyundai Europe, previously said Türkiye should be treated fairly and included in the “Made in EU” process.
“If Türkiye is not included, we may have to look at alternative scenarios. But I think that would create a lose-lose situation for everyone. If some vehicles that can be produced in Türkiye have to be produced in Europe, they will certainly become more expensive. In the end, if customers can no longer afford to buy certain vehicles because they have become too expensive, then Europe also loses,” Martinet said.
The compromise between France and Germany marked a turning point in discussions over Europe’s protectionist legislation. However, there is still no final European Union decision. If Türkiye is left outside the framework, industry representatives say the cost of the protective wall Europe wants to build against China could ultimately be borne by European consumers. Last year, the EU exported 812,000 cars worth 18.8 billion euros to Türkiye, while Türkiye exported 798,000 vehicles worth 18.2 billion euros to the EU. Total two-way automotive trade reached 37 billion euros. Europe accounts for 73.7 percent of Türkiye’s automotive exports, while Eu-origin vehicles represent 73 percent of Türkiye’s imported car market. Automotive products account for 26 percent of total Türkiye-eu trade. Türkiye has been a destination for investment by European automakers for 55 years. Total investment over the past 55 years has reached 21 billion euros.

articles.title: Phosphate Water System Inhibitors Market To 2035: Water-Reuse Mandates Drive Demand - News and Statistics - IndexBox
articles.summary: Phosphate Water System Inhibitors Market To 2035: Water-Reuse Mandates Drive Demand - News and Statistics  IndexBox
articles.full_text:
Abstract
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Phosphate Water System Inhibitors market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The world market for phosphate water system inhibitors is entering a structurally supported growth phase, with demand projected to expand at a compound annual rate of 4.5–5.5% over the 2026–2035 forecast period. These specialty formulations, which form passivating films on metal surfaces to prevent corrosion and scale in water loops, are increasingly critical as industrial operators confront tighter phosphorus-discharge limits and higher water-reuse rates. More than 60% of global demand originates from three end-use clusters: conventional power and steam generation, chemical processing, and semiconductor fabrication.
The latter is growing 1.5–2 percentage points faster than traditional heavy-industry applications, as fab investments in Asia and North America raise the installed base of high-purity water circuits requiring stabilized phosphate blends. Supply remains moderately concentrated, with the top five multinational producers accounting for roughly 40–45% of global capacity, while regional blenders and distributors serve the remainder through contract manufacturing.
The market is also witnessing a shift from orthophosphate to stabilized phosphate blends—such as zinc-phosphate and organophosphonate hybrids—driven by stricter discharge rules and the need for higher thermal stability in closed-loop cooling systems. Raw-material cost volatility, particularly for phosphoric acid and technical-grade monoammonium phosphate, remains a persistent margin pressure point, while regulatory fragmentation across regions complicates product registrations and compliance planning for global suppliers.
The baseline scenario for the phosphate water system inhibitors market assumes a continuation of current regulatory trajectories, industrial water-reuse adoption, and capital investment patterns in key end-use sectors. Under this scenario, global demand is forecast to grow at a 4.5–5.5% CAGR from 2026 to 2035, with the market index reaching approximately 155 (2025=100) by the end of the forecast period.
Growth is not uniform across segments: electronics and precision manufacturing are expected to outpace the broader market, expanding at a rate 1.5–2 percentage points above the aggregate, as semiconductor fabrication capacity expands in Asia-Pacific and North America and as precision-component rinsing requirements tighten. Conventional power and steam generation remains the largest volume segment but faces moderate growth as plant additions slow in mature markets; however, retrofit and maintenance demand in existing cooling towers and boilers provides a stable base. Chemical processing follows a similar pattern, with demand supported by ongoing capacity additions in Asia and the Middle East.
The supply side is expected to remain moderately concentrated, with the top five producers holding 40–45% of capacity, though regional blenders will continue to capture share in price-sensitive markets. Pricing is likely to remain volatile in the near term due to phosphoric acid and monoammonium phosphate cost swings, but contract structures with service-level agreements are expected to stabilize revenue for formulators. Regulatory fragmentation—particularly between EU phosphorus-discharge limits and less stringent regimes in parts of Latin America and Africa—will continue to shape product portfolios, favoring suppliers with flexible formulation capabilities and local registration expertise.
Demand Drivers and Constraints
Primary Demand Drivers
- Tightening phosphorus-discharge regulations in the EU and North America, which push operators toward stabilized phosphate blends and higher-performance inhibitor formulations.
- Rising industrial water-reuse rates, particularly in cooling towers and boiler systems, which increase the need for corrosion and scale protection in closed-loop circuits.
- Accelerated semiconductor fabrication investment in Asia-Pacific and North America, driving demand for phosphate inhibitors in ultrapure-water and precision-cooling applications.
- Growth in blended procurement models combining standard-grade inhibitors with monitoring and dosing service agreements, expanding the addressable market for formulators.
- Expansion of chemical processing and power generation capacity in Asia and the Middle East, supporting baseline demand for conventional phosphate inhibitor formulations.
- Transition from orthophosphate to stabilized phosphate blends (zinc-phosphate and organophosphonate hybrids) that offer higher thermal stability and lower phosphorus discharge.
Potential Growth Constraints
- Raw-material cost volatility, especially for phosphoric acid and technical-grade monoammonium phosphate, creating margin pressure and frequent contract price adjustments.

articles.title: Why the Mercosur-EU deal faces resistance despite gains - Valor International
articles.summary: Why the Mercosur-EU deal faces resistance despite gains  Valor International
articles.full_text:
Why the Mercosur-EU deal faces resistance despite gains
Nearly six months after taking effect provisionally, the pact is boosting trade but remains politically sensitive in Europe
Atualizado
As it approaches its first six months in effect, the Mercosur-European Union Agreement is gaining commercial momentum but still provokes strong reactions and mistrust across the Atlantic. Since taking effect on May 1, the agreement has become something of a taboo subject in European newspapers. It has acquired a political dimension that makes openly defending it difficult amid the current zeitgeist.
Mercosur has become a target because of the perceived threat it poses to Europe’s heavily subsidized agricultural sector, which accounts for 5% of the region’s GDP. Farmers wield significant political influence, make their voices heard, and can cause considerable electoral damage. Brazil’s meat industry knows this all too well. Many French people say the Southern Cone bloc will wipe out their livestock industry.
That was the mood late last year, when the EU ordered hundreds of cattle slaughtered because of an outbreak of lumpy skin disease.
“Now Brazil will bring in all the meat it possibly can,” actress Marine Bordet said at a cocktail reception, before being surprised to learn that, under the agreement’s quotas, Brazil cannot sell France more than the equivalent of one hamburger per French person each year.
Remnants of stickers bearing the word “Mercosur” crossed out with a thick black slash can still be seen on road signs in the French countryside. In supermarkets, signs and references emphasizing products’ local origins are prominently displayed.
Europeans have yet to grasp the significance of the agreement, which was painstakingly brought to fruition, or have not been convinced of its merits. That may reflect Brussels bureaucracy’s perennial difficulty communicating with citizens. The agreement was signed only after a quarter-century of negotiations, propelled by the climate of uncertainty created by the sweeping tariffs and unilateral measures adopted by Donald Trump’s United States.
The problem is that the agreement is in force only provisionally and still requires approval from the EU Court of Justice. The European Parliament demanded the review, as it is responsible for giving the agreement its final approval.
“It is an agreement that is easier to envision from a multinational and multilateral perspective. But once it enters each country’s domestic politics, it becomes much harder to envision or justify. Many politicians have remained silent about it. In part, the hope is to get it through quietly, without people really noticing or mobilizing,” said Christopher Sabatini, a Latin America expert at London-based think tank Chatham House.
The lack of enthusiasm and understanding so far could heighten a risk identified by experts interviewed by Valor: with elections scheduled in Brazil and key EU countries in 2027, the agreement may be approaching its most delicate phase. Sabatini called it “a dangerous period,” as some European leaders will be reluctant to defend the agreement, speak publicly about it, or press for its approval.
Sabatini said some groups affected by opening their markets to Brazilian agricultural exports or imports will mobilize and use their concerns to justify opposing the agreement. That may not be well received in Brazil, particularly under a potential Flávio Bolsonaro administration.
“Attempts to impose restrictions related to deforestation, cattle traceability, and all these measures designed to ensure there is no illegal farming will face resistance from a significant portion of Bolsonaro’s electoral base,” he noted.
Immersed in what seems like a permanent existential crisis, the European bloc is confronting the rise of the far right while seeking to define its place on the geopolitical map between the United States and China.
France will hold a presidential election next year, and the far right appears to be thriving. Although Emmanuel Macron has shown sympathy for the agreement and told Lula and his advisers as much, the political narrative has become so dominant that it is now difficult for the French president to reverse his opposition to the pact.
On January 8, about 100 tractors entered the French capital before dawn despite a police ban. Some reached the Arc de Triomphe and the Eiffel Tower before farmers gathered outside Parliament carrying flags and banners warning of growing pressure on their livelihoods. “Mercosur mort à coup sûr”—a play on words roughly meaning “Mercosur, certain death”—read one prominent sign.
The argument resonated in several EU countries, including Poland and Ireland. Poland sought to suspend the agreement’s provisional application before the EU Court of Justice, which rejected the request on September 29. In Bulgaria, an article in the newspaper “Trud” argued that the agreement’s true nature was not partnership but political opportunism, turning European agriculture into a bargaining chip to secure better access for industrial goods—including cars, chemicals, and machinery—to South America’s vast market.
There are exceptions, however, such as Austria, whose exports to Mercosur totaling €1.9 billion supported at least 32,000 direct jobs in the country even before the agreement. In September 2019, the Austrian Parliament’s EU subcommittee voted almost unanimously against the proposed agreement, arguing that the Southern Cone countries did not meet sustainability requirements.
Austria’s national industry federation pushed back, warning against “populist scaremongering and free-trade myths” and emphasizing that the agreement includes commitments to the Paris climate accord and efforts to combat deforestation in the Amazon.
EU data shows that small businesses account for 95% of all Austrian exporters and stand to benefit most, as they often struggle to export outside the EU because of additional costs and administrative procedures. Even the president of Austria’s central bank supported the agreement late last year.
In the small state of Salzburg, local industry associations have also emphasized that its international orientation is one of the state’s principal strengths and that the agreement creates new market opportunities for the local economy in sectors that will be critical in the future, “particularly in the green transition, since Mercosur countries could become important partners because of their raw materials and rare-earth resources.”
Two-way trade between Brazil and the EU totaled $49.9 billion between May, when the agreement took effect, and September. That was a 16.6% increase from the same period in 2025. Brazilian exports drove the result, rising 30.7% to $27.3 billion. Imports from the EU rose by a smaller percentage, 3.1%, but climbed to $22.6 billion.
Brazil recorded a $4.7 billion surplus during the period, a significant reversal from May through September 2025, when it posted a trade deficit of $965.9 million.
With a large share of tariffs eliminated immediately in the initial phase, some products recorded triple-digit or greater increases in shipments to Europe. In other categories, gains were equally substantial, or even larger.
Data compiled for Valor by the Ministry of Development, Industry, Trade and Services (MDIC) shows exceptional growth in some categories. Exports of tanks, vats and similar containers made of cast iron, iron or steel and holding more than 300 liters, for example, surged 14,695% between 2025 and 2026. Exports of other dryers for wood, paper pulp, paper or paperboard increased 4,325%.
Transformer exports reached $39.1 million, while machinery and equipment used to manufacture paper or paperboard generated $3.4 million and other gas turbines accounted for $2 million. Those products, whose tariffs fell to zero from 3.7%, 1.7%, and 4.1%, respectively, had not been exported during the same period in 2025, according to MDIC data.
“We are talking about Brazil’s most important trade agreement in the past 30 years. It is still too early to assess all its effects, but the initial results are very encouraging, with strong growth in two-way trade driven by Brazilian exports,” said Tatiana Prazeres, the ministry’s foreign trade secretary, who described the negotiation of the agreement as a historic step.
The priority now, Prazeres said, is implementation. “That is where tariff preferences, negotiated rules and greater predictability for trade must translate into investment, competitiveness gains, and new opportunities for companies,” she said.
The gains have come primarily from the first round of tariff reductions. Brazilian exports in this group rose particularly sharply, from $1.8 billion between May and September 2025 to $2.6 billion during the same period in 2026—an increase of 40.9%, according to MDIC data.
Many tariffs will be eliminated only over the coming decade. Beatrice Peanuts, one of the world’s largest peanut producers, estimates that its exports to Europe will rise by at least 30% by the end of the tariff phaseout period for its processed products, which will take about 10 years.
Pablo Javera, the company’s director, is optimistic. Europe is the largest market for Brazilian peanuts and pays the highest prices. The gains are primarily tariff-related, he said, because the industry has already undergone a rigorous process of adapting to European rules, which change fairly frequently.
Brazil’s largest competitor in the European market is Argentina, which is also covered by the agreement. The neighboring country, however, does not yet meet all control requirements. Javera said membership in the agreement provides no sanitary advantages, but it does create an institutional framework with rules that must be followed.
Beatrice’s products were hit by the sweeping U.S. tariffs, which were imposed suddenly and forced the company, based in rural São Paulo state, to redirect its products primarily to the EU.
