articles.title: EU Tightens 'European-Made' Rules in IAA, Threatening South Korea - 조선일보
articles.summary: EU Tightens 'European-Made' Rules in IAA, Threatening South Korea  조선일보
articles.full_text:
Germany and France, Europe’s two leading automotive powers, are pushing to tighten the criteria for recognizing “European-made” products in the European Union’s proposed Industrial Acceleration Act (IAA), a form of trade barrier, deepening concerns in the global automotive industry. While the move targets Chinese eco-friendly vehicles, South Korea—a country with a free trade agreement (FTA) with the EU—could also face unintended repercussions if the regulations become overly stringent.
The IAA includes non-tariff barriers aimed at expanding EU production of eco-friendly vehicles and secondary batteries. For eco-friendly vehicles, the draft law stipulates preferential treatment, such as subsidies, if the final assembly occurs in an EU member state and at least 70% of components (excluding batteries) are sourced from Europe.
According to industry sources on October 20, Germany and France agreed on October 16 to narrow the scope of “European-made” components to the EU’s 27 member states and select European countries like the UK. The March draft of the IAA had initially proposed extending European status to parts produced in FTA partner countries, including South Korea. However, recent factors such as France’s fiscal challenges and Volkswagen’s historic restructuring have reportedly influenced the two nations to advocate for stricter origin criteria.
Hyundai Motor and Kia sold approximately 200,000 electric vehicles in Europe from January to September this year, with 37% produced locally, including in Turkey. However, Turkey is not an EU member state, raising concerns that its components might not qualify as “European-made” under the final IAA. Additionally, Hyundai and Kia’s factories in EU member states like the Czech Republic and Slovakia rely heavily on Korean-sourced parts, meaning they may need to increase local procurement to meet the 70% threshold. This could necessitate costly expansions of European component facilities and negatively impact South Korean auto parts exporters.
In response, the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources launched a public-private task force on October 15 to address the IAA. It has also urged the EU to treat South Korea, as an FTA partner, equally with EU member states. The ministry argues that South Korean companies have significantly contributed to the EU’s economy and supply chains through investments in local production facilities, making discriminatory treatment unjustified.

articles.title: French presidential race largely unaffected by unrest, first post-riot poll shows - POLITICO.eu
articles.summary: French presidential race largely unaffected by unrest, first post-riot poll shows  POLITICO.eu
articles.full_text:
PARIS — The first publicly available poll following the violence that rocked France over the weekend showed little change in voter intentions in next spring’s presidential election.
While even some of far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen’s adversaries expected her to get a boost from the rioting and looting that took place on the sidelines of peaceful protests on Saturday, the survey published by Ifop and Fiducial found little change in her support levels.
Nor was there much change in voting intentions toward far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, whom the government has repeatedly blamed for stoking the violence. Mélenchon and his allies have repeatedly and forcefully denied the accusation.

Customers are set to benefit as the Healthy Start top-up for low-income families with young children returns
Sainsbury's has confirmed it will become the "first" UK supermarket to introduce a £3 offer for shoppers - with a new policy. Customers are set to benefit as the Healthy Start top-up for low-income families with young children returns.
The scheme, for shoppers in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, will see customers eligible to apply for an additional £3 a week towards fruit, vegetables, beans and pulses for six weeks.
It is the first retailer to offer it, Sainsbury's has said in an announcement on Tuesday (October 20). Eligible customers can sign up to receive a £3 eGift card by email each week for six weeks from 18 November, which can be used in store and online.

articles.title: Extremists could exploit unrest in France amid violent protests, expert warns - The Jerusalem Post
articles.summary: Extremists could exploit unrest in France amid violent protests, expert warns  The Jerusalem Post
articles.full_text:
France is confronting one of its worst episodes of civil unrest in years after weeks of student demonstrations over deteriorating school conditions converged with nationwide protests against the rising cost of living, culminating in riots, looting, and attacks on public buildings.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Hundreds of thousands of people demonstrated across the country on October 17, with turnout estimates ranging from 550,000, according to authorities, to 800,000, according to organizers. Most participants protested peacefully, but violent clashes erupted in Paris, Lyon, Marseille, and several other cities.
Approximately 2,400 people were arrested over the weekend, nearly 1,000 police officers and gendarmes were injured, and about 3,000 businesses were damaged or looted. In Paris, a demonstrator died after suffering a cardiac arrest, with no reported evidence linking his death to police actions.
Among the most serious incidents was an arson attack on the historic City Hall in Limoges, where flames devastated much of the 19th-century building, causing most of its roof to collapse.
The violence has placed President Emmanuel Macron’s government under mounting pressure. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez acknowledged that security forces had lost control in several cities and offered his resignation, which Macron rejected. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu backed localized curfews, which authorities began imposing on Monday in parts of Paris and other cities to prevent further disorder.
French officials have attributed much of the violence to far-left extremists and opportunistic looters. The scale of the destruction has also prompted wider questions about how social grievances developed into a national security crisis, whether extremist networks are exploiting the unrest, and what the consequences could be for France’s political future.
From economic grievances to violence
The initial student demonstrations began in September over teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms, and inadequate educational facilities. Their grievances subsequently converged with a separate movement against rising fuel prices and living costs, bringing together students, trade unions, and participants in the Yellow Vest movement, which emerged in 2018.
For Sharon Adarlo, a conflict analyst, editor, and operations and research director at Militant Wire, economic hardship remains central to understanding the demonstrations.
Adarlo told The Media Line: “People are motivated by concerns over the high cost of living—the overarching concern. That must fuel rage and feelings that they have little stake in the safety and harmony of commercial corridors in Paris.”
Similar economic pressures have generated protests elsewhere in Europe, including demonstrations over housing, public services, and declining purchasing power, although the immediate causes and political circumstances differ from country to country.
Counterterrorism and extremist groups expert Daniele Garofalo argues that the grievances driving the demonstrations must be distinguished from the actions of those responsible for the violence.
“These grievances explain the support for the protests, but they are not sufficient to explain arson, looting, and attacks against institutions,” Garofalo told The Media Line.
He believes relatively small groups can exert considerable influence over demonstrations, even when most participants remain peaceful.
“The influence of a radical component does not depend solely on its numbers: even a small group can affect the outcome of a demonstration if it succeeds in provoking confrontation,” he explained.
The disorder has exposed weaknesses in France’s security preparations. Despite warnings of possible violence, authorities struggled to protect commercial districts and public buildings. Some local officials criticized the government for failing to provide sufficient police protection, while security officials acknowledged that the size and organization of the demonstrations had proved difficult to anticipate.
Lecornu has accused radical left-wing groups of seeking to destabilize the country ahead of the 2027 presidential election. Left-wing political figures have disputed the allegations and demanded evidence.
Islamist networks and the question of extremist cooperation
The riots have also revived questions about a possible so-called red-green alliance, a term used to describe cooperation between radical left-wing movements and Islamist networks around particular political causes.
Although these movements differ ideologically, some groups have cooperated in opposition to particular policies or political adversaries. Whether such cooperation has played any role in France’s current unrest remains unproven.
Garofalo cautions against attributing the violence to Islamist organizations without supporting evidence.
“Based on verified public sources and the various private channels monitored, there is insufficient evidence to attribute a significant operational role in the violence to the Muslim Brotherhood or other Islamist organizations. Making such a claim today would go beyond what the available evidence supports,” he said.
The potential influence of Islamist networks in France has previously attracted government scrutiny. In May 2025, the French Interior Ministry published a report titled Frères musulmans et islamisme politique en France (Muslim Brotherhood and Political Islamism in France), examining Muslim Brotherhood-linked networks and their influence through associations and local institutions.
The report generated political controversy over the extent of the threat posed by political Islamism, but it predates the current unrest and provides no evidence connecting those networks to the riots.
Garofalo distinguishes between organizing violence and exploiting instability after it occurs.
“Moreover, a network can exploit a crisis without having caused it, using it for propaganda, establishing contacts, mobilization, or strengthening its influence,” he explained.
The possibility that extremist organizations might seek to benefit politically from the disorder does not establish that they directed or coordinated the violence.
Social media and foreign interference concerns
The role of social media has attracted attention because the October 17 mobilization was promoted extensively online before developing into nationwide demonstrations.
The initial call to protest rising fuel prices appeared on TikTok in September. As student demonstrations gathered momentum, the proposed date attracted wider support, including from participants in the Yellow Vest movement.
According to figures published by Le Monde from social media monitoring company Visibrain, approximately 460,000 posts concerning the October 17 mobilization circulated between September 27 and October 16. Videos mentioning the protest date accumulated approximately 132 million views on TikTok.
The expression Gilets Jeunes, or Young Vests, emerged online as a play on Gilets Jaunes, the French name for the Yellow Vest movement, reflecting the convergence of student demands and broader economic grievances.
Adarlo believes the online attention has encouraged some participants to seek visibility through “aura farming,” a social media practice involving efforts to attract attention and enhance one’s online reputation.
“There needs to be a productive conversation about social media. Lots of the protesters are using TikTok and other platforms to ‘aura farm’ during the protests, which is no doubt fanning the flames,” she said.
The possibility of foreign interference presents another concern, given Russia’s history of using online influence operations to exploit divisions within European societies.
Adarlo warned: “In regard to a green-red alliance, the protesters have valid claims, but we can’t dismiss the possibility of foreign interference stoking underlying social unrest, particularly on social media. Russians are adept at using social engineering techniques to amplify societal tension.”
There is no established evidence that Russia organized or directed the current protests.
In September, France’s foreign digital interference monitoring agency, Viginum, told Le Monde that it had detected only limited and largely opportunistic foreign activity surrounding the original online calls to protest. Some suspicious accounts promoting the demonstrations appeared to be seeking followers or commercial visibility rather than advancing a coordinated foreign political operation.
The policing dilemma and France’s political future
For the French government, restoring public order without further inflaming tensions has become an urgent challenge.
The destruction has prompted demands for tougher policing, while serious injuries during police interventions have intensified scrutiny of crowd-control tactics.
In Saint-Étienne, a 17-year-old demonstrator lost his right hand during the October 17 protests after a grenade launched by security forces exploded. Investigators are examining the circumstances, including reports that the teenager picked up the grenade before it detonated. The Saint-Étienne prosecutor’s office opened an investigation, assigning it jointly to France’s national police and gendarmerie oversight agencies, the IGPN and IGGN.
Garofalo warns that both inadequate policing and an indiscriminate crackdown could deepen the crisis.
“An insufficient response may reinforce the perception of impunity; an indiscriminate response may extend the crisis to groups that did not initially support the confrontations,” he said.
The political consequences could extend beyond the immediate security response. Garofalo considers it plausible that the violence could strengthen demands for tougher immigration policies and border controls ahead of the 2027 presidential election. Such measures, he cautions, would not necessarily address violence involving individuals already living in France.

articles.title: The rioting across France is a symptom of a much larger public and political crisis - Egypt Independent
articles.summary: The rioting across France is a symptom of a much larger public and political crisis  Egypt Independent
articles.full_text:
“We have a mess on our hands, to put it bluntly,” French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said Monday.
If anything, he might be guilty of understatement. After widespread rioting at the weekend – estimated to have cost several hundred million dollars in property damage and theft – France faces a toxic mix of urban rebellion, drift and economic crisis.
The disorder at the weekend occurred in major cities across the country, leading Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez to offer his resignation because of the police’s failure to contain the rioting.
There was rampant looting in Paris, Marseille, Bordeaux and other cities, while the city hall in Limoges, which survived two world wars, was badly damaged by fire and its clock spire collapsed.
The violence at the weekend, which led to some 2,400 arrests, followed weeks of protests by French students angry about crumbling schools, a lack of teachers and dismal job prospects. More than 6,000 arrests were made during the school protests that began at the start of the fall term and more than 100 schools were damaged.
More demonstrations are scheduled for next weekend. In November, labor unions plan to strike.
France faces a winter of discontent in the run-up to a presidential election next spring. The far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is leading in the polls.
Political drift
In a national televised address Sunday, President Emmanuel Macron condemned the violence but did not set out ideas to deal with it or seize the initiative. Instead, he warned of politicians seizing on the chaos for political gain – before leaving France for a three-day visit to the Gulf states.
Lecornu similarly deployed the blame game. After far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon accused the government of “opening the door to chaos” with its policing tactics, Lecornu shot back: “You cannot call for an end to the violence while providing excuses to those who commit it. This is YOUR political responsibility.”
Le Pen, who is standing in the presidential election for the far-right National Rally party, has sought to inject the issue of migration into the debate, blaming the violence on delinquents from France’s banlieues, poor urban areas where much of the country’s migrant population lives.
“Our country is caught in a vice…between violence and powerlessness,” she said, suggesting only her firm hand could restore order amid Macron’s “chaos.”
The president of her National Rally party, Jordan Bardella, poured fuel on the fire, demanding that “Antifa militias, far-left extremist groups and Black Bloc groups” be designated as terrorist organisations.”
Black Bloc groups wear matching or similar black clothing along with face masks during protests to hide their identity.
Analysts say this political fragmentation, which led to the paralysis of parliament after snap elections called by Macron in 2024 backfired, is likely to persist – and is at the core of France’s deepening crisis.
The political center in France has evaporated, allowing the National Rally and Mélenchon’s far-left France Unbowed party to harvest growing public exasperation, while Macron’s successive prime ministers have been unable to pass a budget through Parliament.
The multitude of candidates in the center, “most with relatively few supporters, will ultimately help secure the second-round election for one of the two contenders who represent the greatest danger to democracy in France,” wrote Robert Zaretsky, a professor of modern French history at the University of Houston, in an essay for the Atlantic.
Debt and déclinisme
The current crisis has polarized an already deeply divided society. Besides the shock and anger at the weekend’s mayhem, there is an air of defeatism. In a recent Ipsos-BVA poll, 85% of respondents said that France was in decline, and 98% were dissatisfied with the present state of the country.
Whoever governs France next will have shrinking room for maneuver, even if they can stitch together a stable coalition.
The French economy is stagnating. Farmers were hit by an extremely hot and dry summer, while global energy prices stoked inflation.
Tourism remains a strong earner for France, but the videos of violence on the streets circling the globe in the past two days may deter some travelers.
French businesses are wary of the drift and indecision. Investment has fallen about 1% in the first half of this year amid climbing interest rates.
Above all, there is the debt.
“France carries one of the highest government debt burdens in Europe, and deadlock means we expect its debt level to continue rising,” researchers at Oxford Economics said in July.
France will have to issue a record high of €340 billion in medium- and long-term bonds next year, according to analysts. Its debt as a proportion of gross domestic product (GDP) rose to 119% in the second quarter of this year, double the European Union’s target.
Jittery investors sent the country’s 10-year government bond yield up to 4.9% on Monday.
Its reputation in bond markets is not helped by Mélenchon’s plan to freeze or wipe away the French sovereign bonds held by the Bank of France.
“Political fragmentation may persist well after the 2027 elections, meaning that France’s next government will continue to kick the public-finance can down the road,” said Oxford Economics. This would “prolong the existing climate of high uncertainty, weighing on confidence and domestic demand.”
The man most revered by the French, General Charles de Gaulle, once declared that “France cannot be France without grandeur.” De Gaulle had soaring ambitions for the country’s global role and independence.
But during his long presidency he also told an aide: “I keep the theater going as long as I can and then, after me, have no illusion, things will go back to where they were.”
De Gaulle stepped down a year after the 1968 riots that shook France – events that some commentators are likening to today’s shock.
When he became president, Macron was seen as the antidote to what the French call déclinisme (a word that first appeared in the French Larousse dictionary in 2016.)
“He delivers an extremely positive, constructive message, full of hope for the future. He shows that there is also another France,” wrote one commentator.
A decade later, Macron’s approval rating is hovering at about 15 to 17%, according to multiple polls Déclinisme is still very much on the lips of a citizenry that is demanding more from a beleaguered state that has less.

articles.title: Spain versus Morocco: this is how the military forces of both countries stand in 2026 - Euronews.com
articles.summary: Spain versus Morocco: this is how the military forces of both countries stand in 2026  Euronews.com
articles.full_text:
Spain spends three times more on defence than Morocco and leads in air and naval power, but Rabat has more troops and rockets. US-backed rearmament boosts its strength and narrows the gap.
The Royal Moroccan Air Force's first F-16 Block 72 carried out its maiden flight on 6 October in Greenville, South Carolina, Lockheed Martin has announced. It is now progressing through pre-delivery testing after some delays in the programme. It is the most eye-catching piece of a rearmament drive that is being closely watched in Spain.
But, with the numbers in front of us, how much military weight does Morocco actually have today compared with Spain? Spain is still far ahead in terms of budget and easily dominates at sea. Rabat, by contrast, has more soldiers and rocket artillery, a capability the Spanish Army has lacked for the past 15 years.
Defence spending: more than six to one
The clearest gap is in spending. According to the latest report by Sipri (Stockholm International Peace Research Institute), Spain allocated around 34.287 billion euros to Defence in 2025, 50% more than the previous year, pushing its military burden up to 2.1% of GDP. Morocco came to 5.645 billion euros, up from 4.920 billion in 2024. That increase keeps it as Africa's second-biggest military spender, behind Algeria, which spent 22.660 billion.
Behind that lies the size of each economy. Morocco closed 2025 with a GDP of 138.668 billion euros, according to the World Bank, while the Spanish economy was around 1.69 trillion euros. Twelve times larger.
Does Morocco really spend 10% of its GDP on Defence?
It is one of the figures most often circulated, but it does not fit with Sipri's time series. The institute itself puts Morocco's 2025 military spending at 3.54% of GDP. The 10% looks much more like another indicator: Defence's share of public expenditure, which Sipri calculates at 10.28% for 2025.
Something similar happens with the budget figures. Morocco's 2026 finance law authorised future spending commitments for the National Defence Administration of 157.170 billion dirhams, around 14.7 billion euros, a multi-year line that is often presented as if it were spending in a single year. What will actually be disbursed in 2026 in payment appropriations comes to 55.300 billion dirhams (5.157 billion euros).
Spain, meanwhile, hit 2% of GDP in 2025 and aims to consolidate that in 2026, although it remains the only ally to have refused to sign up to the 5% target for 2035.
Manpower: more troops south of the Strait
Here the balance tips the other way. Several sources converge on Morocco having between 195,000 and 200,000 active-duty personnel and some 150,000 reservists. In addition, unlike Spain, Morocco maintains compulsory military service, reintroduced in 2019. In troop numbers, Morocco's military strength comfortably exceeds Spain's.
This is where the oft-quoted 400,000 figure, which has gone viral in various media, should be treated with caution. The number comes from Global Firepower's profile updated on 21 January 2026, which also credits the African country with some 250,000 reservists, and, as of publication, no other independent record backs it up.
The Spanish Armed Forces have a staffing problem. On 1 January 2025 there were 116,739 military personnel in active service, below the legal minimum of 130,000 set by the Military Career Act, and the year ended with 832 fewer troops. The reserve is even weaker: at the start of 2024 there were 3,091 voluntary reservists.
Aviation: Eurofighter versus F-16 Viper
Spain flies more aircraft, but faces a longer-term question mark. FlightGlobal's World Air Forces 2026 directory credits it with 81 EF-18 Hornets and 67 Eurofighters, with another 45 on order. The first Halcón, a twin-seater, rolled out of the Getafe plant on 1 June, and the second batch will start to be delivered in 2030.
The problem is what comes next. Spain shelved the F-35 in August 2025 in order to buy European, and in June 2026 the FCAS, the fighter it was banking on, fell apart between France and Germany. Paris will now develop its own aircraft on its own.
Morocco is taking a different path. Washington approved in 2019 the sale of 25 F-16 Block 72s for some 3.380 billion euros, plus 23 kits to upgrade the F-16s it already operates.
And the F-35? There are signs of advanced talks, but the deal remains in the realm of the possible and would still need final approval from the US administration and Congress. Specialist media have spoken of 32 aircraft costing around 13.5 billion euros spread over 45 years, including maintenance, but there has been no official confirmation.
In helicopters, Rabat already has 12 of the 24 AH-64E Apaches it ordered and is expecting the rest in phases between 2026 and 2027. Spain will upgrade its 18 Tigers to the MKIII standard. Morocco has also completed delivery of the Israeli Barak MX system, with three batteries and 225 interceptor missiles with a range of up to 70 kilometres, according to Sipri's database.
Ground forces: where Rabat presses hardest
It is on land that Morocco's military strength comes closest to Spain's. Rabat operates the US M1A2 Abrams and, although opacity makes an exact count impossible, some 200 units are estimated to be in service and another 150 on order. Spain fields 220 Leopard 2E tanks and around 50 2A4s, and plans to upgrade them to the 2A8 standard.
The most striking asymmetry is in multiple rocket launchers. Global Firepower credits Morocco with 185 systems and Spain with none; the Army lost that capability when the Teruel system was withdrawn in 2011. Morocco, by contrast, combines Chinese systems with Israel's PULS, already in service, and is awaiting the US HIMARS, of which Washington has approved the sale of 18 launchers.
There is a paradox here. Spain's Silam programme was to be based precisely on PULS, but the contract was cancelled because of the embargo on Israeli military technology imposed by the government; on 30 December 2025 Escribano and Rheinmetall Expal presented the Defence Ministry with a national alternative. In the meantime, the Moroccan Army is already receiving 8x8 WhAP armoured vehicles assembled in the country.
At sea, the gap is vast
The Navy is Spain's big safety cushion. Its backbone consists of five Álvaro de Bazán-class F-100 frigates, whereas Rabat's flagship is a single FREMM frigate. On top of that Spain has the LHD Juan Carlos I, which serves as an aircraft carrier, and two Galicia-class amphibious assault ships.
Under water there is simply no comparison, as submarine capability is one of Morocco's historic shortfalls. The S-81 Isaac Peral has been in service since November 2023, and the S-82 Narciso Monturiol has been undergoing port and sea trials since the summer, with delivery scheduled for the last quarter of the year; it will be the first to be fitted from the outset with air-independent propulsion. On the surface, the F-111 Bonifaz frigate, first in the new series, will join the fleet in 2028.
The Washington factor in Morocco's military strength
What has changed in 2026 is the political backing behind the purchases. Morocco and the United States signed at the Pentagon a military cooperation roadmap for 2026-2036, and by February the Royal Armed Forces had already tested the Link-16 tactical communications system, until now reserved for NATO members.
The US Senate has gone a step further: a clause in its defence bill instructs the Pentagon to deliver within 180 days a ten-year plan to turn Morocco into its most capable military partner in Africa. The United States already accounts for around 60% of Morocco's arms imports.
Rabat also wants to manufacture at home. The government has authorised ten defence industrial projects worth around 231 million euros in investment, and a letter of intent envisages producing in the country a long-range autonomous strike system, the Irifi, with a declared range of around 2,000 kilometres.
Spain has other cards to play. Its defence industry places it among the few countries capable of designing and building its own conventional attack submarines, and it belongs to NATO, although the geographical scope set out in Article 6 of the Washington Treaty does not explicitly include Ceuta and Melilla.
What the rankings don't measure
In the 2026 Global Firepower index, Spain ranks 18th out of 145 and Morocco's military strength appears in 56th place. It is the most frequently cited ranking, but it does not publish an auditable methodology and acknowledges that it relies on the CIA World Factbook and unidentified sources.
The trend, in any case, is upward. Morocco's military strength was ranked 59th in the 2025 edition and 61st in 2024. Nor does the index keep pace with deliveries: it gives Spain zero tanker aircraft, even though the Air Force is taking delivery of its third A330 MRTT this year.
The real friction between the two countries has not, moreover, involved fighters or armoured vehicles. At the end of July, the arrival of migrants in Ceuta led to a mass crossing by sea and over the breakwater at the border, the most serious crisis between the two countries since 2021.
The next figure to be scrutinised in Madrid will arrive soon. Mohammed VI on Saturday chaired in Rabat the Council of Ministers that approved the general guidelines of the 2027 budget, and the Defence allocation will be known once the draft reaches Parliament.

articles.title: Nexfibre and Virgin Media O2’s £2bn Netomnia UK broadband deal in trouble UPDATE2 - ISPreview UK
articles.summary: Nexfibre and Virgin Media O2’s £2bn Netomnia UK broadband deal in trouble UPDATE2  ISPreview UKVirgin Media O2 owners push CMA to reconsider £2bn broadband deal  Financial Timesnexfibre challenges regulator in £2bn Netomnia takeover review  Broadband TV NewsBroadband investors warn blocking takeover would undermine UK’s image  The Timesnexfibre refuses to blink as CMA deadline for remedies passes  Telco Titans
articles.full_text:
Full fibre network operator nexfibre has today issued a joint statement with shareholders InfraVia, Liberty Global (Virgin Media) and Telefónica (O2) to confirm that they do not plan to submit any remedies to the Competition and Markets Authority over their £2bn acquisition of Netomnia (Substantial Group). The move comes after the CMA found significant competition concerns.
Nexfibre, which is being backed by InfraVia Capital and shares some of their parentage with VMO2 (i.e. Liberty Global and Telefónica), had originally argued that the deal would have expanded the coverage of their network to 8m premises by the end of 2027 and unlocked a £3.5bn investment in the UK market – assisting in the upgrade of 2.1 million of Virgin Media’s premises from cable (Hybrid Fibre Coax) to full fibre (FTTP) broadband.
However, critics of the deal, such as CityFibre, which had also been attempting to acquire Netomnia before nexfibre tabled the most attractive offer, stated that there was a lot of overlap between the nexfibre / Virgin Media and Netomnia broadband networks. A recent Point Topic study put the overbuild figure at 832,000 premises when looking at the FTTP side of these networks (here), but there’s much more overbuild with HFC (see below).
The CEO of CityFibre, Simon Holden, previously warned that the proposed agreement would “significantly reduce competition and the choice available to consumers, as well as force hundreds of thousands of Netomnia customers back to VMO2” – potentially raising the prospects of the UK returning to a duopoly between Virgin/nexfibre and Openreach.
The situation started to reach a head in early October 2026, after the CMA published their initial report, which showed that they had not been persuaded by nexfibre’s arguments. Instead the competition regulator rejected some of the operators claims and found that the transaction amounted to a relevant merger situation (RMS), which they said was “expected to result in a substantial lessening of competition (SLC) in the wholesale supply of fixed broadband services.”
The CMA’s report was particularly tough, especially given how the UK Government had previously welcomed the agreement, and left nexfibre with few potential options in terms of viable remedies that could be proposed as a resolution.
Statement from InfraVia, Liberty Global and Telefónica:
“The CMA’s Interim Report is fundamentally flawed. Its conclusions rely on counterfactuals that do not reflect the commercial and financial reality of the UK fibre market. In particular, the assumption that CityFibre will acquire Netomnia is not a credible basis on which to judge this transaction. Nor is the assumption that the billions of pounds of investment enabled by this deal would simply happen anyway.
Since the Interim Report was published, that position has become even harder to sustain. BT’s acquisition of TalkTalk is shrinking the available wholesale market, while CityFibre’s latest accounts and debt restructuring raise further questions about its financial viability. The market has moved on and the CMA’s analysis must move with it.
We engaged in good faith on potential remedies, including commitments on investment and wholesale access. But there is no remedies package that can address the CMA’s current counterfactuals, and on that basis we have not submitted one.
The UK now faces a stark choice: a real, funded plan to unlock £3.5 billion of investment and develop a scaled and sustainable challenger to Openreach, or a fantasy future that will never come.
We remain ready to engage constructively with CMA once the counterfactuals reflect the reality of the market.”
As it stands the CMA has yet to publish their final decision, which is working to a statutory deadline of 15th December 2026, although on the surface nexfibre’s decision today would appear to make it increasingly likely that the deal might be formally blocked by the competition authority. Virgin Media will also need to revise some of their plans for upgrading their old HFC (coax) network to FTTP, part of which had become dependent upon the Netomnia deal.
Such an outcome will have wider impacts across the sector as many altnets had been anticipating that approval would help to open the floodgates to further market consolidation. But now any agreements between larger players will need to pay much closer attention to the negative competitive impacts of network overbuild between parties, so as to avoid the same fate as the above deal.
On the flip side today’s news represents a fresh opportunity for CityFibre to make a renewed offer for Netomnia (something they seem to be preparing), albeit one that may not be as financially attractive to the operator’s owners as their agreement with nexfibre (i.e. a lack of competition in the bidding process gives CityFibre more power). This does at least make it more likely that the market will end up with at least three major providers of broadband infrastructure, as opposed to the longer-term risk of a duopoly returning.
The alternative is that the CMA could, having listened to nexfibre’s strongly held objections to their decision above, still have a change of heart.
UPDATE 4:46pm
Just prior to today’s statement an earlier report had indicated that nexfibre were seeking to reopen the CMA’s assessment by raising questions about CityFibre’s financial position (i.e. questioning the viability of the CMA’s counterfactual to their deal), which is a strategy that has worked before and promptly attracted a response from CityFibre.
A spokesperson for CityFibre said:
“The CMA has already examined CityFibre in detail and is well aware of our financial position, our intentions to recapitalise and of the new £900m contribution from our shareholders. All that evidence is already reflected in the CMA’s Interim Report.
Over recent years, CityFibre has invested some £7bn in the UK fibre market and the company expects to invest a further £5bn by 2040. This is on the basis of a clear and consistent regulatory policy, and a robust and independent competition regime.”
CityFibre does have a valid point here, but at the same time nexfibre’s strategy also puts more pressure on them to reach a final agreement on shoring up their finances, ideally sooner rather than later. Failing to do this in a timely fashion now could lend at least some credit to nexfibre’s argument.
The CMA has today effectively already issued an invitation to comment on the possibility of blocking the proposed transaction, partly on the basis of no remedies being offered, which is only open to responses for a week.
UPDATE 21st Oct 2026 @ 8:25am
Just to give a bit of extra context to nexfibre’s strategy above, which wasn’t initially made clear enough. The operator appears to be attempting to follow the same approach as the recent ABF/Hovis merger. The parties involved in that case challenged the counterfactual featured in the Interim Report, prompting a second version to be created and published, which ultimately found in favour of the merger.
As above, this is nexfibre trying to show that CityFibre’s financial situation has changed and that they may struggle to mount a serious bid for Netomnia (a justified aspect to test), which the operator has already responded to above. This is why we’ve suggested yesterday that it will now be much more important for CityFibre to get their underlying finances in order as quickly as possible.
The difficulty here is that the ABF/Hovis merger is not a perfect mirror for the nexfibre/Netomnia case. The two progressed somewhat differently through Phase 2 and for Hovis and ABF, the CMA ruled that the competitive pressure from ABF’s Allied Bakeries would disappear with or without the merger because the business was fundamentally unsustainable.
The situation isn’t quite as clear cut for nexfibre/Netomnia, where the CMA views that the acquisition would harm wholesale broadband competition by removing a critical independent. Granted this does place a lot of focus on CityFibre being the only counterfactual option considered, but Netomnia may also have other prospects for M&A outside of that.
We’re still of the view that nexfibre may be fighting up a hill that’s now already too steep, but then we live in strange times and only recently we didn’t think it was likely that BT would end up taking over TalkTalk either. Today’s market isn’t always predictable.

articles.title: Germany's Agile to make up to 2,000 humanoid robots with Nvidia, CEO says - electronics.economictimes.indiatimes.com
articles.summary: Germany's Agile to make up to 2,000 humanoid robots with Nvidia, CEO says  electronics.economictimes.indiatimes.com
articles.full_text:
AMSTERDAM: Germany's Agile Robots plans to produce up to 2,000 petite humanoid robots next year under a partnership with Nvidia announced on Wednesday targeting universities and corporate research labs, CEO Zhaopeng Chen said in an interview.
Production of Agile ONE S and ONE SN models will begin by the end of this year, Chen said, adding that the company expects to produce 1,000-2,000, with Stanford University and ETH Zurich among potential customers.
At 1.4 meters tall and weighing about 34 kilograms, the robots are smaller versions of Agile's full-sized humanoid models, making them easier and safer for researchers to handle.
The partnership combines Nvidia computing and "GR00T" AI model with Agile's hardware to give researchers a ready-to-use system for gathering data and testing skills intended for later use in factories and warehouses.
Spencer Huang, product director for robotics at Nvidia, said having bots with the standardized pre-configuration could save researchers two or three months spent getting separately purchased components working together.
"If we can bring researchers something that's already 80% of the way there, it accelerates their development," he said.
